p.emphasis: Cape Erimo, July of the twenty-eighth.

section.subtitle: Prologue
section.p: Cape Erimo held the wind the way one holds a taut string. It did not tear the string and did not let go. For three days running, twenty-three meters per second from the southwest stood over the cape, and the fishing pier beyond the village, built in the sixty-third and set on stone piles in the seventy-first, held that wind the way it had always held it—shoulder-on.

Kurosawa came alone, by car, in a black coat below mid-thigh, in leather shoes with soles resoled twice. He left the car at the parking lot by the lighthouse and walked down to the pier. Two terns shifted on the path and did not fear him.

Nine columns stood in a row beneath the lower edge of the pier, on the seaward side, sunk into the concrete of the lower platform. Thick cedar piles, cut off level at a man's height, black from damp below and gray above, with bronze brackets that had once held lanterns and now held only the memory of them. The lanterns were taken down in the two-thousandth, when Erimo-Misaki was moved to autonomous power.
He counted the columns from the shore.
At the eighth he stopped.

A bronze lantern bracket, with a ring at the top and an angled clip below, was held on four bolts—two of them rusted red, two new, of the kind sold in Otaru at the shop on Denuki Boulevard, four or five years old, no more. Kurosawa saw this from thirty meters. Coming up, he laid his palm on the inner face of the pile—where the bronze clip entered the wood—and the clip gave.
Behind it was a niche.

He did not examine it for long. Twenty centimeters deep, cut into the body of the column, lined with one sheet of heavy gray paper, the same paper sold in Otaru at the stationery shop on Denuki. Inside the niche—two things.
One—a small child's collarbone. The right one. With a thin crack through its very center, old, calcified—ten years ago, or maybe fifty. Kurosawa was not a forensic examiner. Endo would have been.
The other—one sheet of paper, folded in four, inscribed in black pen.

He stood over the niche for a long time. The wind took him from the seaward side, tugged at the skirts of his coat, did not catch in his hair because his hair was short. The two terns came back and settled on the far column—the ninth, the empty one.

He put the collarbone back. Lowered it deeper into the niche, closer to the back wall, the way one lays a bone in a coffin that is not to be taken out. The bronze clip—back into place, pressed with his palm until it clicked.
The sheet he kept.

He did not unfold it. He folded it once more, from four to eight, and put it into the inside pocket of his coat—the same pocket that held the yellow slip from the department about the new duty roster. Two things side by side, in a coat.
The road to the last room began here.

title.p: The Department. August of the Twenty-Eighth

p.emphasis: The new chief wanted the case closed. Kurosawa said neither yes nor no.

section.subtitle: Chapter One
section.p: The Hokkaido Prefectural Police Headquarters stood on the same corner it had stood on thirty and ten years ago. In August it held the same faintly stifling warmth that September did not always manage—ceilings high, windows narrow, the air conditioners loud but holding the damp.
Kurosawa entered at eight forty-seven.

The guard behind the partition was new. Not Mori. Mori had been transferred to Hakodate in February. The new one—Kobayashi, thirty-two—straightened at the desk when he saw a lieutenant's rank on the coat, and made a formal bow of fifteen degrees. Kurosawa nodded. He committed the new guard's name to memory the way one writes down in a notebook things that will be needed in five days.

The elevator smelled of wet cloth from somebody's jacket. On the wall inside—a new poster, white on black, with a red band at the bottom: "Internal Investigation into the Shichijō Tractor Incident: Conclusions on August 25." Kurosawa looked at the date longer than he meant to. Eleven days remained until the twenty-fifth.
The elevator chimed on the fourth.

The Missing Persons unit held the same stifling warmth as last winter, and the winter before, and two weeks ago, when he had opened this room for the last time before his leave over the death of Ogawa. Three desks in one room. A glass partition in the right corner—only now Ogawa did not sit behind it. Behind it sat a man in a gray suit, in a white shirt with the top button undone and no jacket—the jacket hung on a peg by the window—and he did not raise his eyes when Kurosawa came into the unit.
Sasaki, at the middle desk, did raise them.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Sasaki-junsa-buchō."

She stood. Not at once—a half-second late, the way people stand who are weighing whether it will be unnecessary. Then she stood anyway. A short bow, five degrees. Kurosawa returned it in the same measure.
"Good that you are back," she said.
"Good that you are here."

He hung his coat on a peg. The scarf he tucked into a side pocket; this scarf was not the one whose wool had held fine cuts in winter—this one was light, summer, cotton, dark gray. He set the thermos on the desk. Second coffee of the morning. He drank standing.
The calendar on the wall was crooked on one pin—a new one, August—with a photograph of the Teshio River. Teshio did not please him. He preferred the January bridge.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
The voice from behind the glass partition. Quiet. Tokyo standard, no admixture.
He turned.
Tanaka Ryosuke was already at the door of his office—the same door where a year and a half ago Ogawa used to lift his chin and say "sit down." Tanaka's right hand rested on the handle.
"You have a minute."
"Yes."
"Come in."
The office was the same and not the same.

The bottle of water on the lower shelf behind the desk—was not there. The desk—without the two stacks of folders Ogawa always kept on the left and right of himself—now held one stack in the center, level, with a single soft red plastic tab on the top folder. The visitor's chair—the same wooden one with black cloth—remained. The ashtray on the sill—taken away. Tanaka did not smoke.
Kurosawa came in, closed the door behind him. He did not sit.
"Sit down, Kurosawa-keibuho."
He sat.

Tanaka did not sit for another ten seconds. He stood by the window, hands behind his back, back to Kurosawa. Beyond the window—the portico, beyond the portico—the intersection. A truck went by below. On the wall behind Tanaka—the same framed certificate that had hung in Ogawa's office: "For thirty years of unblemished service, Kurosawa Yukio, 2020." Tanaka had not taken it down. That held Kurosawa for a second. Ogawa had kept that certificate right above Kurosawa's own head, the way one keeps an old nail from which one can hang a coat. Tanaka had left it there the way one leaves in a room the things of the previous occupant, until the tidying is done.

"I assume the functions of head of this unit from the twenty-sixth of June," Tanaka said to the window. "Ogawa-san died on the second. The interim rotation lasted three weeks. From the first of August I am here permanently. You know this."
"Yes."
"You were on leave for six weeks. By permission of the deputy prefectural chief. You know this too."
"Yes."
Tanaka turned. Walked to the desk. Sat straight, the way people sit who have long trained themselves to sit straight.
"I wanted to see you before you opened the first file. That is why I asked Sasaki-junsa-buchō to inform me when you entered the fourth floor."
Kurosawa did not show that he knew this.
Tanaka set his palms on either side of the top folder on the desk. He did not open it.
"Kurosawa-keibuho. Did you rest well?"
"Yes."
"That is good."
A pause.
"I will not summarize for you what I read in the folder. You wrote it. I want you to hear me on one short sentence."
Kurosawa was looking at the top folder.
"I am listening."
"The Doll Maker case is closed."
Silence. One second. Two.
Kurosawa did not move.

"The primary subject—by our data—is dead," Tanaka said evenly. "The network—uncovered. Families—waiting. There is no open line that would, in the understanding of the NPA and the Ministry, keep this case alive."
He paused.
"I know that you do not agree with this."
Kurosawa did not move.
"I know that you went to Cape Erimo in July. Alone. Without clearance. On leave."
Kurosawa did not move.
"That is your right as a man on leave. But in my part of things I take it into account. Kurosawa-keibuho, I have no grounds to carry that trip further. I did not see it."
A pause.

"I only want you to understand: if by the end of this week a line appears on your desk that points to the Doll Maker alive—that is, if you initiate operational action that takes us beyond the closed case—you do that under your own responsibility. Without internal backing. And without Ogawa—" Tanaka allowed himself a short, barely audible breath, "—under the phrase Ogawa-san would have covered this from behind my shoulder."
He put his palm on the top folder.
"I am not Ogawa."
"I know."
"You will say that you need to know something else."
Kurosawa was silent.
Tanaka looked at him for ten seconds. Then leaned back in his chair. Took the folder, opened to the second page.

"I have two inquiries on my desk this week from district stations. Ito Kazuo-san's wife wrote a note of thanks—the body was found in April, the case is closed. Nakamura Aoi-san's mother sent a letter about the return of personal effects—I will pass it through Sasaki-junsa-buchō. That is what you close. That is what I want on my desk by Friday. That is your current work. You hear me."
"Yes."
"Go."
Kurosawa stood.
At the threshold—he turned.
"Tanaka-san."
"Yes."
"Thank you."
Tanaka did not lift his eyes.
"Go, Kurosawa-keibuho."

Outside the office Sasaki sat at her desk and did not look in his direction. Her fingers on the keyboard moved evenly. Kurosawa walked to his desk. Sat. His coat remained on the peg. Thermos on the desk. Coffee still warm.
He laid his palm on the right inside pocket of the coat—then he reached through the shoulder, drew out the sheet. Folded in four. Then in eight. Then in sixteen. He did not unfold it.
He only held it in his palm.

The sheet had lived on him for six weeks. Two weeks in the coat. Four—in the bottom drawer of the chest in Maruyama, beneath a shirt Kurosawa had not worn since January. He knew the sheet was there and therefore did not open that drawer—not because he did not want to see the sheet, but because he knew that if he opened it he would not close it the same evening. On Friday last he had, in the end, opened the drawer: he tucked the sheet into the inside pocket of his coat, put the coat into the wardrobe. The coat had hung in the wardrobe until this morning.
Then he put it into the top drawer of his desk, under a thin folder with two reports Tanaka wanted by Friday. He did not lock it. He pushed the drawer shut.
He lifted his eyes.
Sasaki at the keyboard was still for one second.
"Sasaki-junsa-buchō."
"Yes."
"In five minutes—at my desk. With the folder on Nakamura-san."
"Return the mother's effects to that address?"
"Yes. And write down Yamada-san's number in Niigata. We'll have a conversation with her on Tuesday."
"Yamada-san?"
"Ayano-san. My brother's daughter."
Sasaki nodded.

She did not ask, the way she had asked five months ago, in January, when he had said something for the first time. She simply opened her notebook, wrote down the number he dictated from memory, and closed the notebook.

Kurosawa did not look at her as he spoke. He looked at the calendar with the Teshio River, and thought that the Teshio flowed north, toward Otaru, only from the other side of the peninsula—and that the town where his case with his father had begun in two thousand and five lay not on a river but in a bay, on the seaward side, where Pier Two was.
Then he opened the drawer and looked into it once. The sheet lay as he had left it.
He closed the drawer.
The coffee in the thermos had gone cold.

p.emphasis: She knew he had gone alone. She did not ask why. She asked what.

section.subtitle: Chapter Two
section.p: At six forty Sasaki came into the unit with two paper cups in her hands.

Coffee from the machine on the ground floor. Not from the canteen: canteen coffee came with powdered milk, and Kurosawa did not drink it. From the machine in the lobby—one button, black, no sugar, hot. One cup with a red lid, the other with a red lid too, with a small mark from her nail near the rim. The mark was Sasaki's, so she would know which was hers.
Kurosawa came in at six forty-seven. He hung the coat. He did not take out the thermos.
Sasaki set one cup on his desk. She said nothing. She walked to her own. Sat. Opened her notebook. Did not start writing.
He looked at the cup for five seconds. Then sat. Took it. Pulled the lid off with two fingers by the rim. Drank a little.
"Thank you, Sasaki-junsa-buchō."
"You're welcome."
Tanaka was not in his office. Tanaka came in at eight sharp. That was his rhythm.

Kurosawa set the cup down beside the thermos. He had not brought the thermos today—he had forgotten, and that surprised him a little, the way a thing surprises a person when they have kept it in the kitchen for nine months in a row and have not set it down.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"You went to Cape Erimo," Sasaki said evenly. "In July. The ninth. Or the tenth."
Kurosawa returned the cup to the ring of damp it had left.
"The eleventh."
"The eleventh," she repeated. "July eleventh."
"Yes."
She did not look at him. She looked at the notebook. She held the pencil the way one holds a cup—by the top, carefully.
"You did not tell me you would go."
"No."
"You did not tell Ogawa either."
"Ogawa was already gone."
"I know."
A pause. Under the baseboard a thin current of cool air from the concrete slab held, as always. Through the air conditioner the rustle of turning blades could be heard.
"Kurosawa-keibuho." She lifted her eyes. "Tell me what you found."
He was silent for about five seconds.
Then he pushed the thermos aside, drew a key from the lower pocket of his trousers—small, brass—set it into the lock of the top drawer of his desk. Turned. Opened.
Took out the sheet.

Folded in four. Not unfolded for five weeks. The paper lay flat, unyellowed—heavy gray, the same paper sold at the stationery shop on Denuki in Otaru. Kurosawa looked at this paper and knew where it was from and did not want to say it aloud.
He stood. Walked to Sasaki's desk. Set the sheet down in the middle, on her open notebook. Did not unfold it.
"One time."
She nodded. Set the pencil aside.
Took the sheet between two fingers. Unfolded to eight. Then—to four. Then—to two.
One sheet of B5 format, folded in four. One word, written in black pen, in the center.

Not Ogawa's hand. Not Toshi's. Not the earlier clipping—that had been red felt-tip, a ring around the face. This—black pen, a dry hand, a Japanese upright register. The same register as the five words on the envelope at Sato's, that long-ago morning in the izakaya.
Sasaki looked at the sheet for eight seconds.
Then she lifted her eyes.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"So he is alive."
"Yes."
"So we continue."
Kurosawa said nothing. Not yes, not no. He looked past her—at the calendar with the Teshio River—and nodded once. A small nod, the kind one gives when a word is not needed.
Sasaki folded the sheet back. Into four. Then into eight. Not into sixteen—there was no need. She held it out to him.
"Take it."
He took it. Put it back into the top drawer. Closed it. Did not lock.
"Does Tanaka know?"
"No."
"Tanaka knows that you went."
"He knows."
"But not about this."
"No."
She folded her hands on the notebook.
"Kurosawa-keibuho. You understand that if we open this line without Tanaka's knowledge, Tanaka will close it on us at the first operational request."
"I understand."
"You understand that if we open it with Tanaka, he will close it before the first data."
"I understand."
"You understand that between those two options is a narrow corridor."
"I understand."
"Kurosawa-keibuho. You have already chosen."
"Yes."
"Say which."
He looked at her. Not at once.
"We go the corridor," he said quietly. "Three weeks. Then I tell Tanaka in person, when there is data."
"Three weeks," Sasaki repeated.
"Yes."
"Who else?"
"Kenji."
"Yamada-san."
"Yes."
"He is in Sapporo?"
"Yes. I called him yesterday evening from a private phone. He knows he is coming to our unit today at nine. He knows Tanaka does not know about it."
"He is with us."
"He is with us."
She nodded. Took the pencil. Wrote three things in the notebook. Kurosawa did not see what—she held the notebook at a slant.
Then she raised her eyes.
"Kurosawa-keibuho. I want to tell you one thing."
"Tell me."
"In July I knew you were going to Erimo. I did not ask before you went, because I knew you would say no and go anyway. I decided that of the two—better that I let you go than that I made you lie."
He was silent.

"But when you did not come back by morning," she said evenly, "I drove to your house in Maruyama. At six. I stood in the courtyard under the lamp for four minutes. Then I rang your mailbox—there was an advertising flyer in it about a new candy store in the metro—and I took it out and put it back. Then I went home. You came back in the evening at nine. I knew you had come back, because in your apartment on the third floor the light came on in the kitchen window."

Kurosawa did not ask how she knew which was the kitchen window. He knew how. Last winter they had come back together from a scene on Kita-24, and Sasaki had driven him home, and had waited in the car until he went up, and the light in the kitchen window came on. She saw it. She looked at it steadily until he drew the curtain aside.
Now he set his palm on the ring of damp from the cup.
"Thank you, Sasaki-junsa-buchō."
"You're welcome."
"I should not have left you alone."
"No. You should not have."
"It will not happen again."
"I know."

He looked at her notebook. Sasaki's notebook cover was new—light brown, with a thin white sticker in the lower right corner on which she wrote in pencil "From" and the date. In the corner stood: "From 12 July 2028." That meant she had closed the previous notebook the day after his trip to Erimo. Kurosawa did not ask how many pages of the previous notebook she had filled that day. He knew how Sasaki wrote—in an even line of seven or eight signs, with side notations—and he knew that something in the previous notebook was there that he should not go back to.
"Sasaki-junsa-buchō."
"Yes."
"You started a new notebook from the twelfth of July."
"Yes."
"That is a choice."
"Yes."
"I am not asking about the previous one."
"I know."

She turned the page of the notebook to a clean one, with a short motion of her left hand—the way one turns a page in a book from which one is not going to read aloud. Then she set the pencil down beside it, level with the fold.
She was not looking at him. She looked at the notebook. But the corner of her mouth for a moment went inward—not a smile, only what goes in place of a smile in people who do not smile at work.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"Kenji-san is coming at nine. We have an hour and twelve minutes."
"Yes."
"Will you tell me in that time what you saw in the niche of the eighth column?"
Kurosawa looked at his closed desk. At the top drawer. At the key in the side pocket of his trousers.
He did not look into the desk.
"One collarbone. The right one. A child's. A thin crack through the center—old. The collarbone I put back. The sheet I took."
"A child's."
"Yes."
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"A child's collarbone—that is a new line. Not from the network. From something deeper."
"Yes."
Sasaki nodded. Wrote one phrase in the notebook. Closed the notebook.
A pause. One second, two.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"You will tell me one thing I did not ask, and will not ask."
"I will tell you."
"The collarbone—from a child. In eight of nine columns on the pier. You put it back."
"Yes."
"That is a choice."
He was silent.
"You could have taken it. You saw a child's collarbone. You knew that to some parent that collarbone would weigh more than one sheet of paper. You left it."
"I did not want him to know I had taken it."
"He will know anyway. You left it not for him."
Kurosawa looked at the bottom of the cup. There was a small crystal of sugar at the bottom that the machine had mistakenly poured in. He had not eaten it.

"I left it," he said quietly, "because on the eighth column of nine it had to be. That is his drawing. If I take one collarbone out of the drawing, I change the drawing. I am not ready to change it. Not today."
"So you see his drawing whole."
"Not whole. But I see it."
Sasaki nodded. She did not write this in the notebook.
"Let Kenji-san come ten minutes late. I will go down for ten minutes to the machine and bring you another coffee. You will drink it before he comes in. And then I will come in again."
"All right."

She stood. She took Kurosawa's empty cup—the one with the red lid and no nail mark, that is, his—and threw it into the bin under the desk. This morning, at six, when she had stood for five minutes in front of the machine, she had chosen the way she always chose.
One button.
She went out toward the elevator.
Kurosawa sat at the desk. One hand he kept on the ring of damp. The other—on the pocket of his trousers, where the key to the top drawer lay.
He did not move until she came back.

title.p: Kenji. The Radio and Forty-Seven Names

p.emphasis: Kenji asked for a month. Kurosawa gave him three weeks.

section.subtitle: Chapter Three
section.p: Yamada Kenji came in at nine oh nine.

He always arrived with a surplus of nine minutes or nine seconds—Kurosawa had noticed this once but had not asked why. In Kenji's left hand was a black nylon backpack, in his right—a wet umbrella. He set the umbrella in the stand by the door of the unit, the backpack on the floor beside Sasaki's desk, took off his jacket—the thin gray windbreaker layer he wore from April through October with the same repair seam on the shoulder—and hung it on the peg.
"Kurosawa-san. Sasaki-junsa-buchō."
"Kenji-san."
"Yamada-san."

Not "Yamada-keibu," not "Yamada-junsa-buchō." "Yamada-san." Kenji had been a civilian consultant on digital traces two years ago and now, after Ashibetsu, was a sergeant of the operational group attached personally to Kurosawa. But there was no sergeant's suffix between them. Between them it was "san."
Kenji did not sit at once. He stood straight, backpack at his feet.
"Tanaka in?"
"Not yet. Comes in at eight—" Sasaki glanced at the wall clock, "—that is, already."
"Then quickly."

He opened the backpack. Took out a black external hard drive, a USB cable, a thin brown spiral notebook, and one paper folder. He put it all on Kurosawa's desk, pushing the thermos and the cup aside with the motion of a man who does not ask permission when he is in a hurry.

"Two lines," he said. "Radio and the Yoshidas. Radio I began on the sixth of July, when Kurosawa-san was still on leave. Yoshidas—on the twentieth. Both unfinished. But something can already be seen."

Kurosawa pulled up a chair. Sasaki brought her own—from behind her desk—and set it on his right. All three sat around his desk the way they had sat long ago, when Ogawa was not watching through the glass behind and no one was sitting behind the glass partition. Only now behind the glass partition someone was sitting, and all three remembered that.
Kenji spoke quietly.

"Radio. Between the twenty-seventh of May and the eighth of July, three signals were logged on the shortwave over Hokkaido, not from our repeaters. Not from JMH-2, not from the Sapporo-Wakkanai relay. Not on the fishing bands. One tone—short, eight point two hertz above the standard CB frequency—then three seconds of silence, then the tone again. Each session lasts from ninety seconds to two minutes."
"Timestamp?"
"May twenty-seventh at twenty-three nineteen. June fifteenth at twenty-three twenty. July eighth at twenty-three eighteen."
"Same time."
"Twenty-three nineteen, plus or minus a minute. Yes."
Kenji plugged the external drive into a laptop he took from the backpack. He opened the laptop on his far side of the desk. Kurosawa and Sasaki turned to see the screen.

On the screen—a map of Hokkaido. Three points. All three—in southern Hidaka, in the triangle of Shizunai, Erimo, Urahoro. The westernmost—near Cape Erimo, in the mountains above Genshō-an—but Kenji did not know that name.

"Triangulation from three JARL stations. Error—plus or minus a kilometer or three-five. But in Hidaka the mountains, so in reality—three-seven. The westernmost point falls on the massif above the Genshō valley. That is monastic territory, no road in, only on foot from the Midori-tsuka side."
Kurosawa was looking at the screen.
"Why one hour?"

"I don't know. The same time—that is either a ritual, or a protocol, or the habit of a person who does not want to fall into a new habit. Nobody runs a business broadcast at twenty-three nineteen. That is not professional work. That is a person who wants someone else to know she is there."
"Who is listening."
Kenji raised his eyes.

"Don't know. I checked three stations that could have been listening at that hour in Hokkaido and that log. None of them received these signals. That does not mean no one is listening. It means whoever is listening is not in my registry."
"Could be Niigata."

"Could be. But in Niigata the air is dead at that hour. In Tokyo too. In Kansai—the same. This is not two-way, Kurosawa-san. This is one man speaking into the empty and hoping that a particular person, at that minute, is sitting at a receiver."
"Or he is the receiver. And the transmitter—is another."
Kenji nodded.
"That I did not check. I only checked Hokkaido on transmission. Reception—a new line."

Sasaki wrote something down. Kurosawa looked at the westernmost point. Genshō. He knew that name—from the abbot of Reisen-ji's report—only as the name of an old monk in Sōunkyō. Now a point on a map. The mountains above Erimo.
"Kenji-san."
"Yes."
"You said two lines."
"The second—names."
Kenji closed the map. Opened a spreadsheet. Excel, three columns, four hundred and twenty-one rows.

"Yoshida," he said. "That is the most common surname on Hokkaido. In the driver's registry—thirty-two thousand. In the voter registry—forty-seven thousand and ninety. I took the voters, narrowed by age—fifty-five to seventy on the ninth of July twenty-eight. I narrowed by region—Hokkaido as registered address for no less than ten years. I got four hundred and twenty-one individuals."
He scrolled down. Kurosawa looked at the list. The characters 吉田 repeated evenly, row after row.

"Then I narrowed by one feature that was not in Tanaka's." Kenji revealed a fourth column that had been hidden until now. He opened it. "Men only. The Doll Maker—a male voice in the audio recording Ogawa left in the safe two days before his death. Audio—Toshi fragment, three seconds, from Ashibetsu-yama, from the dictaphone. Endo confirmed it. So—men. I got one hundred and ninety-eight."
"Next."

"Then I excluded those registered permanently in cities over a hundred thousand. Sapporo, Hakodate, Asahikawa, Kushiro—excluded. Our profile is not urban. The Doll Maker is in Hidaka, in the mountains, from a monastery or from beneath a monastery. I got eighty-three."
"Next."

"Then I excluded those who over the last five years had gone for an annual medical checkup at a city clinic." Kenji looked at Sasaki. "That matters. The Doll Maker, if he is in a monastery, will not go for a checkup in Sapporo. That excludes people with a settled medical history. I got sixty-two."
"Next."

"Then I excluded those who pay property tax at a fixed address in city districts for more than twenty years. That is, those who lived somewhere in a city in a settled way and put down roots. The Doll Maker changed addresses at least twice in the last ten years. I got forty-seven."
He opened a new tab. Showed the list.
Forty-seven rows. First column—surname and given name. Second—year of birth. Third—last known address.
"These," Kenji said evenly, "are forty-seven people on Hokkaido who at the second level of check still fit the profile. None confirmed. This is a candidate list. It has to be narrowed to one."
"How long."
Kenji pressed his lips together. Looked at the list.

"A month. Manual work. The pension registries—those are paper archives in Sapporo and Otaru, not fully digitized for Hokkaido. I have access, but I have to travel. I have to read career sheets. I have to cross-check with the registries of children's homes, schools, teachers' unions. I have to cross-check with an updated photograph—and photographs in the pension records there are none, we have only the paper sheet with name, date, addresses. I have to find someone who can describe the appearance. A month—realistic."
"A month we do not have," said Kurosawa.
"I know."
"We have three weeks."
Kenji did not answer at once. He looked at the list. Then raised his eyes.
"Three weeks I will not hold up, Kurosawa-san."
"You will."
"I need to sleep."
"You will sleep here."
Kenji smiled. It was not a smile of joy. It was the smile of a man who understands he will not argue further.
"Three weeks."
"Yes."
"Kurosawa-san. One thing."
"Yes."

"The pension records in Otaru—I have another source. Not official. I have an acquaintance in the archive there—Suzuki, from the Otaru municipal library—he can give me photocopies of the field surveys the municipality does not digitize. On Friday, when he is alone on shift. That is forty-seven rows down to twelve in two days. I will give you the list in ten days, not three weeks."
"Take that line."
"I'll take it. Only one thing."
"What."

"Suzuki—five years ago he lost a child. Since then he is in such a state that he does not like anyone asking him about the archive of wards. He will see me only if I do not mention orphanages. I approach him on a neutral turn—pensions by appointment. He will give it to me. But I cannot ask about Jindai-en, or about Mori, or about anyone's room."
"Ask about pensions."
"I ask."
Sasaki closed the notebook. Then opened it. Wrote "Suzuki" in pencil.
"Then I take two helpers from the Sapporo district. One—Tanabe. The other, younger—Hara, out of the internship. Silent. Not from our unit."
"Take them."
"Will Tanaka give them?"
"Do not ask Tanaka. Say it is carrying out his order on closing the case. He will not object."
"All right."
Sasaki, who had been silent for the last six minutes, now spoke.
"Kenji-san."
"Yes."
"One row is bothering me."
Kenji looked at her finger on the screen. Row nineteen from the top, third column.

"Yoshida Hiro. Year of birth—nineteen sixty-two. Last known address—Otaru, Temiya district, with the note released from post for reasons of health, twenty-sixth of March, twenty-seventh. Post not specified—column empty. In our forty-six others the post is specified. Here—no."
Kenji nodded, as if he had been waiting for that mark.
"That bothered me too," he said. "I stopped on that row. But in the source—the Otaru registry—there is also a gap. I put another tick."
He set one small red mark in the far right column beside row nineteen. Kurosawa saw it, but did not speak.
Sasaki looked at the screen. Then at Kenji. Then at Kurosawa.
"Three weeks."
"Three weeks," Kurosawa repeated.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"In that time you will tell me why you went to Cape Erimo on the eleventh of July, and not the tenth or the twelfth."
He was silent.
"You will tell me either now or before we go to Tanaka in twenty days."
"Before Tanaka."
"All right."
Kurosawa nodded. Kenji closed the spreadsheet. Unplugged the drive. Folded the laptop. Put everything into the backpack.
He stood beside the desk with the backpack in his hand.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"One thing I will tell you now because I will forget later."
"Tell me."
Kenji looked at the list of Yoshidas, which was now closed on the monitor but still open evenly in his memory to all forty-seven rows.

"In two thousand and eight I was in Otaru for two weeks at a summer OSINT circle. I don't remember who my instructor was. One of them cried at the farewell. A grown man. One word stuck in me—sensei—in the tone of an older ward who then went into crime. I don't remember the word exactly. But looking at the list—at row nineteen—I thought it might be him."
"Yoshida Hiro."
"I don't know. I could be wrong. I tell you this not as a fact. I tell you this as a shadow."
Kurosawa looked at him.
"A shadow is already something."
"Yes. A shadow is already something, but not evidence."
"I know."
Kenji nodded. Took the backpack. Walked to the door. On the threshold—he turned.
"Do not tell Tanaka I was here."
"He is coming in ten minutes."
"Then tell him I came for the copies on Nakamura-san."
"I will."
Kenji went out.
Sasaki closed the notebook. Not at once.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"We are now not looking for one man. We are looking for one man among forty-seven."
"Yes."
"With a shadow on the nineteenth."
Kurosawa looked at the monitor that Kenji had closed. Then at the top drawer of his desk, in which lay a sheet with one word in black pen.
"With a shadow on the nineteenth."
He did not open the drawer.

p.emphasis: One of them he knew by name. The other he knew by family record. One of them sent the parcel.

section.subtitle: Chapter Four
section.p: The parcel came at ten forty-two.

The courier—Yamato, in a black vest with a yellow stripe—brought a box seventeen by twelve by ten centimeters, wrapped in plain brown kraft paper without pattern, tied crosswise with two lengths of twine. The address on the top face—by hand, black pen, Japanese calligraphic characters: "Hokkaido Prefectural Police Headquarters, Missing Persons unit, Kurosawa-keibuho, personal."
Stamp—Memuro, Tokachi, ninth of August. Memuro—a small town a hundred and forty kilometers east of Sapporo, in the foothills of Hidaka.
Sender—not specified. In the 送り主 field stood only two characters, inscribed in a thin black pen:
綾乃.

The secretary from the ground floor brought the box up to the unit in white gloves, the way parcels with undetermined senders had been brought since the twenty-sixth, by Tanaka's order. Tanaka was in his office, closed off, with the phone. The secretary set the box on Sasaki's desk, bowed, went out.
Sasaki did not touch the box for a minute. She looked at the upper face.
Kurosawa came over. Stood beside her. Said nothing.
"Kurosawa-keibuho," Sasaki said quietly. "Ayano."
"Yes."
"This is that Ayano."
"No."
She raised her eyes.
"Not from Niigata?"
"I don't know."
"Not from Jindai-en?"
"I don't know."

On that "I don't know" he held his palm to the corner of her desk, where the corner was worn to a slightly darker shade from where Sasaki had set her notebook on it a hundred and eighty times a year. He knew about that, and Sasaki knew he knew.
"Sasaki-junsa-buchō. We have two Ayanos."
She was silent. Then nodded—briefly, the way a person nods who knows more than she wants to and does not want to admit it aloud.
"That is."

"That is, one—Ayano the nurse. Clinic in Niigata. I saw her in interrogation last November. She told us nothing then. She was dismissed for family reasons two weeks later. Then hired back. No one raised the question. The prosecutor recorded nothing."
"And the other?"

"The other—my brother's daughter. Kurosawa Ayano. Born in Otaru, in two thousand and eight. Raised by her father until two thousand and twenty-two. After her father's disappearance—by her widowed mother, that is, by her mother's parents. Her mother had left the family earlier. Ayano—a ward of her grandmother and grandfather in Niigata, now she is twenty. She is in her second year of the master's program at Niigata University, art history faculty. Interning in Sapporo this summer. Lives in a dormitory near Hokkaido Daigaku."
Sasaki placed her palm beside the box. Did not touch. Just laid it there.
"Kurosawa-keibuho. Twenty minutes ago you said tomorrow—Yamada-san from Niigata."
"Yes."
"Then you were speaking of Ayano-the-niece. Not of Ayano-the-nurse."
"Yes."
"And the box—is from Ayano-the-nurse. Or."
"Or."
A pause of ten seconds.
"Or from Kurosawa Ayano."
"I cannot rule it out."
"Your niece could not have done this."
"Could not. But I cannot rule it out."

Sasaki nodded. She took gloves from Kurosawa's side drawer—latex, white, for contact with things not yet passed to forensics. She put them on. Then she put on a paper handkerchief—thin, folded once—covered the upper edge of Kurosawa's box, undid the twine. Not tore—untied. Kurosawa watched.
Inside the box—a thin layer of cotton wool. And one figure.

Small, eight centimeters tall. Porcelain. A child's—with arms spread to the sides, in a kimono with a lilac pattern. The head—the shape of a ball. There was no face. Smooth bone color, like ichimatsu dolls without paint. No brows. No eyes. No mouth.
Such was the doll from the shelf above the altar in Kamishiroi. Such was the doll from Hachirodate. Such was the doll from Sato's.
Now—such.
Sasaki did not touch it with her fingers. She only tilted the box.
Under the figure, on the second layer of cotton—one sheet.
B7 format. The same heavy gray paper from the stationery shop on Denuki in Otaru. Black pen. One word.
綾乃.
And one line beneath it:
Silence.
Kurosawa looked at the sheet for nine seconds.
"Not Ayano-the-nurse," he said quietly. "The nurse wrote in Latin script. This is not her hand."
"So."
"Either Ayano-the-niece, or the one who writes under her name."
"The Doll Maker."
"Yes."
He stepped back from Sasaki's desk half a pace. Looked at the calendar with the Teshio River. Not through the calendar—past it.

Ayano-the-niece. Twenty years old. Hair—light chestnut, cut short in spring, as his mother-in-law had told him on the phone in May. Nose—Ren's. Eyes—Ren's. Not the father's; not the grandfather's. Kurosawa's father and grandfather were not in the eyes—they had left the eyes into the family that same morning when Ren was witness and Yukio was the object of the beating—and in the niece the nose and eyes were the mother's, that is, Yukari's, and Yukari had left the family in the ninth. Kurosawa had seen Ayano last in April, at the cemetery in Niigata, when they buried her grandfather—Yukari's father—and Ayano had stood there in the black schoolgirl dress of a first-year master's student, with a black ribbon in her hair, and had not cried.

Ayano-the-nurse—forty-seven. Or forty-six by the documents. Kurosawa had seen her at interrogation last November. Face—plain, without sharp features. Eyes—dark, deep, clear. Speaks quietly. Never raises her voice.
Kurosawa looked at the calendar.

"He is dividing us," he said. "He is showing us that we do not know which of the two Ayanos to turn to. He wants me to go to the niece and be unable to put the direct question. Or to put it and hear no. Or to decide the niece is with him. He wants me to make a mistake in this place."
Sasaki was silent.

"Sasaki-junsa-buchō. I will go to the niece. On Tuesday. But before that—you will get a telephone check from Niigata. I want to know whether Ayano-the-nurse is at work today or not. I want you to know that by the end of the workday."
"I'll do it."

"And I want you to write down one line for me. In the notebook. Two Ayanos. One—nurse, age forty-six, real name not yet established. The other—Kurosawa Ayano, twenty, niece, art history, Niigata. One—from the network. The other—from the blood. One of them sent the parcel. One of them—is a victim."
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"A third is possible."
He looked at her.
"The third is."
"The third is when he writes under her name and Ayano herself does nothing. Not the first, not the second. Not a victim, not a sender. Just a name he hangs a signal on."
Kurosawa looked at the sheet in the box. Then at her.
"You are right."
"I am not right. I have a variant."
He nodded.
Tanaka behind the glass partition raised his head. Saw the box on Sasaki's desk. Looked through the glass. Did not come out.
Kurosawa waved to Sasaki—a short gesture: cover it. Sasaki covered the box with the handkerchief and pushed it under the edge of the desk.
Tanaka watched for another five seconds. Then lowered his head back into the papers.

At six in the evening Sasaki closed the notebook. She took her coat off the peg—the same thin one, dark blue, to the knee—put it on. She washed the thermos in the canteen and put it into the lower drawer. Kurosawa was still sitting. Kenji had not come back; Tanaka—still in his office, with the phone.
"Kurosawa-keibuho."
"Yes."
"I'll be by from the morning. At seven. With coffee."
"Thank you."

"Yamada-san from Niigata. The check I finished at four. Ayano-the-nurse is at work today, from eight to seventeen. Not dismissed. Has not seen the head of the clinic since May. That is the standard mode."
"Good."
"Then I'm off."
"Yes."

She went out. Kurosawa sat for another fifteen minutes. Then he too rose. Tanaka behind the partition was already without his jacket, with the phone at his ear. Kurosawa nodded through the glass—a short nod that needs no answer. Tanaka nodded back the same way.
Kurosawa left the unit at six seventeen.

Sasaki lived on the second floor of a small building in Hotsumi, near Kita-24-jō station. Five minutes on foot from the metro exit. One entrance, three apartments on the floor, hers the far one on the left. Above her door was one small nameplate with the characters of her surname, and one iron plate with the number—two hundred and three.

She came up the stairs at six forty-two. In her mailbox was tired summer mail. One advertising flyer about a new candy store in the metro—the same one Kurosawa had had in his mailbox in Maruyama six weeks ago. One gas bill. One paper envelope—heavy, brown, kraft, no stamp, no postmark, no address. Only one word in black pen on the front.

Sasaki stood in the hallway with the envelope in her hand for twenty seconds. She did not open it. With her fingers she felt that inside was something solid. Small. In the shape of a ball with two little arms spread to the sides.
She knew what it was.
She set the envelope on the small table in the hallway. Did not open it.

She went to the kitchen. Put the kettle on. Took a cup from the lower shelf of the refrigerator—blue, with a small crack along the inner side—brewed a bancha with the tea dust that had been in the tin since April.
She stood over the cup for five minutes.
Then she came back to the hallway. Took the envelope. Did not open it.
She went into the bedroom. Set the envelope on the bedside table, beside the photograph of Nao in a frame—Nao in her master's-program uniform, with a black belt on her head—and lay down in bed.
She did not turn on the lamp.
She looked at the envelope in the dark.

Outside the window the last bus went by—route eight hundred and eight, from Kita-24 to Heiwana—with the same drawn-out horn as the last bus of two thousand and eleven, when she had first rented this apartment.

Nao in the photograph, in the master's-program uniform, had a black belt on her head and a light smile. The picture had been taken by one of her classmates in November last year, in Niigata—Nao had sent it to Sasaki over LINE with the note "elder sister, I finally set this stick on top after three years"—and Sasaki had printed the photo in a mini-photo lab on Kita-24 a week later. The frame was cheap, with a thin wooden rim; on the underside of the frame Sasaki had stuck a small piece of tape that had turned yellow in half a year.

She kept her palm on the envelope. Through the paper she felt the rounded, hard line of a small head without a face, with two little arms spread to the sides. She knew the form by touch, because she had seen it in three cases in a row. Now—on her own bedside table, two steps from the frame in which her sister was smiling.
"Kurosawa-keibuho," she said aloud, quietly, into the dark, as if he would hear her ten kilometers away across Maruyama. "I will not call."

She would not call, because calling would mean admitting that in this case she was not only an officer. This she admitted without a call. Not only an officer. A sister. There is a younger sister too, and she is in Niigata.
She took her hand off the envelope.
She closed her eyes.
She fell asleep at two forty.
Not today.

section.subtitle: Chapter Five
section.p: The prison at Tsukigata stood forty kilometers north of Sapporo, in a field where onions had once been grown. In winter the field was white. In August—level, green, with low light-gray administrative barracks, to which Kurosawa drove up at ten in the morning.

He came by bus. The car would have stood two hours in the parking lot in the sun, and Kurosawa did not want to return to a heated car. The bus from Ebetsu station—forty minutes, two stops, wind from the field through the open window. Kurosawa sat in the front seat, the thermos between his feet. In his bag—notebook, passport, a visit permit signed by prosecutor Fujiwara.
He did not drink on the bus. Did not read. Looked out at the field and thought of nothing.

Prosecutor Fujiwara revoked Toshi's bail in March. Toshi did not appear for his weekly check-in—that week Kurosawa had taken him to Shiretoko for the operation at one of the network addresses, and the schedule collapsed. Fujiwara signed the warrant within the hour. Toshi did not argue. He got on the bus to Tsukigata himself, in his gray pullover, with a small bag of books in his hand, the way one goes to retirement.
The Sapporo pretrial center held Toshi a year. Tsukigata had held him seven months.
Kurosawa had come three times. Toshi was silent for the first twenty minutes three times.
The guard was the usual one—Kawaguchi-san, fifty, with a small scar on his upper lip. He knew Kurosawa. Knew to bring water, not tea—that mattered. Knew not to remind about the time.
"Kurosawa-keibu." "Kawaguchi-san." "He is in the second room. Reading." "What." "Don't know. A thin book. In Ukrainian he doesn't show us."

Kurosawa nodded. Toshi had read Ukrainian in the Sapporo center—Zbigniew Herbert in someone else's translation, secondhand, from the Furano library. One of the guards had let him have it. Kurosawa had not asked which.
He passed through two metal detectors. He handed over his watch, his pen, his phone. The thermos was opened, sniffed, closed. Let through.
The visiting room at Tsukigata was smaller than at Sapporo—three meters by two, no window, two chairs, a low metal table. Ceiling in square panels. One lamp behind a grille.
Toshi was sitting.

In seven months at Tsukigata he had lost another three kilos. His shaved head kept its color. Skin—dry, as always. Kurosawa thought that Toshi looked the way he would have looked if he had never left the monastery—a body made for stillness.
"You came." "I came."
Kurosawa sat. Set the thermos on the table. Unscrewed the cap. Poured water into a cup—his, plastic, from his bag. Set it between them, closer to Toshi.
Toshi looked at it. Did not thank. Did not take.
Kurosawa screwed the cap back on.
Toshi was looking at the wall to Kurosawa's left. Kurosawa—at the wall to Toshi's left. That was how it had been from the first day.
"Kawaguchi-san says you are reading." "Herbert." "The same one?" "The same one. Mr. Cogito."
Kurosawa nodded. Was silent.
Toshi said:
"You went somewhere." "I did."
A pause. Toshi did not ask where. He knew Kurosawa would say himself.
Kurosawa opened the notebook. Set his palm on the sheet. Did not write. He looked at his own palm for about ten seconds, as if to check it was his. Then he said:
"Toshi. I found a collarbone at Erimo."
Toshi did not move.
Kurosawa waited.

Toshi was breathing—evenly, the way people breathe who have counted breath for years. Behind the wall someone walked down the corridor—soft steps, rubber—and vanished. Toshi sat longer than he had been silent last time. Kurosawa counted the beats of the second hand on the guard's wall clock: forty, sixty, ninety. On the hundredth Toshi shifted his eyes—not to Kurosawa, but to the cup between them.
"How many columns." "Nine. Eight had one each. The ninth—empty." "The eighth was to be yours." "Yes." "The sheet." "There. I took it."
Toshi nodded. Once.
Kurosawa said:
"You knew about Erimo." "No." A pause. "I swear."
The word "swear" was not one Toshi used. Kurosawa heard it from him for the first time in two years. He did not raise his eyes. Toshi did not raise his.
"But you knew something." "Yes."
Toshi went on breathing. Kurosawa gave him time. After a minute Toshi said, in the same quiet voice, in which there was neither resistance nor relief:
"Kurosawa-san. I did not know about Erimo. But I knew there is a place he always comes back to."
"Where."
"I don't know the address."
Kurosawa waited.
"He drove me blindfolded. Three times. In childhood. I did not see the road."
"You remember what."
Toshi thought.

"Smell of the sea—a couple of weeks. Not constant. The way it is when the sea is close but not from a window. Wood—old, dark, damp. Stairs—two flights. One straight, inside. The other—down, into concrete, steeper. In the concrete it smelled of rust and floor-cleaning fluid. The kind sold in the seventies. Still smelled."
He stopped. Kurosawa did not hurry him.
"And what else."
"A roof of a train," said Toshi, "once every fifteen minutes. Freight. Long. Went low above the house."
"Freight." "Yes. No whistle. Only the clatter. Distant, then close, then distant again."
Kurosawa was writing. Toshi did not ask whether he was writing.
"Did you see anything?" "Once." A pause. "I was eight. He untied the blindfold for a second so I could drink water. I saw the ceiling. A beam with a mark. Red. Three signs."
"Which."
"I do not remember the characters. I only remember—red. And—decoration. Shinto type. Not Buddhist."
"Gohei." "Yes. One. And a mark under it. A child's hand. Scrawls."
Kurosawa was writing. Toshi looked at the wall.
"And?"
"And—a city." Toshi paused, after which he would have added nothing if Kurosawa had been silent.
"Which."
Toshi looked at the cup.
"Kurosawa-san." "Yes." "All I know: Otaru."
Kurosawa laid the pen aside.

The word "Otaru" stood in the room—not loudly—with that particular weight with which the name of a city rises in a conversation when both sides have something lying in that city. Kurosawa had been born in Otaru. Kurosawa had buried his father in Otaru in two thousand and five. Kurosawa had buried Ren in Otaru in the twenty-second. In Otaru prosecutor Fujiwara had signed his first case. In Otaru Sato had married Michiko. In Otaru Yoshida Hiro had lived sixty-six years, in the same Temiya district Kurosawa used to come to as a boy to visit his uncle at New Year.
Kurosawa thought about this for five seconds. No more.
He set his palms on the table. Toshi did not move.
"You knew this from the start." "I knew from the day you came to me the first time." "Why did you not say." "You did not ask the right way."

Kurosawa nodded. Slowly—not to Toshi—to himself. To ask the right way meant to ask what Toshi could answer without betrayal. Otaru—that was not an address. That was a city of two hundred thousand souls. Toshi had given him what did not amount to direct betrayal of the Doll Maker—but that narrowed the search the way a funnel narrows a stream of water.
"The children's home," said Kurosawa quietly.
Toshi did not answer.
"The children's home in Otaru. Mori Katsuya. Director until nineteen ninety-eight. Yoshida—after."

Toshi looked at the cup. Kurosawa ran a finger along the edge of the notebook. He knew—when Toshi did not object like this, he confirmed slower than by an affirmative. Toshi had held the name Yoshida on his tongue for years. Kurosawa heard it in the pause.
"Toshi." "Yes." "Yoshida is alive." "Yes." "He is in Otaru?" "Not always." "Where else." "In the mountains. A hermitage. Hidaka." "Genshō-an." "Yes."
Kurosawa wrote out the word. Did not show it.
"You saw him after?" "After—no." A pause. "Before—many times. The last time—two weeks before my arrest at Kamishiroi."
"He knew you would remain." "He knew I would remain." "He set you." "Yes."
Toshi's voice did not change. Kurosawa thought: seven months of silence at Tsukigata, and none of these phrases now sounds like a confession. It sounds like reporting the weather.
Kurosawa drank from his cup. Toshi did not drink from his.
"Toshi." "Yes." "I will stop him." "I know." "You understand that you are a witness." "I understand." "You understand that Fujiwara can open a review." "Yes." "Do you want that?"
Toshi looked at the cup for a long time.

"Kurosawa-san." "Yes." "I do not fear him." "I know." "I do not hate him." "I know." "Will they return me to Furano?" "Not in the coming years." "All right." "Toshi." "Yes." "Do you want to go back to Furano?"
Toshi did not answer at once. Kurosawa waited. Toshi looked somewhere at the ceiling—not at the lamp, but to the side of it—and said:
"I would like one day to see the forest again. Not now. Now the forest is not what I need." "Then what."
Toshi turned his eyes. Not to Kurosawa. To the side, the way one turns them when searching for a word.
"Kurosawa-san." "Yes." "I do not want anything." "Toshi." "I would like—" he corrected himself, slowly, "—for him to go not the way Sato went. And—for Ayano not to be left alone."
Kurosawa closed the notebook.
"Ayano is in Niigata. She is twenty. She is in the master's program, art history."
Toshi nodded. For the first time in the conversation his head lowered—briefly—not a bow—only a movement down—and rose again.
"Thank you."
"That is not a gift." "I know. It is—information. Thank you."
Kurosawa sat another twenty minutes. He asked no more. Toshi looked at the cup. The water in the cup had not gone down.

Kurosawa had thought before that he knew how silence held at Tsukigata: with the same weight as it held in Sapporo, only with the effect of a field around it—because there was empty land, not city. Now he thought otherwise. He thought silence at Tsukigata held slower—not because of the field—but because Toshi in seven months here had let go of one more skin. The one in which he came to meetings in Sapporo. In Sapporo Toshi had sat like a man who waits. In Tsukigata Toshi sat like a man who has already finished waiting.
At the forty-first minute Kurosawa screwed the thermos shut. Took the notebook. Stood.
"Toshi." "Yes." "I will come again." "Do come." "With tea." "Thank you. Green."
Kurosawa nodded. Walked to the door.
"Kurosawa-keibu."
He stopped. Did not turn.
"Yes."
Toshi said quietly, in the voice with which he had spoken haiku on 5channel at Thursday eleven:
"Yoshida-sensei is warm. It is not a trap. It is the truth. Prepare for warmth."
Kurosawa was silent.
The door locked behind him. Kawaguchi-san walked him to the first checkpoint. Kurosawa took back his watch, pen, phone. He put on the jacket only at the exit.
The bus to Ebetsu left at two. Kurosawa sat on the bench at the stop, set the thermos between his feet. Took out the notebook. Wrote two lines:

p.emphasis: Otaru. Roof of a freight train. Shinto gohei, three red signs.

section.p: Closed the notebook.
The field lay level, green. Wind passed through it—low, soft—and went on, into the forest.
Kurosawa waited for the bus. He did not smoke.

p.emphasis: The children's room was long. Three tatami. One low bed with a checked blanket. One nightstand. One window, high, in a boxed frame. On the window—bars of four wooden slats, so no one would fall.
Michiko sat on the blanket. Seven years old.
She took each sock off slowly. First the right. Then the left. Folded one inside the other. Put them under the pillow—under the pillow they did not get lost.
The evening was quiet. The other children were having supper downstairs. She was not having supper. Her stomach ached. Kobayashi-san had given her a cup of warm water and told her to lie down.
Someone went by in the corridor. Steps soft. Not Kobayashi-san—Kobayashi-san walked loudly.

Yoshida-sensei stood in the doorway. In a gray suit. No jacket—only the waistcoat. Shirt sleeves rolled to the elbow. Hair short. He had washed his hands before supper—Michiko knew the smell of that soap. They sold it at the shop on the corner. Her mother used to buy that kind.
Her mother had died last year.
She did not answer. She folded her hands on her knees.
Michiko bowed her head. Once. Low. That was how Kobayashi-san had taught her—to say yes without words when the guest is older.
Yoshida-sensei came in. He closed the door behind him quietly. He did not sit on the bed. He sat on the tatami—on his heels—to be at her level. He set his hand on his own knee.
In his hand was a small box.
Yoshida-sensei placed the box on the tatami between them. The box was white. With a paper ribbon. The ribbon light red.

Michiko looked at the box. The ribbon shone under the lamp. Michiko did not know what was inside. She wanted to ask. She did not ask. Kobayashi-san had said—when a grown-up brings something, first you bow, then you open.
Michiko reached out. Her fingers were small. The ribbon slipped. She undid the knot.
Inside—a small porcelain doll. Without a face. Head smooth. Body in a white kimono. Hands folded in front.
Michiko bowed her head. Not because she understood. Because she did not know how else.
He placed his hand on her shoulder.
The palm was warm. Not heavy. Not holding—resting.
Michiko bowed her head. That meant no. It also meant I am listening. Yoshida-sensei understood.
He kept his palm on her shoulder. Very quietly.
"You can wait. A long time. Can you?"

Michiko counted on her fingers, on her knees. She did not show. She only counted. Three months. Mother had been in the hospital three months. Michiko had come every Sunday. She sat by the bed. She did not talk. Mother did not talk. Michiko waited until the nurse said, "time."
Yoshida-sensei took his hand off her shoulder.
The word "yes" she said aloud. Thin. One syllable.
"When I call you, you will come."
Yoshida-sensei looked at her. Eyes dark. Calm. Not sad, not glad. Michiko thought—that is how a person looks who knows what he wants.
Michiko bowed her head. Then she said:
"I must wait. A long time. When you call—I will come."
He placed the box with the doll beside her pillow. The doll looked at the ceiling without eyes.
Yoshida-sensei stood. His suit was slightly creased at the knees. He smoothed it with his fingers.
He went to the door. He did not turn.
Yoshida-sensei went out. The door closed. His steps went down the corridor. Quiet. Farther. Farther. Gone.
She lifted the doll to the window. The porcelain held the lamplight. There was no face. Michiko looked for a long time.
Then she put the doll into the box. The box—under the pillow, next to the socks.
Kobayashi-san came in half an hour later. Asked if her stomach ached. Michiko bowed her head. Kobayashi-san turned off the lamp. Went out.
Steps from the yard. Steps from the dining hall. Someone's voice. Someone's laugh. Then silence.
She took out the box. Opened it. Took out the doll. Put it beside her. The doll looked at the ceiling.
Michiko looked at the ceiling with it.
The next day Kobayashi-san did not notice the doll. Michiko kept it under her pillow. In the daytime she played with the others. In the evening she took it out. Held it to her cheek. Put it back.
Yoshida-sensei walked down the corridor every morning. Nodded to the children. Michiko bowed. He nodded to her the way he nodded to everyone.
Michiko understood. The word was theirs. No one had to know.
Another month. Another half a year. Another year.
The years began to grow long.

Michiko grew. Learned to read. Learned to count. At ten—to write characters. At thirteen—to speak to adults without swallowing her words. At fifteen—the junior administration gave her the younger children, and Michiko led them to wash their hands before supper, showed them how to fold a towel, how to hold chopsticks.
She kept the doll in her desk. In a drawer behind the notebooks. Sometimes she took it out.
Yoshida-sensei became director. Walked the corridor less often. Now he had an office.
At eighteen she entered a nursing school in Niigata. Yoshida-sensei signed the recommendation.
He passed the paper through Kobayashi-san. Kobayashi-san did not read it—only brought it.

Inside the envelope, separately, was a small box. White. With a paper ribbon. Michiko opened it. Inside lay a second doll. The same size. Without a face. Michiko placed the first and the second side by side. The doll looked at the ceiling. The second—the same.

In Niigata Michiko trained as a nurse. Did not marry. Rented an apartment alone. Bought soap at the same shop—with the same smell she remembered from seven. In the apartment there was nothing extra. In the drawer—two dolls.
Yoshida-sensei did not write. Did not call.
The years passed not fast. She did not add them.
Michiko-san. That was how they called her at the clinic. She kept her back straight. Head—a little down. Voice—level. The patients liked her. The management did not notice her. That suited her.
Michiko-san came to work at seven. Left at six. Slept at ten. Woke at six. That way—for forty years.

Every weekend she washed the floor in the apartment. One room. One stove. One toilet. Rag wet. Cloth on the knee. Michiko-san washed the floor kneeling on the cloth—the way Kobayashi-san had washed it in seventy-one.

Every second Sunday Michiko-san ate lunch at a minimart. One serving of rice. One fish. One small glass of barley tea. In the minimart there was a table under the window. She sat so as to look at the glass. She looked at people—not at them—but at the way they passed.

On the thirtieth of every month Michiko-san transferred half her salary to the postal bank into an account "O"—Yoshida's account—the one he had opened in her name in ninety-nine and on which he was signatory to this day. Michiko-san did not know where the money went. She knew—it had to. She did not ask.
She never had a dog. Never a cat. Never a houseplant.
She had two friends. One nurse from Yokohama who came once a year. One widow on the floor below who borrowed sugar. Michiko-san gave sugar without words. The widow thanked her. Did not come in.
Yoshida-sensei called her the first time in two thousand and three.
Yoshida-sensei called her the second time in two thousand and twenty-two.

From the twenty-second—seven trips to Otaru, every five months. Michiko did not ask to whom. She placed the cannula. She prepared the injections. She went back to Niigata. In the apartment she washed the floor kneeling on the cloth.

section.subtitle: Chapter Seven
section.p: Kenji's office was in the side wing of the unit—a small room with no window, with blinds no one bothered to close, and three monitors set parallel on a wide metal desk. Kenji liked his office. He said that without a window it was easier to concentrate; Kurosawa suspected Kenji liked the office because no one dropped in casually. People came only on purpose, with something.

At ten on Monday evening he was sitting alone. Coffee at the corner of the desk—the fourth. Glass of water—touched twice in the hour. One monitor turned off—Kenji turned the right one off when he was focused—that left a dark rectangular slab on the desk that narrowed the field of view.
On the middle monitor stood the list.
Forty-seven rows.

p.emphasis: Yoshida—year of birth—prefecture of registration—last address per driver's registry.

section.p: The list was printed out in the format Kenji liked—plain text on a black background—no sorting, no colors. It scrolled with one brush of the mouse. Kenji did not sort—sorting was the next step.
He read.

Yoshidas in Hokkaido, per the driver's registry, aged fifty-five to seventy as of August of two thousand and twenty-eight—there were four hundred and twenty-three. Kenji cut those with registered addresses outside Hokkaido in the previous ten years. That left two hundred and ten. He cut those with steady work biographies at one firm over twenty years, on the grounds that the Doll Maker could not have been an office worker. That left one hundred and eighteen. He cut those registered permanently in Sapporo, Hakodate, Asahikawa—three large cities—on the grounds that Toshi had mentioned a freight train, a roof, a ceiling with red marks. That left eighty-three. He cut those with a living spouse—Yoshida, by profile, lives alone. That left forty-seven.
Forty-seven was still many. But it was already accessible to the eye.
Kenji went through the list a second time. Then a third. On the third pass he stopped on one row.

p.emphasis: Yoshida Hiro—1962—Hokkaido—Otaru, Temiya, exact address not updated since 2019.

section.p: He looked at the row. Reached for the coffee.
The coffee was cold.
He set it down.
He looked at the row.

Every professional knows that feeling—that something is familiar—is bad currency. Kenji knew this better than most, because he had studied himself on it more than once: a computer face-recognition network confused a neighbor's face with a suspect's in three cases out of ten—and the human brain had the same error, only with a longer memory. Kenji did not trust recognition. Kenji trusted documents.
But the word Otaru held him.

He opened his own drawer. Not the right one—there lay the USBs, disks, a clean folder. The left one—there lay an old notebook in a soft cover, with paper glued to the spine. On the paper, in a faded marker, "2008–2010." He had not opened this notebook since two thousand and twenty. He kept it because he never threw things away.
He opened it.

The first pages—notes from second-year university analytics. Further—salaryman lunch recipes. Further—telephone numbers, crossed out two or three deep. On the forty-fifth page—a page from July of two thousand and eight, brief: "Otaru. OSINT club. Course. 1–29 July. Instructors: Honda, Takeuchi, Yoshida. Lunch—700 yen. Room—3200 a night, guesthouse Marumi."
Kenji looked at the word "Yoshida" in his own hand. His hand of eight years ago. Then—a little upright. Now he wrote at a slant.
He turned the page. On the fiftieth—"Yoshida-sensei cried at the farewell. Gave me a haiku collection. Did not remember the publisher."
Kenji closed the notebook.
Set it on the desk.
Sat.
He thought about Kurosawa.

Kurosawa was asleep at home. This was not the hour to call Kurosawa. Kurosawa had been sleeping badly for six weeks—since the day of Erimo—and Kenji knew this not from stories but from how Kurosawa spoke in the morning. Kurosawa had two registers of tiredness: the first—when he spoke in shorter sentences, and the second—when he spoke in the same sentences, only with longer pauses between them. The second register was a signal that he had slept less than four hours.
Kenji knew Kurosawa would come to him at seven thirty in the morning.
Before then—he had to decide.

He opened a new window. Typed the query: "Yoshida Hiro, 1962, Otaru." Three hundred hits. Most—another man. Kenji sorted by registry number. Filtered out those with a permanent address outside Otaru. Two remained. One—the owner of a door-and-frame shop, still working. The other—"former caretaker / educator, pension since 2019, no registered employment."
The second row had no photograph.
Kenji checked the local newspaper archive, Otaru Nippō. Over fifteen years—three mentions:
1. "Honoring veterans of pedagogy ceremony, 2011: Yoshida Hiro, educator." No photo.
2. "Summer seminar on information literacy for young people in 2008, the 'Otaru OSINT' circle, instructors: Honda Takashi, Takeuchi Hiroshi, Yoshida Hiro." No photo.
3. "Farewell evening for the director of Jindai-en, 2019: Yoshida Hiro handed leadership over to Inoue Satoshi after twenty-one years of work." No photo either. Only text.
Three lines. The word "Jindai-en."
Kenji looked at the word "Jindai-en" for a long time.

He knew the children's home Jindai-en existed. He had once walked past it with friends, on the way to Pier Two, and had thought then that the Taishō-period building, wooden, with a well-kept facade, looked cared for—someone was tending it. He had not remembered the director's name then. He rarely remembered such things.
But that had been in the summer of two thousand and eight. He had come to Otaru for a month. He had been studying OSINT. Three instructors. One of them cried at the farewell.
He did not remember the face.

He remembered only how this man had stood on a small dais in the hall of the guesthouse Marumi on the second-to-last evening, talking about reading memory through things, and how at the end, when everyone was rising, he—Yoshida-sensei—had remained standing on the dais and looked silently at the room. And how there was water in his eyes. Kenji—that twenty-three-year-old Kenji then—had thought: "this is not sentimentality, this is—something else." He had not dug down to what, exactly. Now, twenty years later, in the night silence of the office, with the black rectangle of the switched-off monitor to his right—Kenji tried to dig it out.
He did not dig it out.
Memory gave the image of the back of a head. Narrow shoulders. Gray suit. Short hair. The face memory did not give.
Kenji closed the notebook.

He opened a very old folder. Photographs from the course. A group shot in the yard of Marumi, taken hurriedly—thirty-two people in three rows. Kenji found himself—second row on the right, in a white shirt, thin. Found Honda Takashi—smiling into the camera, hand raised. Found Takeuchi—standing to the side, arms folded. Yoshida Hiro in the group photo was not there.

That is, he was. Kenji checked three times. It was the third row. But in the third row stood a man whose face was covered by the shadow of the canopy over the entrance. Only his shoulders, brow, and the angle of his chin were visible.
Kenji zoomed in. The pixels scattered. He zoomed out.

He compared the angle of the chin with dozens of chin angles that the police knew from various records of the Doll Maker. The records were of poor quality—fragments from public cameras—and in three of them one could see a fragment of the left side of a face. The angle of the chin—approximate. It might match. It might not.
Might does not work.
Kenji closed the window.
Kurosawa came in at seven twenty. He knocked once. Came in.
"Kenji-san." "Kurosawa-keibu." "You haven't slept." "Slept two hours." "The list?" "Here."
Kurosawa sat on the second chair—the one Kenji kept so that someone could sit—and looked at the monitor. Kenji scrolled.
Kurosawa was silent.
"How many," he asked. "Forty-seven." "Can you cut it down in a week?" "In a week I will have twenty. In two—eight. In three—five." "There are no three weeks."
Kenji nodded.
Kurosawa looked at him. Kenji held the gaze. Kurosawa read something in his face—Kenji did not know what—and said:
"You found something." "Not found. Saw." "Saw—what."
Kenji laid his palms on the desk.

"Kurosawa-keibu. In two thousand and eight I was in Otaru. A month. Summer OSINT course. Circle level, teenagers up to twenties. I came from Sapporo for a day or two, then stayed a month—my previous job let me. One of the instructors was named Yoshida."
Kurosawa did not move.

"Name?" "Hiro." "The same as on the list." "The name matches. But Yoshidas in Hokkaido are in the thousands. Yoshidas Hiro aged fifty-five to seventy in Hokkaido—forty-seven. In Otaru—two. One—a shop owner. The other—a pensioner, former educator. No photo. No active contacts. One line of mention in the paper—Jindai-en."
Kurosawa looked.
"You saw him?" "About four weeks. He came to the classes, taught, left. Cried at the farewell. Gave me a haiku collection."
"Do you remember the face?"
Kenji was silent.
"No."
Kurosawa waited. Kenji finished.
"I remember shoulders. Hair. The suit. The shadow he stood in on the group photo. Face—no."
"It is the same man." "I don't know." "Kenji-san."
Kenji lifted his eyes.

"Kurosawa-keibu. Yoshidas in Hokkaido are in the thousands. Yoshidas Hiro of the right age—forty-seven. Two in Otaru. But this—is not yet him. I could be wrong. I want to be wrong. I will not tell you it is him until I cross-check through the pension registry. That is three weeks."
"We have no weeks." "I know."
Kurosawa sat silent. He reached for Kenji's cup—only to occupy the hand. Did not drink.

"Kenji-san." "Yes." "You went to his classes." "Yes." "He knew your name." "Yes." "You had conversations." "Once. He asked where I was from. I said Sapporo. He said, very good that you came to us. Beyond that—nothing. He did not hold conversations. He held the course."
"You did not stay in his memory." "Him—I don't know. Me—yes."
Kurosawa set the cup back on the desk. With his fingers. Very precisely, onto the same ring he had lifted it from.
"Kenji-san." "Yes." "Do not get into a car with me for Otaru." "Kurosawa-keibu." "I will not take you. You are not a witness. You are—doubt. Doubt I need here. In Sapporo. With a keyboard."
"I understand." "You cut it to eight. In three weeks." "In two." "In two."
Kurosawa stood.
"Do you remember what he said on the dais?"
Kenji thought.

"Reading memory through things. That is a phrase." "The subject?" "Three sessions. On doing OSINT not through people but through their objects. Glass. Keys. Wrappings. He said: a man forgets to say, a thing does not forget to be."
Kurosawa nodded. For a long time.
"That—is him."
Kenji lowered his head. Not a bow—a little. The way one bows to oneself when confirming what one does not want to confirm.
Kurosawa went to the door.
"Kenji-san." "Yes." "You did not expose him. You only saw him." "Yes." "That—is not your fault." "I know."
Kurosawa went out.
Kenji sat. The right monitor—dark. The middle—with forty-seven rows. The left—with one row. Yoshida Hiro. 1962. Otaru. Jindai-en. Pension since 2019.
He opened a window. Wrote:

p.emphasis: Cried at the farewell. OSINT course. Guesthouse Marumi. July 2008. "A thing does not forget to be."

section.p: Saved.
He put the notebook in the left drawer. Did not close the drawer. The coffee stayed cold. The glass of water—touched twice.
He looked at the middle monitor.

He thought about Kurosawa. Not today's—the one who had just gone out of the office and was walking the corridor now to the stairs. Kurosawa had not said either "thank you" or "shame." He had said "that—is him." That was the firmest thing Kurosawa had ever said to Kenji. It was also the softest. Kenji knew the difference.

He did not want to be wrong. But he also did not want to be wrong in the opposite direction—did not want to be silent at eight percent certainty when at another twenty percent it was the hand that had crushed a pencil into his shoulder after the farewell session. Yoshida-sensei had touched his shoulder. Kenji remembered this. The hand had been warm.
He stood. Switched off the middle monitor. Switched on the left. On the left he had a plain text editor in which he wrote what he did not show. He wrote one line.
Did not save.
Closed the window.
Outside the window that was not there, dawn was coming.

section.subtitle: Chapter Eight
section.p: Hiraoka Cemetery lay on the slope south of Sapporo—a place from which the city below seemed a chance occurrence among the hills—and Kurosawa had come here twice a year since two thousand and thirteen: once in spring, in the April week of remembrance, and again in August, when the heat held the cicadas in one long note. He came to his father's grave—not out of love—out of duty. His father's grave stood three rows from the road, beneath a small maple—the stone plain, low, the name carved in an inexpensive script. Kurosawa laid one branch of cypress, refilled the water in the bowl, and left.
Today he had not come to his father.

Ogawa Tatsuo's grave stood on the new side—the one opened in the twentieth—in the twenty-fourth row from the gate, under the plaque "Ogawa, house in Sapporo." The stone was new, dark gray, not yet stained by moss. The name—fresh. The date—March of two thousand and twenty-eight. Five months ago.
He stood.

Ogawa had died under a tractor. It was a stupid death—the kind whose family does not know how to tell. He had gone to his nephew's, in a village outside Asahikawa, for the Saturday. The nephew was plowing a plot. Ogawa was walking the field, looking. The tractor was old, from the nineties. The brake failed, the machine started down the slope. Ogawa stepped aside in the wrong direction. The wheel went over his chest. Fifty-three years old. A quiet man. He had wanted no harm.

Kurosawa had buried him in March. Then Tanaka Ryosuke had come from Tokyo—Tanaka had been a colleague of Ogawa's from the academy, had known him longer than Kurosawa—and by Tanaka's own account it was the one instance in which he had put off his own assignment. Tanaka had stood at the funeral beside Kurosawa. Silent. Kurosawa was silent. Ogawa's wife, Toshiko, held Ogawa's small son—eight-year-old Hiro—by the hand. Hiro did not cry. Toshiko cried quietly, into a white handkerchief.
A week later Tanaka received the appointment to Ogawa's post. He came from Tokyo temporarily. "Temporarily" was five months ago.

Kurosawa thought of Ogawa only when Tanaka came into the office. That was not fair to Ogawa. But it was fair to Kurosawa's head—it held the image of Ogawa only through the silhouette of Tanaka in the doorway.

He crouched before the stone. The water in the bowl—stagnant. Ogawa had a wife who came—Kurosawa knew that—but today was Wednesday, and Toshiko came on Sundays. Four days had been enough for the water to bloom.

Kurosawa unscrewed the cap of the plastic bottle—he had brought water from home—poured out the old, poured in the new. He laid one branch of cypress on the low shelf. He had cut the branch that morning, a block from the unit, from a live hedge—did not ask permission. Ogawa had loved cypress. Ogawa had once said his father kept one in the garden. Kurosawa had remembered—not because he was planning to remember.
He set his hand on the stone. His palm was dry. The stone—cool.
Did not speak.

After a minute he took from the inside pocket of his jacket the sheet. The same one. Folded in three. Worn corners. "Kurosawa" written in the flourish he had known for seven months. Written on heavy paper the Doll Maker had used from some reserve lot of the two thousands—the paper still smelled of an old chest of drawers—and Kurosawa noticed the smell every time the sheet came near his face.
Kurosawa smoothed the sheet. Read for the twentieth time what he knew by heart. One line. One word. A name.
He laid the sheet on the stone.
Stood another minute.
Then lifted it—did not leave it—folded it—and put it back into the pocket. He spoke—to the stone, quietly, not for the stone's sake:
"Not yet, Ogawa-san."
An ant ran along the branch of cypress. Kurosawa watched until it was gone.
He walked to the road on foot. The car was outside the gate, beside two others—a silver sedan and a white minivan.
The phone vibrated in his pocket as he opened the door.
Kurosawa looked at the screen. A "03" prefix—Tokyo. Unfamiliar. He knew what it was.
He answered.
"Kurosawa." "Kurosawa-keibu." "Endo-san." "Do not interrupt, please. I am brief."
Endo's voice was the same as seven months ago—low, calm, with a minimal tilt at the ends of sentences. She spoke at the pace of a person for whom nothing falls out of the list.
"I am listening."
Kurosawa sat in the car. He did not start the engine. The air conditioning was off. Heat inside was rising. He did not notice.
"Kurosawa-keibu, the exhumation of Ren gave its answer. The body—is not Ren."
"I know."
"You are looking for a live man."
"I know."
Endo was silent.

"Then let me say one more thing," she said. "I have held this file for seven months. Since the day the exhumation gave its result. I did not show it, because it is not my jurisdiction.
