Tokyo put me on a consultative contract from January. I hold access to three databases I would not have in Sapporo. My contract ends in December. Then I will not see these databases."
"Say it."
"In my data," said Endo, "is the surname of the Otaru coroner who signed the body under Ren's name in April of two thousand and twenty-two."
Kurosawa waited.

"Kawai Tatsuya." Endo dictated slowly. "Kawai—河合. Tatsuya—達也. Born nineteen fifty-three, Otaru. Coroner in Otaru from nineteen eighty-two. Over thirty-seven years—more than four thousand certificates. Never charged. Never disciplined. Pension from the twentieth. Died in the twenty-fourth. Oncology. Natural death."
"Natural."
"Yes."
"You are certain?"
Endo was silent one second.
"Eighty percent," she said. "Twenty—I keep in reserve."
Kurosawa nodded to the phone, and said nothing. Endo went on:

"Kawai Tatsuya was in contact with Mori Katsuya, the previous director of Jindai-en, from nineteen eighty-six. This is known from letters in the Mori archive Kenji got into on Monday. Mori died in ninety-eight. Kawai went on working. Yoshida—the new director—inherited Kawai through the channels Mori had used. Yoshida and Kawai were in direct contact at least twice: once in two thousand and three, once in two thousand and eleven. In the twenty-second, when Yoshida falsified the body of Ren, Kawai signed the certificate. That is all I have on Kawai."
Kurosawa closed his eyes. Tired from the sun—the air in the car was already warm—he felt the heat pressing into his palms.
"Kawai is dead," he said.
"Yes. But—Kurosawa-keibu." Endo let a small pause hold. "The son—is alive."
Kurosawa opened his eyes.

"The son." "The son. Kawai Takehiro. Born nineteen eighty-four. In Otaru. Heir to his father's practice—private medical practice in Otaru, Temiya district. Alive. Forty-four years old. Not married. No children. Mother—Kawai Hatsuko, eighty-one, alive, in the Otaru-Kōeikai care home. Takehiro visits her."
Kurosawa was silent.
"Let me guess," said Endo. "His father's practice—is the same one in which Kawai Tatsuya signed the certificate of Ren's death in the twenty-second."
"Yes."
"Let me guess," said Endo again, "that Takehiro has inherited not only the practice."
Kurosawa sat. The water bottle on the passenger seat had sweated onto his palm.
"Endo-san." "Yes." "Thank you."
"Kurosawa-keibu." Endo did not change her tone. "This is not a gift. This is information. I ask only one thing of you."
"I am listening."

"Do not summon him today. He has a practice, a standing clientele. Yoshida will know within an hour. Watch a week. Give Kenji time to set surveillance. Then summon him—but with prosecutor Fujiwara, and with a search warrant on the practice simultaneous with the interrogation."
"I will do that."
"One more thing."
Kurosawa waited.
"Kurosawa-keibu. I have no jurisdiction in Otaru. I got a call today from Sapporo—about a new post. Tanaka Ryosuke wants to bring me back from Tokyo as a consultant for your unit."
"I know. He told me this morning."
"Are you—for?"
Kurosawa thought.
"Yes, Endo-san. I am—for."
"I will tell Tanaka yes, if you say yes."
"Say it."
"I will."
Endo was silent another second. Kurosawa waited—he knew—Endo was silent before saying the last thing.
"Kurosawa-keibu." "Yes." "You are—not alone."
"I know."
"Do not forget."
"I will not."
"All the best."
Endo hung up.
Kurosawa sat in the car another five minutes.
The air conditioning he did not switch on. The heat inside grew thick. He felt sweat at his temples. He pulled his tie loose—did not take it off—loosened it.
He took out the notebook. Wrote:

p.emphasis: Kawai Takehiro. Heir to father's practice. Otaru, Temiya. Not married. Mother at Otaru-Kōeikai. Surveillance—Kenji. One week.

section.p: Closed the notebook.
He looked into the side mirror. In the mirror—Ogawa's stone, a square of dark stone among other squares. The cypress branch lay where he had left it. The ant, no doubt, had already passed and gone.
Kurosawa started the engine. Opened the window on the passenger side. Pulled out of the lot slowly.
On the road to Sapporo—two cars ahead, three behind. He held the middle speed.
Hills slid past the window. The city below began as a gray band—where the skyscrapers cut their notch. Kurosawa was not looking at them.
He was looking at the road.
The sheet was in his pocket. He did not take it out.
Ogawa remained where he remained. The place was new, not yet stained. Toshiko would come Sunday.

Kawai Takehiro sat in a practice in Otaru—Kurosawa had not yet seen him—and Kurosawa did not yet know what the son's eyes were like. He knew only that forty-four years, and that there was a mother whom he visited. That was already something. That was—a lever.
He turned on the radio. He was not listening. The radio was needed to keep from hearing the silence in the cabin.
The silence in the cabin that day was very dense.
Half an hour later the second phone rang in the car—the work one. Kenji.

"Kenji-san." "Kurosawa-keibu. Did Endo-san pass it to you?" "Yes. Kawai's pension, the son, the practice." "I have already set surveillance. One car by the practice, one by the mother's home. One passive—in Niigata, on Ayano—on Michiko just in case." "On Michiko?" "The name matches in two registries," said Kenji. "I checked again this morning. Michiko Takahashi, nurse, Niigata, forty-seven. Ward of Jindai-en, nineteen eighty-five through ninety-three. That is the same Ayano—from the clinic—who supplied the midazolam." "You are sure." "Endo-san's twenty percent reserve. I hold it."
Kurosawa was silent.
"Surveillance—passive." "Only passive," said Kenji. "We will not take her until we take him. Otherwise she warns him."
"Yes." "One more thing, Kurosawa-keibu." "Yes." "Tanaka Ryosuke wants a briefing at six." "I'll come."
Kurosawa hung up.
The road became uniform. Hills, then plain, then hills again, then field, then suburb. Kurosawa looked ahead.
The sheet "Kurosawa" was in the inside pocket of his jacket. He felt it in his shoulder when he turned the wheel. Not strongly. But—steadily.
He arrived at the unit fifty minutes later.
Tanaka was in his office. Door open. Kurosawa walked past, nodded. Tanaka nodded back. He asked nothing.
Kurosawa walked to his own office. Closed the door behind him. Turned off the phone. Sat. On the desk lay the Hiraoka Cemetery visitors' log—he had not taken it that morning, had left it for later.
He opened the log. Wrote his name. The date. Entry time—09:47. Exit—10:22.
Closed the log.
He took out the sheet "Kurosawa." Set it on the desk in front of him. Looked. Did not read. He knew it by heart.
One name.
Not yet. But—soon.

section.subtitle: Chapter Nine

p.emphasis: The morning was high. The mountains stood beyond the window grayish-green. The air smelled of resin and wet earth.
Sato sat on the top step. Outside. The wooden porch was old. Boards washed by hundreds of rains. One board in the middle of the porch creaked—Sato knew which.
He held a cup in his palms. Empty.
A pack of Peace lay by his hip. One cigarette—in his fingers. The second—in the pack. The third and beyond—already smoked.
The house stood on the slope of Ashibetsu-yama. One story. A kitchen. A room for him. A room for Yoshida. A bath. That was all.
Sato did not know whose house it was.
He had come here on the third day. Yoshida had driven. Yoshida was at the wheel himself. The road wound. Sato had looked out the window and had not asked.
Walking on the porch. Sleeping. Eating rice. Listening. Not thinking.
The door behind him slid open. Sato did not turn. Steps soft—bare. Yoshida always walked barefoot in the house.
Yoshida sat on the top step. One over from Sato. The board did not creak. He knew where to sit.

In his hands—a small tray. On the tray—two teapots. One—low, with a rust-green glaze. The other—clear, glass. The glass one was warm, with a small amount of tea inside. Sato saw the color—saturated, dark green, almost herbal.
Sato set his own cup on the tray. Yoshida poured.
The tea came slowly. Very slowly. That is how gyokuro is poured—the bottom of the cup should hold a thin layer.
Sato lifted the cup with both palms.
He did not drink at once.
Yoshida poured his own. Took the cup, also with both palms. Held it by his knees.
The taste was soft. Not bitter. Sweet, like young greens.
Sato looked at the mountains. The green of the mountains was the same as in the tea. He did not say it. That would be a metaphor. He had long stopped saying such things.
Yoshida was silent. Also looking at the mountains.
Yoshida was silent. Sato understood the silence as consent.
"Yes. In your room—as much as needed."

He remembered the room differently each day. Today he remembered it this way: old tatami, a lamp, a book about rabbits Kenta had not liked. Kenta had liked a book about ants. Sato had not bought books about ants—Michiko had said ants were frightening. Now Michiko was long gone. Now Kenta too was long gone. But in the room Kenta was—with a book about ants in his hands. Sato sat opposite. Listened.
He knew this was not Kenta. Yoshida had told him this beforehand. Yoshida had said: "You see what memory will do when you let it." Sato had agreed. Sato had wanted to see.
"Sato-san. You saw how he would have gone on living. That is enough."
Sato sipped again. The cup was still warm.
Sato did not look at him. He looked into the tea.
"You—are not Genshō from the monastery, are you?"
Yoshida waited. He did not take offense. He did not smile.
"No. I am the keeper of Genshō-an hermitage in Hidaka. That is different."
"Genshō from the monastery—is a different person. He is older. He is in Sōunkyō. He and I have never met. The name is close. Not me."

section.p: "One man said it. In Furano. He said Genshō from Reisen-ji. I thought—that was you."

p.emphasis: A bird sang beyond the trees. Far. Silence again.
Sato set the cup down. Empty.
Sato looked to the side. At the board that creaks.
Sato turned his head. Looked at Yoshida for the first time. Yoshida sat straight, holding the cup with both palms. His face—warm—not saccharine—with a warmth that had no hurry in it.
"You are not a prisoner, Sato-san. I do not hold you."
"Sato-san. Say the word and I will drive you to the station."
"Those I chose—not many. Those who chose me—also not many."
Yoshida looked at him. For a long time. Sato did not look away.
"Sato-san. Every morning at forty-two you went out to the pier. Held one cigarette. Looked at the water. Stood twenty minutes. Went back to Kingyo. Drank coffee. Cut fish."
"That was not life. That was a form."

"I could not give Kenta back to you. I could only let you see what he would have grown into. Now—you know that you did not kill him. You did not pull him out of the water—that is not killing. That is a form of grief. You can live on without that form."
Yoshida poured again. The glass pot was empty. Sato drank the second cup slowly. Taste soft. Mountains the same.
Set the cup down. The board did not creak. He was sitting straight.

section.p: "Kurosawa-keibu."

p.emphasis: "I never saw him. Did not see him in the room. Did not see him here."
"He will come. Not to me—to himself. That is another road."
Sato was silent. For a long time.
Yoshida stood. Not quickly. Took the cup with both palms. Went into the house. The door slid. Soft steps on the floor. He set the cups on the kitchen table—Sato heard.
Sato sat on the top step. Smoked one more. Did not read. The mountains stood green-gray. The bird sang again—further.

He thought of Kenta. Not of the room. Of Kenta once—on the pier, with a paper airplane in his hands—a year before he drowned. The airplane was yellow. Kenta had made it himself. Kenta had launched it. The airplane flew for two seconds and fell into the water. Kenta laughed. Sato laughed too. Once. Then.
It was the first time in many years.
He finished the cigarette. Put it out in a tin of water at his feet. Smoke went up in a white thread into the morning air.
He went inside to gather his things.
Behind him on the porch board lay a pack of Peace. One remained. It could stay. Sato did not take it.
He would go back to Kingyo.
He would pour himself green tea.
Yoshida-sensei would go back to his Genshō-an. Sato would not see him again.
The mountains behind the house stood green-gray. The bird did not sing again.

section.p: He gathered his things simply. One shirt. One trousers. Slippers. Two books that Yoshida-sensei had given him—Notes of Solitude and A Small Anthology of Bashō. Sato took only the second. The first he left on the low table. Yoshida-sensei would see, would understand.

p.emphasis: He came out of the room. Yoshida-sensei stood in the kitchen. Making himself tea—different this time, barley. He did not look up when Sato came in.
Sato took them. Put them in his pocket. In the pocket, besides the keys, was a pack of Peace. Yoshida-sensei had put it in earlier.
Yoshida-sensei turned his head. Looked at him for the first time that morning.
Yoshida-sensei smiled. Very faintly. At the corners.
Sato nodded. Went to the door.
At the door he stopped. Did not turn.

section.p: "If he comes—Kurosawa-keibu—will you pour him tea?"

p.emphasis: The door slid shut behind him softly. The board on the porch creaked—the same one—as he stepped on it.
He went down the path. Long. The trail wound. One hour to the road. Two hours to the bus. The bus to Ashibetsu. Then the train.

He came to the first bend of the trail. Turned. The house stood on the slope. The roof was not visible past the trees—only the chimney. Nothing came from the chimney. Yoshida-sensei was not lighting a fire that morning—it was warm.
Sato turned back to the trail. Farther. Farther. Farther.
The mountains held silence at his back.
"The ryokan was bought in the tenth. Through a firm the dead man had closed."

section.subtitle: Chapter Ten
section.p: Kenji came in at seven in the morning—earlier than the unit itself was awake—and was sitting in the corner chair with a laptop on his knees when Yukio and Sasaki walked into the office at the same time, from the corridor, from two sides. Miso in the carrier lay with his nose to the radiator and did not lift his head.
"You slept," said Sasaki.
"Five hours," said Kenji. "That is standard."

Yukio hung his coat. He noticed that Kenji had switched off the desk lamp and left only the monitor. That meant one thing: Kenji had found something, and did not want the cleaner who came in at six forty to read it.
Yukio sat. Sasaki brought three paper cups of coffee from the corridor vending machine and set one in front of Kenji. He nodded, did not look.
"Show me," said Yukio.

Kenji turned the laptop screen toward the desk. On the screen—a gray scan of an old paper registry. Characters photocopied, the line a little crooked. Stamp of the administration of Akaneko-mura, September of two thousand and ten.
"Ryokan Kamishiroi," said Kenji.
Yukio did not move. Sasaki set her cup on the corner of the desk, slowly.

Kamishiroi. The first "room" they had found. Sato-san in a small two-story house on the side of the mountain, with a wooden bath, with a view over the bay, with a portrait of the owner from twenty years ago on the entrance wall. The ryokan in which they had thought they saw the edge of the network—and had turned out to see its entrance.
"Go on," said Yukio.

"The ryokan was bought in the tenth. Not by Yoshida personally—" Kenji opened a second scan, "—by a firm. Yuki-Kōgei LLC. Restoration of traditional architecture. Head office in Sapporo Chūō—I showed it to you last year."
"That is the same network firm from our map," said Sasaki.
"Yes. But—here it becomes more interesting."
Kenji laid an index finger on the name of Yuki-Kōgei's director in the scanned deed.
"Tanaka Hideo. Died in Otaru, September of two thousand and eight. Renal failure."
Yukio nodded. He remembered that.
"The deed is dated the twentieth of September, two thousand and ten. That is, two years after the director's death. Signature on the deed—Tanaka Hideo. Stamp—Yuki-Kōgei."
Sasaki set the cup flat on the desk. Did not drink.
"A dead man signed."

"A dead man signed," said Kenji. "Formally. On paper. In reality—the firm still existed, because no one had reported the death to the tax office. Tanaka-san's son did not report it, because he did not know his father was director of anything. The daughters did not report it, because they had not seen their father for fifteen years before his death. The firm became 'dormant.' The death certificate did not reach the tax office until the twelfth. Only then did the firm move to 'undergoing reorganization.' That is—between two thousand and eight and two thousand and twelve, Yuki-Kōgei was alive on paper, with a dead director who kept signing documents."
"Who signed?"
"The one who had the stamp."
Yukio reached for the coffee—did not take it—and set his hand on the corner of the desk. Sasaki knew this movement. She stood and was silent.
"Mori Katsuya," said Yukio.

"Mori Katsuya," Kenji confirmed. "Director of the children's home in Otaru, died in ninety-eight. Yoshida—his student and successor. Mori, before his death, registered Yuki-Kōgei through the nominee director Tanaka. The stamp remained with Yoshida. The Kamishiroi deed in the tenth—his signature under Tanaka's name, with Mori's stamp. He bought the ryokan with money that lay in the firm's account from Mori's old period."
"How much lay there."

"Twenty-two million yen. The deed—eighteen point seven. The difference—for renovation. Renovation was done in the eleventh. Through Kita-Michi Zaimoku KK, out of Ashibetsu—the same on our map—cedar, Japanese larch. Interior partitions. Plus materials for the bath. Plus roof."
Yukio nodded.
"So the whole network," said Sasaki slowly, "did not grow from a network. It grew from a children's home in Otaru. Through one firm Mori created three months before his death. In ninety-eight."
"Yes," said Kenji.
Sasaki sat. For the first time that morning.

Yukio was standing. He did not sit. He looked into the laptop screen and past the laptop screen at the same time—the way a man looks through glass and through his reflection in the glass—and sees two things, and cannot choose which one to see next.
"Kenji-kun."
"Yes."
"The name of the children's home."
A pause.
"There isn't one."
"How 'isn't'."

"The NGO registry of Hokkaido from nineteen ninety-eight burned in two thousand and two. Fire in the archives of the Otaru administration. There were—paper files. Backup on film—did not survive, the equipment was old, the film had yellowed to unusable already in the nineties. Digitization began in the two-thousands, but without this part. I have only what is in later registries: in Otaru in two thousand and two—seven children's homes. Mori was director of one of seven. Which one exactly—needs either a person who remembers, or a document from another archive—tax, medical—and those are from other years. I am working. Give me three days."
Yukio was silent.

Seven children's homes. One of the seven. Mori—findable by name in retrospective medical declarations—but that is six weeks through the Sapporo state archive, and the state archive works like a state archive—not faster and not more accurate.
"We do not have three days," said Yukio.
"I know," said Kenji. "But this is what I can do. I do not make false promises."
Yukio nodded.
Sasaki lifted her head.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."

"So we do not have a network. We have an origin. Yuki-Kōgei is the bone from which the whole network grew. Kamishiroi is not the edge. It is the continuation. Mori prepared this by ninety-eight, and Yoshida carried it out."
"Yes."
"The children's home he grew up in—that is his frame. That is why Otaru."
"That is why Otaru," said Yukio.
Kenji half-closed the laptop—so the screen would not go out but would not shine in the eyes. He noted aloud:
"Kurosawa-san, I have one more sheet."
"Show me."
"Yuki-Kōgei in two thousand and eleven—besides Kamishiroi—bought three more objects. One in Memuro. One in Shiretoko. One in Hidaka."
"Hidaka."

"Yes. Mountain cottage. One story. One hectare of land. On paper—dacha for the firm's staff. Real staff at Yuki-Kōgei—two nominal ones, both puppets of Tanaka. That is, no one ever came out to the dacha as staff."
"Who pays the electricity."
"Ainu-Tabi Hoshō. Small payment, roughly eight thousand yen a month. That corresponds to one permanent resident. In the cold period—fifteen. That is, someone lived there."
"Since what year."
"Since the twelfth. Permanently."
Yukio nodded.

He did not say it aloud. Kenji did not know the word—it was not on our map. Sasaki knew: it had been in one report of the abbot of Reisen-ji in December of the year before last—the report Endo had taken with her to Tokyo—and in it the abbot had noted that in the mountains of Hidaka there was a small hermitage, "Genshō-an," not officially registered, to which once a year an old monk walks with a letter. The abbot had written it as an aside, without explaining why.
Yukio had marked it for himself then. He had not returned.
Now he did.
"That is his place," he said. "Not Otaru. Hidaka."
"The place he lives in—yes," said Kenji. "But the place where he keeps others—Otaru. Or nearby. A children's home we do not yet know."
"Yes."
Yukio turned to Sasaki. She sat with the tense calm she had before going out into the field—when she already knew where to go and was waiting for him to say it aloud, so as not to run ahead.
"Sasaki-san."
"Yes."
"Where do we go."
Sasaki thought one second.
"To Otaru. The children's home. Through Inoue, if he has access; through Yasuko, if he does not. Through medical exam archives. Through anything."
"No," said Yukio.
Sasaki lifted her eyes.
"To the lighthouse first," said Yukio. "He wants this."
Sasaki did not answer at once. Kenji set the coffee mug on the desk—now he was drinking—and turned his head to Yukio. He did not ask aloud. He asked with a posture.

"That sheet from Erimo," said Yukio, "which only Sasaki-san knows about, because I showed her after I came back. It is addressed to me personally. He expects me to come there. The children's home—that is what I will find after the lighthouse. He plans it that way."
"Kurosawa-san," said Kenji, "this is a trap."
"Yes."
"And you are walking into it."
"Yes."
Kenji laid his forefinger on the edge of the desk. Silent. Then:

"Then the children's home I prepare for your return. By Sunday you will have an address. Yasuko-san—I have already started looking through the Otaru pension registry. That is faster than through the administration."
"Thank you, Kenji-kun."
"Not 'kun,'" said Kenji. "I do not mind 'kun.' I only noticed. You sometimes use '-kun,' sometimes '-san.' It is not important. Go on."
Yukio was silent.
Sasaki stood.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"We must prepare for the lighthouse. And this evening I have to go to my sister in Niigata. It cannot wait. Nao has one thing I must check with my hands."
"One night."
"One night. I return Monday morning."
"All right."

Sasaki nodded. Walked to her desk. Yukio did not ask what the thing was. He knew something about Sasaki and Nao from earlier years. He knew that when Sasaki said one thing I must check with my hands, it meant she had already checked it with her head and did not like what she had found.
Kenji stood in the corner.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."

"One more thing. Ryokan Kamishiroi—bought in the tenth. Renovation in the eleventh. But the furnishings—not from the eleventh. One board on a panel in the tea room—I checked through the restorer Komatsu-san from Sapporo, he did the report for Book One—dates to somewhere between nineteen ninety-eight and two thousand. That is, in Kamishiroi there is one board brought from some house dismantled between ninety-eight and two thousand. Not from the open market."
Yukio did not look at him.
"From what house."
"I don't know. I thought you might guess."

Yukio did not say it. He knew. The annex of ninety-eight—when Yoshida became director, and reconstruction of the annex began in one of the seven children's homes. He had not yet seen it. But he had seen the board that had been pulled from it and carried ten years later to Kamishiroi and set as a panel in the tea room, where Sato-san then sat.
These people saved everything. Nothing was thrown away.
"All right," said Yukio. "Kenji-kun. Continue on the children's home. Sasaki-san—today to Niigata, Monday morning here. Me—the lighthouse. Departure—Tuesday morning."
"Five days," said Sasaki.
"Yes."
Yukio looked at the corner of the desk, where Sasaki had set her cup and had not drunk. Two swallows of coffee remained. It stood cold now.
He took it and drank it in one go.

Outside the window the August rain was falling—thin as a thread—and Yukio thought about one board from an unknown children's home that had held the wall of the tea room in Kamishiroi twelve years after it had been pulled from there.
He did not know from which children's home.
He knew only that he would find it faster than the man hiding it would want.

p.emphasis: "Don't go to Otaru. Not this Saturday."

section.subtitle: Chapter Eleven
section.p: Nao opened the door at six forty-five—without asking who—because she knew one thing: when Yuri came to Niigata unannounced, she stood on the landing exactly the pause with which she listened for whether the television was on inside. Nao switched it off. Nao waited.

The door was old, wooden, with a brass handle, like most first-floor buildings in Minami-Shiomi. Yuri took off her shoes, set them straight, toes to the wall. Hung her coat on the single nail by the entrance. Nao took her bag, set it on the low chest, and looked at her sister's face once—that short attentive look Yuri had once given her at fourteen, when Nao came home for the first time with a broken knee.
"There is onigiri," said Nao. "I'm putting the miso soup on now."
"Thank you."
"You are for one night."
"For one night."
Nao nodded. Did not ask why exactly.

The apartment was one room and a kitchen, as always in Niigata for a graduate student on the minimum stipend with a parental supplement on the rent. On the kitchen table—an open catalog. Nao closed it in a hurry when she saw Yuri's glance—but Yuri had already seen.

An ichimatsu-ningyō. Small, porcelain, in a blue kimono, without a face. Photograph—old, on matte paper. Underneath—a caption in Japanese: "Original from a private collection, Otaru. Exhibition 'The Body and the Form: The Japanese Doll in the First Half of Shōwa,' Otaru Museum, August 14–28."
"You're taking me with you," said Nao.
"I am not taking you."
"You said 'one night.' That means you did not come with her."
Yuri was silent.

Nao set the miso soup pot on the stove. She noticed there was a little too little water and added from the kettle. She sliced leek slowly and evenly with the knife Yuri had given her two years ago. Behind each slice a small wet crescent remained on the board. Nao, when she concentrated, did not look at her hands. She looked at the wall above the sink.
"Nao."
"Yes."
"Tell me about work."

Nao had no time to understand how Yuri had understood—and did not want to, and started. She spoke calmly, with the slow clarity of a twenty-four-year-old telling of her first major research to a person she loves.

"I am writing my master's thesis on ichimatsu-ningyō of the first Shōwa period. Twenty-eighth to forties. Not about the dolls themselves—about their bodies. About proportions. About how proportions changed after the Kantō earthquake. Bodies became heavier. Heads—a little smaller. As if before then dolls were held by the head, and after—began to be held by the hips."
"Does it have an explanation?"

"It does. The explanation is collective trauma. It is said that people after Kantō held children on their arms differently, and the masters saw this and applied it. But that is, of course, a hypothesis. No one has proved it."
"You are proving it."

"I am collecting. The exhibition in Otaru—fifty-eight dolls from private collections. There has not been anything like it since the nineties. I bought a ticket last week. For Saturday. I want to take you."
Yuri was silent.
"You pay, I accept," Nao said with a thin smile. "That is a rare gesture on my side. Take advantage."

Yuri did not smile. She set her elbow on the corner of the table, propped her forehead on her fist. That was how she did when she was thinking how to say. Nao knew that. Nao put the leek into the pot and turned the heat down a little.
"Nao."
"Yes."
"Don't go to Otaru. Not this Saturday."
Nao set the ladle in the bowl. Not at once. She turned her head to Yuri. Did not ask.
"Do not ask," said Yuri. "Please."
Nao looked at her. One second. A second.
"You are on work."
"Yes."
"It is serious."
"Yes."
"All right."

Nao turned back to the stove. Stirred. Yuri saw her cheek in profile—the cheek that did not tremble. Nao had this capacity: if someone important said do not ask, she did not ask. It was not obedience. It was trust, and Yuri knew that trust was what she was obliged to guard precisely because Nao did not ask the price of it.
"Nao."
"Yes."
"I will tell you everything. Later."
"I know."

Nao ladled rice into two small ceramic bowls. On top—one onigiri each, the ones with umeboshi that Yuri liked. She poured miso into two smaller bowls from the wooden ladle. She set everything on the low table in the corner of the room. She sat on a cushion opposite.
They did not speak for fifteen minutes.

Nao ate slowly. Yuri ate the way she always did—fast, focused, without pleasure. The onigiri was soft inside and level at the sides. Nao, among other things, shaped a good onigiri. Yuri had never said it aloud.

After supper Nao left the bowls in the sink—did not wash at once—turned off the overhead light and left only the desk lamp by the window. The same yellow circle in which Yuri, when she visited, would read the paper before sleep, and Nao would work.
Nao opened the laptop.
"I will show you three pages from my master's," she said. "Only three. I will not tire you."
"Show me."
Nao turned. On the first page there was a large photograph of one doll in a blue kimono with a bow at the waist. A porcelain face, fine. Glass eyes, dark.
Yuri looked.

"This one," said Nao, "is from the Otaru collection. Nineteen thirty-four period. Master unknown. Believed to be a private commission. The body is unusually heavy—two hundred eighty grams for a height of twenty-two centimeters. That is an anomalous ratio. As if she is held in the ground."
"How many like this in the exhibition."
"With heavy bodies—eight. With truly heavy—only this one."
"From a private collection."
"Yes. The owner's surname is not given in the catalog. Only 'private collection, Otaru.'"
Yuri was silent.

Nao turned to the second. The photograph was contemporary: a shelf in some unfamiliar interior, three dolls in a row, under soft light. The second—not porcelain, you could tell by the texture. Composite. There was no face.
"And this one?"

"This one is not from the exhibition. This is from another chapter of mine. Reconstruction of dolls to the traditional recipe, but without a face. These are being made now, in some workshops in northern Hokkaido. These are not antique—they are modern. But by an old method."
"Who makes them."
"Names not given. One workshop—in Otaru. One—in Hidaka. Another—near Asahikawa. It is not banned. It is simply rare."
"Hidaka."
"Yes."
Yuri turned her head to Nao. Nao did not notice the pause—she scrolled on.
"The third."
This was not even a page of the master's. It was a screenshot of a museum database. Nao switched to the adjacent window.

"Here is the inventory. I have access through my department. This is not public. In Otaru, in the depository, lie twelve faceless dolls from the early nineties. Recorded as donation of anonymous donor. The donor gave them in three lots: nineteen ninety-three, nineteen ninety-six, two thousand and one. Four each time."
"Nao."
"Yes."
"Let me scroll."

Nao gave way. Yuri slowly scrolled the record. Doll size—twenty-two centimeters. Material—porcelain plus wooden armature. Face—absent. Clothing—dark blue. Date of manufacture—not established. Author—not established.
Yuri scrolled to the last accession date. Two thousand and one.
Two thousand and two—fire at the archive of the Otaru administration.
She set the laptop on its side. Did not close.
"Nao."
"Yes."
"Who runs this database."
"One senior curator. Yamamoto. He is sixty-three. He knows me. Well disposed."
"Do not ask him anything extra."
"I won't."
"I am not joking."
"Yuri—" Nao for the first time said her name, without "-nēsan," "—I know. I hear you."
Yuri nodded.
Nao closed the laptop.

Yuri sat in the yellow circle of the desk lamp and thought of one thing she did not intend to say aloud, not today or ever in front of Nao: that twenty-two centimeters, two hundred eighty grams, a dark-blue kimono, and an absent face—that is exactly the figure Kurosawa-san Yukio kept on his kitchen sill from that winter. He had taken it from Toshi's hut and he did not know himself why.
He had not thrown it out in two years.

She had begun then to understand that Kurosawa had a life before her—not one life, but several, layered one over the other, like the transparent films of an old slide projector, she was thinking now, as she wiped her hands on the towel in the corner of the kitchen. Nao in the other room was laying out the guest futon—Yuri could hear the sound of her movements through the thin partition.

She remembered one winter night—after Ogawa's death—when Kurosawa had been sitting in his office on the small settee and did not want to go home, and she had brought him coffee from the corridor vending machine, and had sat on the settee opposite, and he had been silent, and silent, and silent, and then said, without lifting his head:

p.emphasis: "I had a brother. I did not tell you about him. He died six years ago. I thought so then."

section.p: Yuri had not asked and now? then. She took her coffee and drank, and let him go on.

Kurosawa had not gone on then. He had gone on a week later. He had told her about Otaru in two thousand and five, when he had gone on his father's case—and when his elder brother Ren was already teaching at an art school—and how Ren, in the conversation in a café, had said something about one person who knows too much, and how Kurosawa had not caught the name. Had not thought of it for twenty-two years. Had not held it as information.

He was telling me that then not because, Yuri thought, it made things easier for him. He was telling me because he knew: I had to know. I am his partner. I have to know why he does not sleep at three in the morning. He was not making me his listener—he was making me his witness. And that is different.

She came back from the memory when Nao came into the kitchen, took a glass from the sill, poured water from the kettle, and went silently back to the room. Yuri noticed that Nao had not asked whether Yuri would sleep—Nao knew Yuri would sleep—and had not asked whether Yuri would turn off the light in the kitchen—Nao knew Yuri would.
The package came thirty minutes later.

The Yamato courier, in a black cap, quietly, without a knock, left a small cardboard box by the door and went. Yuri met him in the corridor, signed, took the box. The name on the slip—"Sasaki Yuri, temporary address." Sender—"Ayano, Niigata clinic, hand delivery." Stamp—Niigata, that same evening. Time—seventeen forty-two.
Ayano the nurse. From the Niigata clinic. From the fall in Ashibetsu. Now—here.

Yuri did not go into the room to Nao. She went into the bathroom, closed the door behind her—Nao would hear the water in the pipe and think that her sister was washing her hands after the road—and opened the box on the lid of the laundry basket.
A small porcelain ichimatsu-ningyō. Twenty-two centimeters. Two hundred eighty grams by weight—she put it on her palm; she felt the weight. Dark blue kimono with a thin white edge. Face—none.
Inside—a small piece of paper, folded in two. Handwriting thin, calm, female.
Yuri stood over the basket for a minute. She did not move.

Then she folded the paper, put it into the inner pocket of her jacket, the one she had come in. She wrapped the doll in the same paper wrapping in which it had arrived, and put it back in the box. The box—under the sink, behind the basket. Nao did not look there.
Yuri turned off the light in the bathroom and went out.
Nao from the room:
"Yuri, the futon is ready."
"Thank you."
"I put out water for you."
"Thank you."

Yuri went into the room. Nao was already lying on her side, shoulder covered by the blanket, reading a book—small, paper, from a shop in Asakusa she liked. Yuri sat on the futon on the other side of the room. She took off her coat. She set the holster on the low chest.
Nao looked at her once. Saw the holster.
"You have a weapon."
"Yes."
"Yuri."
"Nao. Do not ask."
Nao nodded. Went back to the book.
Yuri lay down. She looked at the ceiling—the ceiling was white, with one stain from a leaking roof—and heard Nao turn a page. One—then a minute later a second.
Yuri set the phone on the nightstand beside her, silent, with vibration on. She looked at the screen for one second—expecting something—and expected nothing in particular.
The doll in the bathroom she decided to take with her to Sapporo in the morning. Not to throw away. To show Kurosawa after the lighthouse. Not sooner.
Nao closed the book five minutes later. Turned off the light on her side.
"Nao."
"Yes."
"You are a good onigiri master."
Nao laughed quietly in the dark. One short sound.
"I know," she said.
Yuri closed her eyes.

p.emphasis: "It can be put together only at the lighthouse."

section.subtitle: Chapter Twelve
section.p: The letter lay on the kitchen sill.

Yukio did not notice it at once—he had come home from work at twenty fifty, taken off his coat, set the thermos on the sideboard—and then, when he was going to the kettle, he saw the white corner between the curtain and the glass. The curtain shifted slightly in the draft from the fanlight—and the corner emerged, and stayed standing. Yukio had not closed the window earlier. Whoever had placed the letter knew there would be no need to lock behind him.

He stood for two seconds, looking. Then he pulled a latex glove from the inside pocket of the coat still hanging on the chair. He took the envelope with two fingers—by the corner—and carried it to the kitchen table. He raised the shade of the desk lamp. One lamp, the way he liked it when he ate.
The envelope—plain, white. No stamp. No postage. No address written. Only one word in the middle, in pencil, small: "Kurosawa." The same hand that had been on the sheet from Erimo.

Yukio laid the glove on the other side and looked at the kitchen clock. Twenty-one oh two. He allowed himself ten seconds of silence—not because he was hesitating, but because he wanted to remember what he had done in those ten seconds—and then he opened the envelope.
Inside—two things.

The first—a photograph. Old, black and white, with serrated edges as they used to be trimmed by lab scissors. The Erimo lighthouse, shot from the sea, from a boat, at a small distance—three hundred meters—in a light that was either very early or very late. The rotating optic on the drawing of the lighthouse was not on. No people on the platform. No gulls in the sky. Only the concrete of the tower and a small rock behind. By the grain of the film—sixties, with certainty. By the type of paper—Fuji of that time, lab print. On the back—no inscription.

The second—a thin strip of paper cut from something larger. Width—about two and a half centimeters. Length—twelve. Printed on it in an old machine typeface, without punctuation, three words and two numbers:

p.strong: "Seven days. One. Or two. No more."

section.p: Yukio laid the strip on the corner of the table, parallel to the photograph. He looked. He did not move anything. He did not read a second time—once was enough.
Then he reached for the phone.
One ring. Two. On the third Sasaki picked up.
"Kurosawa-san."
The tone of her voice was the one with which a person answers a call after nine in the evening: quiet, ready.
"Sasaki-san. Are you still in Sapporo?"
"I came back at six. I have been home."
"Come."
The pause was short. Exactly one breath.
"I'm on my way."

He put down the phone. Did not say anything more. He knew she would not ask aloud. He knew she would come in forty minutes—Sasaki's apartment was in Higashi-ku, two bridges and one overpass away, and she drove evenly and quickly.
Yukio returned to the table.

He set beside the photograph of Erimo another—from the inside pocket of his coat. The one he had carried these last six weeks and had not shown to Sasaki or to Kenji: a small cut-out fragment from the old school album of Otaru, which Endo had handed him before leaving for Tokyo. In the photo—the class of the children's home in nineteen seventy-five. Back row, fourth from the left—Yoshida Hiro, thirteen years old, thin, with a shaven head (for some childish reason, not by tradition). His face clear. His gaze straight.
Yukio set this photograph to the left of the lighthouse.

Then he took from the side pocket a second—from the same batch of Endo's. Misako Yoshida, eighth class, nineteen seventy. A girl with two small braids. Taken two weeks before her death. Yukio had not known that. He knew only one thing: the face was the same as her brother's—and not the same; the cheekbone the same, the lips different; he now knew they were twins, and he saw in that face a trait of Yoshida's—but so far he could not find, exactly, which. He had kept this photo in his coat for no reason—he could not throw it out.
To the right of the Erimo lighthouse he set the sheet "Kurosawa" from the eighth column. The same one. The one that had brought him here.

Further—three contemporary photographs: —Kurosawa Ren, two thousand and sixteen, at Chitose airport, laughing (the same one that stood on the desk in his home office); —Kurosawa Ayano, Ren's daughter, twenty years old, from the Niigata passport system, taken in December two years ago; —One small porcelain figure without a face—a digital photograph, taken by Yukio on his phone in his kitchen last week, when he had for the second time in half a year taken it from the sill and turned it over to see if there was a maker's stamp on the bottom. There was none.

The eighth photograph—was not a photograph. It was one sheet from Kenji: a list of four firms from their map, now widened by one row—"Yuki-Kōgei LLC—Kamishiroi deed 2010—signature of a dead director." Yukio added it to the right of the others.
Eight elements. A rectangle on the table. Like a tarot layout, like a mosaic, like—it turned out in the pit of his stomach when he looked at it from above—both at once.

He stepped back one pace. Pulled out from under the sink a stool, set it by the kitchen window, sat. He drank cold tea from a glass that had stood there since morning. Not hungry. Did not want to move his hand.
He knew he knew a lot. He knew he lacked one thing.
Sasaki arrived thirty-six minutes later.

She had a key—Yukio had given her one back in November, after the night when he had caught cold and she had brought a doctor at four in the morning—and she came in without knocking. He heard the lock turn—and heard the front door close behind her—and heard her take off her shoes and set them down neatly—and walk down the corridor to the kitchen without hurry.
Yukio did not stand.
Sasaki came into the kitchen.

She saw the table before she saw him. She stood three seconds—exactly the pause with which people begin to understand when they are shown not a separate scene but a laid-out game. Then she set her bag on the corner of a chair. Did not take off her coat. Did not take off her scarf.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
He indicated the envelope with the corner of his chin.

Sasaki came closer. She took—she had gloves too, she pulled them from the side pocket of the coat and put them on—the photograph of Erimo. Looked. Did not ask. Then put it down. Took the strip with the words. Read. Put it down.
"Seven days."
"Yes."
"One. Or two. No more."
"Yes."

Sasaki looked at the table. Her gaze went left, then up, then right, the way the gaze of a person who has been trained to read a crime scene systematically moves. Yukio noticed she had switched off one extra emotion—the one she had had at the entryway—and was now working.
"Yoshida," she said. "Misako. Erimo. The sheet 'Kurosawa.' Ren. Ayano-the-daughter. The figure. Yuki-Kōgei."
"Yes."
"Eight."
"Eight."
Sasaki slowly nodded. Then dropped onto the chair opposite him. Did not take off her coat. Did not take off her scarf. The way one sits down when one has come not as a guest but on the job.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I don't know how to put this into one picture."
Yukio was silent.

He did not notice that he had said the same thing he had been about to say—but she said it first, with the even clarity with which she had spoken about Nao in the winter office five months after Ashibetsu. Yukio only repeated aloud:
"I don't know how to put them into one picture."
Sasaki raised her eyes at him.
"It can be put together only at the lighthouse."

Yukio did not answer at once. He looked at the table. At the strip with four phrases. At the photograph of Erimo, the sixties, taken from the sea, from a boat, at the distance from which a person shoots who is going to sail back. Whoever had taken this photograph—perhaps Yoshida himself, at thirteen or fourteen—had sat in a boat and looked at the lighthouse knowing he would come here at seventy to call his man here.
He had known it already then.
"Yes," said Yukio. "It can be put together only there."
Sasaki nodded.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"We do not ask Tanaka-san for permission."
"No."
"We do not write an official route plan."
"No."
"We do not take a team."
"No."
"We take only the two of us."
"Yes."

Yukio noticed that on "only the two of us" she had for a second covered with her voice the pause in which she might have added "and Kenji." She had not added. Because she already knew that Kenji would not go. Kenji had to hold the center while they were on the periphery. That was how this team had always worked, from the first day.
Sasaki set her fingers on the strip with "seven days."
"The seventh day is the seventh of August."
"Yes."
"We leave Tuesday morning."
"Tuesday morning."
"The drive—five hours, with a stop. Arrival at the dawn of Wednesday."
"Yes."
"That is 'one' day of the seven. We enter the lighthouse on 'one.' We will not stay there longer."
"Yes."
Sasaki nodded.

Yukio for the first time since she came in noticed that she was holding, in her left hand under the coat, the edge of something hard. The holster. She had not taken it off, because she was not going to sit long.
"Sasaki-san."
"Yes."
"Thank you for coming without asking."
"Not 'thank you.' It is simply work."
"All the same."
Sasaki was silent.

Yukio turned back to the table. He had wanted to ask one thing—about Nao, about the trip to Niigata, about that one thing she had had to check with her hands. He did not ask. He knew: if Sasaki had wanted to say aloud, she would have. She had not—so she was keeping it, and had reason to keep it. He was her partner. He would not draw out of her what she was not ready to place.
He looked at her briefly. Sasaki held the gaze.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"You are not showing me something."
Yukio did not answer at once. Then:
"You are not showing me something either."
Sasaki nodded.
"Then," she said, "after the lighthouse we will each put one more thing on the table."
"Agreed."
"Agreed."

Yukio took from the lower drawer of the chest under the sill a small cardboard box. Inside—three postal envelopes in which he kept documents prepared just in case. In the first—a will (drawn up a year ago at the Maruyama notary's office, short: apartment—to his aunt Kiyoko, photo archive—Endo, documents—Sasaki, cash—a charitable fund for the families of those whose loved ones did not come back from the taiga). In the second—pension data and the notary's phone. In the third—one sealed letter addressed to "Kurosawa Ayano, Niigata," no stamp. Yukio had never shown it to anyone. He had written it in January two years ago, when he had come back from Ashibetsu and could not sleep for two months.

He put all three envelopes back into the box. Did not take them out. Did not show them. But set the box in a visible place, on the upper shelf above the sink, on the right side—so that Sasaki, if needed, would know where to look.
Sasaki noticed the movement. Did not say anything.
"All right," she said. "I'll go."
"Yes."
"I'll come by tomorrow at seven."
"All right."
She stood.
Yukio stood too. They did not shake hands. That was not their custom. Sasaki went to the door. In the corridor—she put on her shoes, neatly again—and set her hand on the door handle.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I have one thing I must show you. Not today. In the car on the way."
"All right."
"Good night."
"Good night."
She went out.
Yukio heard the front door close behind her. Then—heard steps along the corridor. Then—the entry doors open and close. Then—her car start below, on the street, and go.
He came back into the kitchen. He stood over the table. He looked at the eight elements.
He knew there would not be a ninth.
He knew that the ninth had to become himself.

section.subtitle: Chapter Thirteen
section.p: Monday. Twenty-seven hours before departure. Yukio called Kenji into his office at eight in the morning—not seven forty, as usual—and not from the corridor but through the phone, because he did not want Tanaka Ryosuke behind the glass to see him get up in his booth and walk to Kenji's corner desk. Tanaka had noted every route Yukio took inside the unit over two weeks of observation; he knew which corner was five minutes without him, which was thirty seconds. So Yukio had rebuilt the routes.
Kenji came in a black hoodie, laptop under one arm, a can of Boss Coffee in his left hand. Miso in the carrier stayed at his own desk—Miso was sleeping today.
Yukio closed the office door. Not the blinds.
"Sit."
Kenji sat on the visitor chair to the right. Set the laptop on the corner of the desk. Did not open it.
"Kenji-kun."
"Yes."
"You are staying."
Kenji did not react at once. He, as always, took five seconds—not from not understanding, but from some inner processor Yukio had noticed a year ago. Then he nodded. Once.
"I knew you would say that."
"Keep contact with both Ayanos, with Otaru, with Endo, with Tanaka."

"With the two Ayanos—differently. With Ayano-the-nurse—I watch the mailbox at Niigata-Minami-Kunigi that appeared at hers on the seventeenth. I did not put a picket, that is not permitted, but there is a camera across the street, I have access through the housing complex. I know her schedule through Friday. With Kurosawa Ayano, your brother's daughter—I do not watch and will not. That is not my line. If needed—either Sasaki-san or you speak with her."
"Yes."

"With Otaru—Yasuko-san. I have her son's phone, he lives in Sapporo. He says she is mostly home, goes to the supermarket on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Yoshida has not visited her in the last six months. The son knows this because the mother said so herself."
Yukio nodded. That was new.
"With Endo—I passed it last night. She will make a call from Tokyo on Friday. Tanaka will not know about it."
"With Tanaka?"

"With Tanaka I keep formal contact. I give him reports on methodological support. Five pages a day, ten on Friday. He does not read more than half. He reads only when there is a number that seems to him wrong. I give correct numbers."
Yukio smiled slightly.
"You have learned to handle him."
"He underestimates me. That works both ways."
"Yes."
A pause.
Kenji opened the Boss Coffee can. Took one short swallow. Set it back on the corner.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"This is a trap."
"I know."

"Yoshida is waiting for you at the lighthouse. Not Yoshida—whoever he will call himself. He is there alone, or almost alone. He wants a conversation. He does not want shooting. But he has one exit and one insurance, and we do not know which."
"I know."
"Then why go."
Yukio did not answer at once. He knew the answer. He did not like to say it aloud, because it sounded simpler than it was.
"Because he said so."
Kenji was silent.
"Kurosawa-san," he said after a minute, "I know you know this. But I have to say."
"Say."

"If at the lighthouse you remain without Sasaki-san or without yourself, the team falls. Not because we do nothing without you—but because we built this operation from you. Endo has Tokyo, I have this desk, Sasaki—a sister. Each of us is held by something of our own. But what holds us together is you. If you are not there—Sasaki-san will pick up my half, I will pick up hers. But that is another team, and it will work differently."
Yukio nodded.
"I know, Kenji-kun."
"Then," said Kenji, "let me hand you one thing."
He opened the laptop. Took from the inner pocket of the hoodie a small gray flash drive. USB type A. Unmarked.
Set it before Yukio.

"Here is everything I have for six weeks. Forty-seven Yoshidas. Career sheets. Last known addresses. Scans of registries. Medical exams where they exist. Pensions, where there is half of it. Transcripts of phone calls I could listen to—that is sixteen of the forty-seven. Nothing confirmed. Not one Yoshida of these forty-seven is the one we are looking for—I say that responsibly. None of them."
Yukio looked at the flash drive. Did not take it at once.
"None."

"None," said Kenji. "I checked. Not the age, not the geography, not the year in Otaru, not the profile. I lay the forty-seven as cover. If Tanaka asks—I show him this flash drive. He will read for three days and find nothing, because there is nothing there. This is my camouflage."
"And the real Yoshida," said Yukio, "is not among the forty-seven."

"Not among the forty-seven. He is among the non-Yoshidas. That is—Yoshida with an archive entry release from post for reasons of health, 2019, but with no pension trail in Hokkaido—did not make it through my first filter—I saw him yesterday in a passive sheet where the Yoshidas were not entered because they are formally not active. I have him. Not yet confirmed—I need the pension registries 1998–2019, which come in Wednesday morning—but I have him."
"Yoshida Hiro," said Yukio quietly.
"I will not say," said Kenji. "Not today. Not until there is pension confirmation. I do not give you names without confirmation, Kurosawa-san. That is what you taught."
Yukio nodded. He looked at the USB for a minute.
"Kenji-kun."
"Yes."
"Continue through the night."
"I will continue through the night."

"On Wednesday morning," said Yukio, "when the pensions come in, you write an SMS to Sasaki-san. Not to me. My phone is in a state the Doll Maker may be able to track. You write to Sasaki-san on her personal number, not the work one, with confirmation or denial. Three words is enough."
"Understood."
"You write at four in the morning."
"At four I will already be asleep. The pension registries come in at three forty."
"So much the better. Do not write from a code we use in the team. Do not write key names. Only what is needed."
"Understood."

Yukio took the USB. Did not put it in his pocket—put it in the central drawer of his desk, locked it, put the key in his wallet, the wallet into the inside pocket of his coat—the one he would go out with on Tuesday morning.
"Kenji-kun."
"Yes."
"You did this alone for six weeks."
"Alone."
"I have not thanked you aloud once."
"There was no need."
"Thank you, Kenji-san."
A pause.

Kenji lifted his head. He did not look Yukio in the eye fully—he had no such habit—he looked at the corner of the desk beyond the interlocutor's shoulder, where Yukio had a small porcelain figure he had brought into the office from the apartment last month. But this time—after "san"—he raised his gaze for one second to the bridge of Yukio's nose. Not into the eyes. At the bridge of the nose.
One second—and back.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I have prepared one more thing for you," said Kenji. "For the evening."
"Which."

"My number. Direct, not through the switchboard. From this moment—twenty-four seven. If at the lighthouse you have a chance to dial one digit—dial one. Automatic call to Erimo fire station through my server. That is a fifteen-minute delay, but faster than without it. I tested it."
"All right."
"And one more."
"Yes."
"The holster. You have it on your right. I know you carry one spare magazine. Take two. Not because you will need the second, but because I ask you. One magazine—by protocol, two—by me."
Yukio looked at him.
"All right, Kenji-kun. Two."
"Thank you."
Kenji closed the laptop. Took the Boss Coffee can in his palm. Stood. Then, still not moving:
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"If at the lighthouse it happens that you come back without Sasaki-san."
Yukio did not answer.
"I want," said Kenji, "you to know. She went not because you took her. She went because she chose. That is different."
Yukio nodded.
"I know, Kenji-kun."
"All right."
Kenji stood up. Walked to the door. On the threshold—he turned briefly.
"And," he said, "if you both come back—I am ordering both of you sushi-maki with tuna from Kyoto. The shop by the station you both like. That is my promise."
Yukio smiled at the corner of his mouth—the rare movement Kenji had already seen once or twice a year.
"All right."
Kenji went out.

Yukio remained at the desk. For a minute he did not move. Then he took out of the inside pocket of his wallet a small piece of paper—a receipt from the Maruyama notary's office, received a year ago—unfolded it, laid it before him, looked at it for one second.
He did not tear it. Folded it in two. Put it back in the wallet.

Outside the window the August morning was going on—the cicadas had not yet started—and Yukio thought about that one second when Kenji had raised his gaze to the bridge of his nose—not to the eyes—and said san back to him.
He knew Kenji would remember that.
He knew he would remember it too.

p.emphasis: "If something goes wrong—say I decided myself."

section.subtitle: Chapter Fourteen
section.p: They left at twelve forty-five in the morning.

Sasaki at the wheel. Yukio in the passenger seat. The car—a dark gray Nissan Skyline from the administrative pool, whose plate Kenji had reissued to a different series that morning—not for evasion, but through a standard documentary procedure—so that patrols on the road, checking against the database, would see the series "service, on rotation," and not "Missing Persons unit." Evasion of the Doll Maker's number cameras, if they existed—Kenji did not know whether they did.

The route—the Dōshin Expressway to Chitose, then Erimo highway south. Five hours with one intermediate stop. Arrival—around five forty in the morning. Sunrise in these August days—at four forty-five. That is, they would arrive by daylight.
Yukio had planned it that way. He was not going to walk into the lighthouse at night. He needed daylight to see a person.
For three hours they did not speak.

Sasaki drove evenly, holding a steady ninety—the speed at which she would not attract the attention of speed cameras or patrols on the night Dōshin. She had a habit of keeping her left hand in the lower corner of the wheel and her right on the shift lever—the way old-school detectives had done—and Yukio had never asked where she got it. She did not drink coffee on the road. Did not listen to the radio.

Yukio looked out the window. Forest on both sides of the road—dark, tall, in places lit through by the moon. Once a small billboard from some Asahikawa sanatorium flashed past—a red crane on blue. Yukio remembered that crane from childhood. He had thought then it meant the sanatorium was good. He did not know why he still thought so.

At four oh eight they pulled off at a Cosmo filling station by the Hidaka-Yūbari pass. They filled up. Yukio went out for coffee to the thin metal booth in which two vending machines stood—one for hot drinks, one for cold. He bought two. One—with milk, for Sasaki; one—black, for himself. Sasaki stood by the car. Did not go into the booth.
Yukio came out and handed her a cup. She took it.
They drank standing. Coffee from the machine was not good—it had never been good on this stretch of road—but it was warm. That was enough.

The sky to the east was starting to unfold—a thin strip of gray over the dark blue—and Yukio saw the strip through Sasaki's silhouette, standing to his left, with coffee in her right hand, in a North Face down jacket, with short-cropped dark hair—Sasaki had not changed in two years, and Yukio had not noticed until this moment.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I have a sister."
"I know."

"Nao. Twenty-four. Niigata master's, art history. Lives alone in Minami-Shiomi, third floor, corner of the building. Parents in Komagata—that is Niigata prefecture—not close to Nao, but in the same prefecture. They come see her once every two months."
"Yes."
"I want to tell you," Sasaki set the cup on the top of the fuel pump, slowly, "if something goes wrong—you will find her. Tell her I decided myself."
Yukio did not look at her. He was looking at the strip of sky.
"I will tell her."
"Thank you."

Sasaki did not add anything. Did not explain what something wrong meant—because both knew—and did not explain why decided myself—because both knew that too. Between them it was not work and not friendship. It was something between a work oath and something they had never named, because they had no word for it.
Yukio slowly finished the coffee. He crumpled the cup in his palm. Threw it into the bin by the booth. Sasaki threw hers as well.
"All right," said Yukio. "Fifteen minutes."
"Fifteen."
They got into the car.

Erimo Highway was narrower than the Dōshin. In places two-lane, with an interrupted line. On the right—forest, tall cedar and larch, which Kita-Michi had once transported into the network. Yukio thought of that and did not think of it at the same time.

At five oh two they passed a small Shinto torii on the shoulder—old, with peeled red paint—with the inscription "Kamishiroi-mura" on the side post. Two hundred meters further, an exit into a small village where five years ago the ryokan Kamishiroi had been. Sasaki held the right turn. Yukio in the side-view mirror saw her cheek in profile—the same cheek that had not trembled at Nao's in Niigata—and thought that now, with that same look, she was passing the place where it all began.
He did not say it aloud. She did not either.
Fifteen minutes of silence.

At five twenty-seven Sasaki slowed at the entrance to Samani. The town was asleep. On the main street—yellow lamps, three of ten lit. Yukio noticed the ENEOS station they had driven past ten years ago on a case still stood in the same place, with the same sign and the same small rubber hose insufficiently coiled at the second pump.
Beyond Samani—a narrow road up, to the cape.

Sasaki reduced speed to forty. The road—with turns, with paint worn away in places. The wind—already different. Yukio heard it through the seal of the window—that low humming with which the Atlantic wind on Erimo turned into the other, from the Kurils side.
At five forty they came to the last turn. The lighthouse was beyond it, three hundred meters ahead, over a low ridge.
Sasaki stopped the car.
She switched off the headlights. But not the engine—she left it on idle—so all electrics would work, and so it could be killed instantly.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Five more minutes."
"Yes."

Yukio took from the inside pocket of his coat the elastic band in which he carried the second magazine, and slipped it into the right pocket of his trousers—easily reachable, as Kenji had promised. The main magazine was in the holster. He checked the safety—on.
Sasaki kept both hands on the wheel. Did not move.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Thank you for taking me."
Yukio was silent.
"Not for the trip," said Sasaki. "For everything."

Yukio turned to her. He looked not into her eyes—but at the spot under her right eye, at the mark where she used to put a cosmetic dot when she did not have one—that is, at a neutral place on her face she knew—and said:
"You are not 'taken,' Sasaki-san. You are—a partner."
Sasaki nodded. Once.

Then she opened the glove compartment. She pulled out a small black flashlight—tactical, narrow beam, battery for nine hours. She set it between the seats. Pulled out a second—the same—set it there too.
"One for you, one for me."
"Yes."
"We go in together," said Sasaki. "We come out together."
"Yes."

Yukio nodded. He took from the breast pocket a small card—a slip with the Erimo fire station's phone number and one number of Kenji's—and set it on the dashboard, under the sun visor. If something happened to him, Sasaki-san would know what to dial.
Sasaki did not say anything. But noticed.

She pulled from the inner pocket of her jacket a thin strip of paper and set it under the same visor, on the right side. On the paper—in an even hand: "Sasaki Nao, Niigata, Minami-Shiomi 3-14-2, apt. 306, +81 25 2XX XXXX. Key at the downstairs neighbor's, Tanaba-san."
Yukio nodded.

Then she pulled from the same pocket a small bundle—of soft paper, the size of a child's fist—and set it on the dashboard next to the slip. She did not explain. Yukio did not ask. He knew: the same "one thing" she had spoken of in his kitchen two days ago. Later. If they came back. If not—he would find it himself.
"All right," said Sasaki. "Let's go."
She turned the key. Turned the headlights to low. Put it into gear.
The car rolled to the last turn.

Above Cape Erimo the sky was already gray. Gray with that thin pink at the very eastern edge—the color of blood dissolved in water—which Yukio had once seen on a Kuroshio children's excursion steamer at seven, and had thought it was not a color but a mistake of the sky.
He held the holster with his right hand—the sleeve did not press on it—and thought of one second, in which he would say to someone at the lighthouse you.
Sasaki parked the car behind a low ridge, in a blind zone from the sea. She killed the engine.
The wind came into the car from below, through the crack of the door. It was loud.
Sasaki looked at him once. She did not speak.
Yukio nodded.
They opened the doors at the same time.

section.subtitle: Chapter Fifteen

p.emphasis: The Abe Clinic stood on the corner of Higashi-Sanchōme in Niigata—a small private general-practice clinic on the ground floor of a five-story residential building from the sixties. Three examination rooms, one reception, one pharmacy behind double doors.
Tuesday, October, two thousand and three. Autumn came early that year.

Michiko opened the pharmacy at seven ten. The key on a soft leather cord under her uniform white blouse. Abe-sensei had entrusted her with this key since April. No one else on the junior staff had such a key.
Checked the expense log. Locked the door. The lock clicked.
At eight forty-three Abe-sensei came out of the first examination room into the corridor.
"He didn't say. Says he's known you a long time. In the waiting room."
Michiko looked at the appointment log. Next patient—nine fifteen. Thirty minutes.
She took off her coat, straightened the collar of her blouse, went out to the waiting room.

A man in a gray suit sat by the window. Forty-one years old—she could tell by the hair: short, dark, with the first threads of gray at the temples. A worn face. Thin lips. Long fingers rested on his knees, backs up.
She recognized the voice before the face.

section.p: He placed a copy of the Coastal Herald of Niigata on the low table. Did not move it—only placed it.

p.emphasis: The words came evenly. She had not prepared them. They had waited inside her since the autumn when she was seven years old, when Jindai-en was her home.
Yoshida nodded. Looked at her calmly.
"I need the key to the pharmacy," he said. "Once a quarter. Propofol. Two twenty-milliliter ampoules. Not from the batch used to write off invasive sedatives. You'll understand which ones to take."
"I'll come myself. Or a person I send. You'll know them by one word."

section.p: "They'll say Memuro."
"And one name," he said. "When they ask you, you'll say Ayano."

p.emphasis: He repeated the name as if placing it in her palm—and she took it.
Yoshida stood. Straightened his jacket with two motions along the edges, from bottom to top—and picked up a small brown bag from the floor. Michiko had not seen it when she came in.
"Goodbye," he said. Did not add a name.

The clinic door clicked shut behind him. Through the glass of the waiting room she saw his back—gray suit in a thin rain—and how he opened a small black umbrella, and how he disappeared around the corner of Higashi-Sanchōme toward the bus stop on Funagaya.
Then she stood. Returned to the pharmacy. Opened the lock. Took the inventory log from the shelf.

"Propofol—20 ml, ampoule." Remaining today—forty ampoules. Written off in October—three. Each with a batch number, with the clinic's internal series number. She ran her finger down the column of numbers. Reached the ninth from the bottom: the batch from the second-to-last restocking, clinic number three hundred forty-five, series V. Ampoules from this batch were written off irregularly. Last write-off—September. Before that—July. Before that—May.
These were the ampoules whose write-off troubled no one.
She closed the log. Locked the pharmacy.

At nine forty-seven she took a spare badge from the lower drawer of her desk—the one that had been lying in a plastic sleeve since April, made at her request at the workshop across the road—and swapped the badge on her chest.
On the new badge, in white kanji on dark blue plastic, was one name.
No one at the clinic noticed.

Michiko walked to reception, took the card for the next appointment—a woman of forty-three, elevated blood pressure—and called the patient in her usual tone, the same voice with which she had called patients three years running.
The voice did not change either.
Only on the badge under her throat was a different name now, and the clinic did not notice, and Niigata did not notice—and Michiko, from this morning on, no longer wore her own.

section.subtitle: Chapter Sixteen
section.p: They arrived ten minutes before dawn.

The last five kilometers of road to the cape ran along a narrow asphalt switchback that held the edge of the cliff on the seaward side and went up and down without dividing lines. Sasaki drove slowly—forty-two kilometers per hour—with the caution people in Hokkaido use when they know a road only from traffic-accident reports, not from their own driving. Kurosawa sat to the right. He looked through the side glass. The wind held the car with a short pressure from the side—steady, not in gusts. The speedometer showed twenty-two meters per second of wind. Higher it could not read.

Sasaki cut the headlights of the Corolla three hundred meters short of the lighthouse—on the brief straight where the road came out from behind the last outcrop of the cliff and spilled onto the plateau—and drove the rest of the way on running lights. The sky to the east was beginning to pull away from black—that slow transition that came early over Erimo—and the headlights no longer had a function.

The parking pad by the lighthouse was empty. Three concrete slabs, gravel, a metal post with a placard "Erimo-misaki. Autonomous lighting since 2013." The post leaned slightly to the north. Beyond the post—the sea. Sasaki parked the car under the east wall of the keeper's cottage, on the side the wind could not reach.
The clock on the dashboard read five seventeen.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"I go first."
"No. Together."
She did not argue.

They got out of the car one at a time—Sasaki on the driver's side, Kurosawa on the passenger's. She held her door with a hand so it would not be torn out. Kurosawa stepped out—the wind took him from the sea side—and thought, briefly, that twenty-three meters per second could be held, but had to be held. He buttoned his coat to the top. Raised the collar.
"I'm behind you," Sasaki said quietly. "One minute."
Kurosawa nodded. Walked to the door of the cottage. Kept his back straight. Right hand on the holster. Did not look back.
Sasaki lingered by the car.

Thirty seconds. She closed the driver's door—pressed with her shoulder so the lock caught evenly—and kept her palm on the handle another half second. The wind held her down jacket from the side. She did not move.
In that second the phone in the inner pocket of her jacket vibrated once, short.
She took it out. One glance at the screen.

p.strong: "Pension registry gave a match. Yoshida Hiro 1962, director of Jindai-en Otaru 1998–2019. Cleaner Yasuko-san, 78, alive. It's him."

section.p: Kenji. Time—five eighteen. He had worked through the night, she knew.

Sasaki stood with the phone in her hand. Three seconds. Inside those three seconds two things held in her. One: catch up to Kurosawa—he was still fifteen meters from the door—and say it aloud. Two: not catch up.
She knew which she would choose.

Yoshida was not the kind who meets an investigator with a ready-made name. Yoshida was the kind who gives the name himself. If Kurosawa walked into the lighthouse with Yoshida's name on his lips, he would take Yoshida's moment from him—and Yoshida would do something else, something she could not predict. Sasaki was not ready to take Yoshida's moment from him. Not here. Not today.
She would play the name after.
Sasaki put the phone in the side pocket—not the inner one—so she could pull it out with one motion when it would be needed. Walked after Kurosawa.
The gravel creaked under her boots. The wind held its note from the sea side.
She caught up to him at the door.
They walked to the tower.

The Erimo-Misaki lighthouse, rebuilt in the fifties after the typhoon, stood at the very edge of the plateau—a round stone tower forty meters high, with rotating optics at the top and a gray concrete base at the bottom. Last painted in two thousand. The paint had come off in patches on the sea side. North of the tower stood the former keeper's cottage—a squat building with two windows, faced with gray stone, roofed with sheet copper that had darkened to black.
The cottage door—metal—was not locked.

Kurosawa saw this from twenty meters out. The spring of the upper lock was set half a turn, the way doors are set by people who know guests are being waited for inside. He did not tell Sasaki. She did not tell him either.
They approached from different sides. Sasaki raised her hand to the holster—and did not draw. Kurosawa gave her a sign with his palm turned down: not yet. She nodded.
He opened the door with his shoulder.

The wind came in ahead of him. Went through the entry hall, knocked a small tin can off the shelf on the left—it struck the concrete and rolled—and quieted somewhere in the depth of the two rooms. Kurosawa stepped in after it.

He did not use his flashlight. Five minutes before dawn the entry hall was already gray enough to see the walls. The shelf on the left, empty. The clothes hook on the right, empty. Further—two doorways. The right led to the first room. The left—to a corridor to the second.
Sasaki came in after him.
"I take the right." Quietly. "You the left."
He did not argue. It was correct—he had the side on which a promise was being awaited.
The first room was empty.

He saw it from the threshold. Bare concrete walls, plank floor, one curtained window on the sea side, an old tin heater in the corner, disconnected since twenty-thirteen. On the floor—a thin layer of dust. In the dust—no trace. No one had entered this room in the last several weeks.
He closed the door.
From the corridor Sasaki said nothing. That meant: she had nothing yet either.

He went down the corridor to the second room. It was at the far end—around a turn to the left, under the wall that gave on the sea. The door was open a hand's breadth. He pushed it with the tips of his fingers. The door yielded evenly, without a creak.
Inside a lamp was burning.

One. A small desk lamp on a low concrete pillar by the far wall. The cord ran into the wall to a socket at shoulder height. The lamp shone toward the desk—an old low wooden desk, worn to gray—and on the desk something lay.
Kurosawa stepped into the room.
It was clavicles.
Six.

They lay in a half-circle, with the convex side toward him—with that verified regularity of intervals with which things are arranged by people who have practiced arrangement for a long time. Each small, a child's. Each with a thin crack through the center, old, calcified. Each in its place—at a slight angle to its neighbor—so that the whole composition resembled an opened fan, or an unclosed ring, or an arc that waits to be closed.
He stood in the doorway. Did not step further in.
He was counting.
One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Six.

There had been nine columns on Erimo. In the eighth—the one he had taken last July—there had been one. It now lay in the department safe with the tag Erimo-8. He had not brought it. These six—not from Erimo. These six—from Memuro. Three earlier ones. Three more from those he did not know—that had not yet risen onto the map—that the Doll Maker had kept for himself longer.
He looked. Very quietly. Very long.
Then he raised his eyes to the wall behind the desk.

On the wall was one phrase. Not a phrase—one word. Written in a plain gray pencil, soft. Size—of a palm. Slight rightward slant. The strokes confident—not fast, not slow—with that barely perceptible pressure at the ends of each stroke that people use who have known this kanji from childhood and never stopped drawing it.

He did not know how to read it. The first kanji—"beauty"—that he recognized. The second—"assistant," or "from the side"—he was not sure in which reading. The third—"child." But their combination did not give him a word. Surname or name—he did not know.
He looked at the wall.
Behind him, from the corridor, Sasaki came up. Stopped by the jamb. Did not enter the room.
"Sir."
"Yes."
"On the desk—six."
"Yes."
She did not say Erimo-8 in the safe, seven together. He knew she had thought it.

Kurosawa turned back to the desk. Came two steps closer. Did not touch. Just looked at them from above. The arrangement—the intervals—the corners. The smallest clavicle was on the left, with the convex side turned toward the north window. The next in size—to its right, with the convex side turned the same way. And further—by size—to the largest.
He calculated to himself: children, from four to nine years old. Not older.

He knew that Endo, when she reached these bones, would sign exactly that. He knew this not because he knew the bone—he knew it because he knew Endo. She went around clavicles in a spiral, from the convex side—he had seen her do it in Obihiro in twenty-five—and she was silent for half a minute before writing down the year. Here she would be silent longer. Here there were six.
"Memuro was four," he said quietly. "Erimo-8 was thirteen. These six are from other years. We'll need to cross-check with the Hokkaido missing-persons registry between ninety-eight and ten."
"Yes."
"Endo will say in a week."
"She will."

Kurosawa raised his hand. Did not touch the clavicles. Ran his fingers through the air above them, ten centimeters up—the way one runs a hand over writing one does not want to smear. Then lowered his hand.
He turned back to the wall. He looked at 美佐子 longer than he had looked at the bones.

Outside the window it was beginning to grow light. The sky over the sea was slowly pulling away from black to blue—that slow transition Erimo makes early, because the sun rises here from the sea with nothing between.
