The two terns he had seen on the pier last July were now sitting on the north sill—not the same ones, of course, but their descendants, or their neighbors—and looked at the glass sideways, with that short, focused look with which gull-birds evaluate whether you have something for them in your coat.
Kurosawa saw this and did not remember it.
Sasaki took a step back from the door. Drew the phone from her inner pocket. Kurosawa saw this with his side vision and did not turn.
She did not look at the screen for a long time.
Then, quietly, she said:
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"There's an SMS. Kenji. Just sent."
Kurosawa did not turn from the wall.

He knew she had received it out there—by the car, in that minute when he went in first. He knew this by the short pause before "There's." He knew she could have spoken sooner—before he entered—and had not spoken.
"Not now," he said.
"Yes."

She put the phone back in her pocket. Did not press. He knew Sasaki never pressed—and that when she pressed, she pressed only when she thought it necessary—this was one of those constants he had carried for her in his head since January of two thousand, when she came into the department.
He looked at 美佐子 one more second.
Then dropped his eyes to the desk. The clavicles lay as they had lain.
Outside the walls of the lighthouse the wind held its note. Did not tear, did not release. Twenty-three meters per second from the southwest—the same one that had held the pier.
Kurosawa turned to her.
"Is there a door in the back wall?"
"Yes, sir. Another room. The door is closed. Not locked—I checked the handle, did not enter."
"He is here."
"Yes."
Kurosawa nodded.

He stood one more second in front of the desk. Then unbuttoned the top button of his coat, took from the inner pocket the small folded sheet of paper—the one from Erimo cape, signed with one word Kurosawa—and placed it on the desk beside the clavicles. Not on them. Beside.
He did not explain to Sasaki why.
She did not ask.
He turned toward the back wall. The door to that room was in the right corner behind the desk—old, wooden, with a brass handle.
Behind it—a step.
Not fast. Not quiet. That even step with which people walk when they know you are waiting.
The lamp on the pillar kept burning evenly.

section.subtitle: Chapter Seventeen
section.p: The door to the back room opened from within.

Not sharply, not slowly. With the motion of someone who has been holding the handle for a while, deciding when. Kurosawa heard the handle slip in its socket, the bolt come out of the mortise, the hinges creak once on the upper axis. Three sounds. Each separately.
A man stood in the opening.

Thin. Not tall—one meter seventy, thereabouts. A shaved head—not smoothly shaved, but slightly grown back, with that gray stubble sheen left by scissors, not by a razor. A worn face, without sharp features—with the kind of face that laid poorly in the memory, that a man passed with in a crowd and no one turned to look after. Dark eyes, deep, clear. Thin lips. Long fingers. On the right index finger—a small old scar under the thin skin, half a centimeter long—the kind of scar left by wood shavings during carving, when a child does not yet know how to hold a knife.

Clothing—a gray wool coat below mid-thigh, buttoned to the top, beneath it a dark gray suit jacket, and a dark sweater with a high neck. The coat was dry—not recently dried, but long dry—with that faded gray into which good English wool passes after fifteen years of wearing without cleaning. Nothing in the right hand. In the left—a small gray umbrella tube, the length of a forearm—the kind sold in stationery shops in Otaru in the eighties.
He was not holding a weapon.
Kurosawa saw this before he began to look—because he began by looking at the hands.
He was sixty-six years old. He looked older. He read as seventy-two, as a ribbon from a monastery, as a long cellarer who had kept silent more than he had spoken.
Kurosawa knew this about him now. Five minutes ago—had not known. Now knew.
Yoshida stepped over the threshold of the back room into the second. One step. Did not hurry. Closed the door behind him with his elbow—did not push it to the click, only closed it.
He stopped at a distance of three meters from the desk.

Sasaki stood half a step behind and to the left of Kurosawa. Kurosawa heard her coat brush against the doorframe when she shifted her weight. Her right hand rested on her holster. He knew this without looking.
He gave her the sign with his palm—the same one as at the entrance: not yet.
She did not take her hand off the holster. Simply waited.
Yoshida looked at Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa-san," he said quietly. "Thank you for coming."

The voice was as Toshi had described. Quiet, warm, restrained. Did not lift, did not stay silent long. That voice teachers use to set a class in place—not because they know how to speak loudly, but because they have never needed to.
Kurosawa did not answer at once.

He looked at him for a long time. He looked the way investigators look who have studied a biography by paper for many months and now for the first time see the face—and at the same time the way people look who have long carried an empty form inside them, and in this second someone puts content into it. Two things happened together. He did not separate them.

He had a first surmise about this face—the one that would be needed later, in Jindai-en—but now he did not have it, and did not have how it would turn out. Now he had before him a man in a gray coat. Now he had only what he stood with.

Then he did something he had not done in any interview across twenty-three years of service. He did not take out a notebook. He did not turn on a recorder—there was one running in his chest pocket from the first minute he entered the entry hall, and that recorder captured the conversation evenly—but Kurosawa was not thinking about it in this second. He made no gesture of fixation. He held his hands along his body. He looked. He knew—and knew evenly—that this would be the only conversation, and that the fixation of it would be himself.
"You killed him," he said.
It came before he had time to think from what place in himself he was saying it. He had not meant to open with this. He opened.
Yoshida looked at him as if a cup had been passed to him with the wrong tea poured in.
"Whom," he said.
"Ren."
Pause. In it the wind outside the walls held its note.
Yoshida blinked once—slowly—and lowered his chin. Did not object with his voice. Objected with the motion.
"No," he said. "I did not kill."
Pause.
"I preserved him."
He said it evenly. Without emphasis. The way people speak who know a phrase will pull the whole conversation after it, and do not want to spoil it by pressure.
Kurosawa did not move. He felt behind him Sasaki breathing shallowly—with the rhythm people breathe with when they are holding something at gunpoint that they do not yet intend to shoot.
"You told my mother," Kurosawa said, "that he was dead."

Yoshida lifted his gaze slowly. There was neither surprise nor reproach in it. He looked at Kurosawa the way old Japanese schoolteachers looked at a teenager who had said something aloud that did not fit the timeline—kindly—with that particular kind of kindness that never crossed into condescension.
"Your mother," he said, "was dead before I met him."
Kurosawa did not object.

He had known this before he said the first phrase. His mother had died in childbirth in seventy-seven. He had known it since he was four, from a photograph in the family album, from his father's account, who would drink and start talking about it one or two times a year—from his father's voice, which never added anything new, and from Ren's silence beside him when the father spoke. He knew this. He said the phrase for something else. He said it to see—and saw—that Yoshida would not confuse the chronology. Yoshida did not confuse it. That said something more about him than the next four minutes could have said.

In that same second he saw one more thing. Yoshida had said before I met him. Not before he was born. Not before your birth. He had said I met him—and into that phrase two things entered. First: a meeting had happened. Second: it had happened in a particular year, which Yoshida kept for himself as a meeting. Not as observation, not as contact. A meeting. That was a day Yoshida remembered and dated. That was a day Yoshida had carried across twenty-three years and placed before Kurosawa in the second room of the lighthouse on Erimo, in the morning.
Kurosawa did not know the date. He knew there would be one.
Kurosawa nodded once—small, barely perceptible.

He knew, in that same corner, that Yoshida had seen it. Yoshida saw everything Kurosawa showed, and saw a large share of what Kurosawa did not show. This came to him evenly—without satisfaction—the way it comes to people who for many years have listened to others without intending to interrupt.
"Where is he," said Kurosawa.
Yoshida held the pause.

He did not look at the wall with the word 美佐子. He did not look at the clavicles on the desk. He did not look at the sheet of paper "Kurosawa" that Kurosawa had put there a minute ago. He looked only at Kurosawa—directly—with the calm of a man who had prepared this second for twenty-three years for a person, and that person had finally arrived.
"You will find," he said.
Pause.
"If you have the strength after today."
Kurosawa did not understand at once.

He felt—with that quiet corner that knew about the future half a second before the rest of him learned it—that Yoshida had said not "if you stay in uniform," not "if you do not stop," not "if you hold up," but if you have the strength after today. The word today carried weight. The word today meant a day in which something would happen. The word today meant it had already happened in plans—Yoshida was only sharing what was known to him.
Kurosawa heard it. He did not show he had heard.

Kurosawa looked at him one more second. He felt—as a man feels the pressure of air before a storm—that Yoshida had said about today something that had not been planned to be said. In Yoshida something ran briefly for that half second—a small inward turn of the fists—and passed.
"You came here without a weapon," he said.
"Yes."
"You came without escort."
"Yes."
"You came to leave."
Yoshida smiled for the first time in the conversation. The smile was brief—corners of the mouth lifted by two millimeters—and faded. In the eyes it held longer.
"Kurosawa-san," he said, "I came for you to see me. You see me. That is all I had to do here."
"You will tell me one more thing."
"I will."
Kurosawa waited.
Yoshida looked at him one more second.
"The name on the wall," he said, "you can leave as it is. You are not reading it yet. You will read it later."
He looked briefly at the word 美佐子 for the first time—only briefly—and turned his eyes back to Kurosawa.
"It is not a trap for you," he said. "It is a record. One of mine."
"For whom."
"For a person who will no longer hear."
Kurosawa was silent.
"One clavicle in your department's safe," Yoshida said. "Six here. Two more in places I will not lead you to. Nine in all. You will return them to the families. That will be good."
Pause.

"Yamagata," he said. "The last two. Ninety-eight and ninety-three. I do not give surnames. You will get them from the archive. The families are alive—both fathers still alive—you will find them in two weeks. Give them what you no longer need to hold."
Kurosawa did not understand at once why Yoshida was saying this.

He understood half a second later. Yoshida was saying it because he no longer needed to hold it. He was handing it over the way one hands papers from one pair of hands to another when clearing a drawer.
"You will say this to a court," Kurosawa repeated.
"I will not say this to a court."
"Why."
Yoshida lowered his gaze.
"Because there will be no court."
He did not say it with defiance. He said it the way a doctor tells a patient the analysis shows something that will not be good—evenly—with that professional warmth in which there is no self-pity.
Kurosawa looked at him for a long time.
"You came to say goodbye," he said quietly.
"No."

Yoshida raised his eyes. There was no defiance in them. There was that brief shine that sometimes appears in people who have long lived with an unsaid thing inside them and in this second speak it, not thinking whether the listener will understand.
"I will say goodbye to him," he said.
Pause.

"You will see him," he added. "That is my promise. It is not for me to keep—for you. You will come and see him. I will not be with you at that. That is important. You will come alone. He is your brother. Not mine."
Kurosawa was silent.

He was not thinking. He was holding his body in the position it had stood in—heels level, weight slightly shifted onto the left foot, hands along his sides—and waited for the second to pass in which one word wanted to be said. The second passed. The word he did not say.
Kurosawa did not ask with whom. He knew. He had known from the minute Yoshida had said I preserved him.

Outside the walls of the lighthouse the wind held its note. In the small interval between him and Yoshida—across the desk with six clavicles—two people who did not move—three things stood. The word 美佐子 behind Yoshida's back. The sheet of paper "Kurosawa" under his right hand. The clavicles laid out in a half-circle.
Kurosawa looked at him half a second more. Then—because in this second it became important to him—he asked:
"Misako."
Yoshida raised his eyes.

It was the first time in the conversation Yoshida changed expression. Not in voice—in face. The corners of his eyes dropped by half a millimeter. In his right hand, in the fingers that held the gray tube—for half a second—a tremor appeared, small, the tremor with which one holds an object one has held for twenty-three years running and has forgotten one is holding.
The tremor passed.
"You remember this name," Yoshida said quietly. "That is good."
"I do not remember it. I read it from your wall."
"You read it."
Yoshida looked at the word behind him—a longer look than the brief nimble check before—and turned back to Kurosawa.
"Misako," he repeated. "You will remember it. Not today. Later. You will hold it in you the way I held it. Not so it will be easier for you. So it will be honest."
Kurosawa was silent.
Yoshida held the pause.
"I am arresting you," Kurosawa said.
"Not today, Kurosawa-san."
"Today."
"No."
Pause.
"You think you can walk out of here now," said Kurosawa. "Because I will not shoot you. You are right. I will not shoot you. But I will not let you out of here."
Yoshida nodded—a small nod, with the respect one shows to a reasonable position one does not intend to agree with.
"Kurosawa-san," he said. "You will not let me out—that is true. But I will leave."
"How."
Yoshida held the pause.
He looked at Sasaki for the first time.

Looked at her for half a second. No longer. In that half second he weighed something—weighed it in himself the way one weighs a precious thing when it must be placed in a pocket not one's own for a few hours. Then he turned his gaze back to Kurosawa.
"I am sorry," he said. "For this."
Kurosawa did not understand at once what for.

He understood a second and a half later—through those second and a half when he understood that Yoshida had shifted his weight from his right foot to his left—that his left foot had come half a centimeter closer to the back door—that with his right hand he had let go of the small gray tube, holding it with only two fingers—and that this meant that the tube in the next minute would no longer be needed by him.
Yoshida looked at Sasaki for one more brief moment.
"Sasaki-san," he said. Quietly. "Not after yourself."
Kurosawa did not manage to understand what that referred to.
He opened his mouth to say "stop."
He did not manage.
Yoshida took one quiet step back—unhurried—toward the back door. A second. On the third Kurosawa moved after him.
Sasaki moved in the same second—from the other side of the desk—her right hand already drawing the pistol.
Yoshida disappeared, back first, into the back room. The door closed behind him.

Outside the walls of the lighthouse the wind held its note at twenty-three meters per second from the southwest, and on that note—embedded in it—half a second before Kurosawa reached the back door—another sound rang out.
Short. Metallic. Quiet.
A click.
Kurosawa heard it.
He knew what it was.
He had time to think one thing—one—brief—not about Yoshida.
He turned his head.

section.subtitle: Chapter Eighteen
section.p: The back door exploded.

Not all of it. Only the lower half—the one where an oil lantern from old fishing gear had stood, with a brass reservoir and a cotton wick, which Yoshida had set an hour before their arrival with a small clockwork mechanism. The mechanism was simple—of the kind sold in Sapporo in radio-parts shops until the nineties. It had been set without an igniter. The igniter was a valve that closed the moment the door opened a second time—that is, the moment Yoshida stepped out.

Forensics would later find three components. A brass fragment of the reservoir, ten centimeters long, in the northeast corner of the room. A wooden splinter from the inner planking of the door, with thin gray paint, in the crack between the desk and the wall. A thin steel band from the housing of the clockwork mechanism—four centimeters long—lodged in the soft fibers of Sasaki's coat, in the left shoulder blade, from the back. It was that shard. Kurosawa would later hold it in a plastic bag on his desk in the department for three days, and would not place it in the file until the third.
Then, in the second of the explosion, he did not know this.
The valve closed. The wick took. The brass reservoir went on the side.
Half a second—for heating. Half a second—for the rupture.
The door flew into the second room by its lower edge.

Shards came from two sources—from the lantern itself, brass and glass—and from the wooden plank of the lower half of the door, splintered into slivers—and from the metal facing, hurled diagonally to the northeast corner of the room. Speed—forty to eighty meters per second, depending on mass. Kurosawa did not know that then. He read it in the forensic's protocol two weeks later—read it—and laid the protocol on the corner of the desk—and picked it up again—and laid it down again. Many times.
In that second he knew something else.
He knew he had turned to Sasaki.

He knew that his eyes had made it to her—to her face, to her right hand, to the pistol in that hand, to her left shoulder—and had also made it to a small detail behind her: the word 美佐子 on the wall, lit by the lamp on the pillar.
The word was where it was. Three kanji. Plain gray pencil.
He saw it—and his eyes lingered on it—and into that lingering entered—before he had realized he was lingering—a small questioning sound in his head: "beauty-assistant-child"?
He did not have the word. He had only three kanji.
He held his eyes on them half a second.
In that half second Sasaki moved.

He did not see her move. He saw only the end of her motion—a body in a black coat passing through the space between him and the wall with the writing. Her left shoulder was lower—she had tilted her torso—and her right hand with the pistol was going up—not to shoot, but for balance. Her head was turned toward him. She was looking at him.
The shard passed through her left shoulder blade.

Kurosawa did not see it. He felt the air push against his own left shoulder—short, sharp, with a pressure he knew from the range—and understood that something had pierced what stood in front of him. He fell to his right knee—not by will, but because the knee gave way—and with his hand in his coat, in the inner pocket, he grabbed to the left—and did not find—and understood he was searching not his own pocket.
He was searching for Sasaki.
He found her on the floor.

She had fallen face down—with the short cornering motion with which people fall whose body has just lost its weight along with one main nerve signal. Her pistol had flown from her right hand half a meter forward. Her left arm remained under her, twisted. Her left cheek on the concrete—not on tatami; there was no tatami here—only concrete, covered with a thin layer of dust and shards.
Kurosawa turned her onto her back.

He did this with hands that did not tremble. He understood that later. Then he was not thinking about his hands. He made the motions his hands made—and his hands knew—made them the way they would not have made them if he had thought.

He put his left palm under the back of her head. With his right he unbuttoned the top button of her coat. The second. The third. Opened the coat. Under the coat was a dark blue uniform jacket. Holster on the right side. Pistol—not in the holster. The pistol lay on the concrete beyond the edge of his right field of vision. He left it there. The pistol was not needed. In that second he did not need any object other than the one he was holding.
On the jacket—on the chest at the left—a dark wet patch, from which air was coming out. Not blood. Air. He heard it.
"Sasaki," he said.
She opened her eyes.
Not at once. The pause was—a second—maybe two. Then she opened them. Looked at him. Calmly.
"Sir."
"Do not move."
"I am not moving."
It seemed to him she smiled—faintly—at the corners—not for him. For something between them.

He drew the phone from his chest pocket. Held it in one hand. With the other he held her head. With the fingers not holding the phone he unbuttoned one more button of her jacket—to find the edges of the wound. Found them. The shard had passed obliquely—entered the left upper part of the chest cavity, in the eighth intercostal space from the back, exited the front wall—with the small exit that punched skin like a stiletto—and lodged somewhere on the concrete three meters behind. Kurosawa did not look for it. That was for forensics.
"Sasaki-san," he said. "Breathe slowly."
"Yes."

He dialed 110. Then 119. Then—with the same finger that had dialed—he took a handkerchief from his inner pocket. It was white, linen, with a monogram K.Y. in the lower corner—a gift from Ogawa's wife for New Year twenty-five, three years ago. He pressed the handkerchief to the exit hole of the wound on her chest. Did not seal it tight. Left one edge lifted—as they showed on the courses—so that air could come out but not go in.
He held it.

Behind the shattered back door he heard a thin metallic rustle. It was the sound of a rope going through an iron ring on the outer wall of the lighthouse on the sea side. Yoshida was descending. Beyond the wall, below—where the cliff went south to the water—there stood a boat. Kurosawa knew this because he ought to know it, and because it was the only thing that made sense. He did not stand up to check.
The rope creaked another twenty seconds.

Then—quietly, very quietly—from below, from beneath the cliff—a short sound of an engine. Small outboard. Eight-horsepower, ten. It started on the first pull. Stalled. Started again. Ran evenly. The sound went south—to open water—to that side of the sea Erimo always looks at.

Kurosawa later knew that the boat was small—metal, a Yamaha, six meters—and that it did not go far: it kept to the cliffs, rounded the cape from the west, and in a little over an hour put in at one of the fishing coves at the foot of the Hidaka, from which a footpath led up into the mountains—to Genshō-an. Beyond that the way was overland. Kurosawa knew this two hours later from a coast-guard radio broadcast he listened to at the end of the third half-hour in the entry hall with a walkie-talkie in his left hand and a towel one of the paramedics had thrown him onto his thigh in his right. Then he knew only that the engine was going south along the shore. That was enough. He understood.
In a minute the engine could no longer be heard.
Kurosawa did not turn toward it.
He held the handkerchief on Sasaki's wound and looked into her eyes.
She was breathing.

The inhale was short and high. The exhale was longer. The right side of her chest rose half a centimeter—no more. The left did not rise at all. Kurosawa saw this by the collar of her jacket—by the way the fabric moved above the right clavicle and did not move above the left.
Her lips grew paler with each inhale. He knew this too. He did not move the handkerchief.
Outside the walls of the lighthouse the wind held its note. Twenty-three meters per second from the southwest.
In the back room, behind the shattered door, the wick of the oil lamp burned down. It had another ten seconds. Then nobody's.
On the wall above the desk, lit by the lamp on the concrete pillar, stood the word 美佐子—three kanji, plain gray pencil.
The word had gone nowhere.
Kurosawa would return to it later. He knew.

He knew one more thing—with that same quiet corner into which things folded before he had time to think them through. He knew what he would be given for this at the department. Tanaka Ryosuke would hear him out under protocol. The internal investigation would last thirty days—after the death of an officer—and Kurosawa would give testimony three times—twice orally, once in writing. He knew what would be said to him, and what would not be said. He knew that in part of the testimony he would keep silent—and that this silence would be entered into the "conclusion regarding further service" line. He knew.
He set it aside.
Now he was holding a palm.

section.subtitle: Chapter Nineteen
section.p: He held the handkerchief.

With the right palm—pressed to the exit of the wound—not by pressure, by weight. With the left—he held the back of her head. The fingers of his left hand found the short hair at the base of her neck that had always been a little longer for her than at the ears—because she cut it herself—because she said once that going to a hairdresser was an hour spent on foolishness for her.
He knew this about her. Many things about her he knew.

He knew that she drank her coffee without sugar. Knew that in winter the left corner of her mouth grew dry and she kept a small tube of medical Vaseline in her desk. Knew she kept a white towel in the glove box of the car for him. Knew she had a sister in Niigata. Knew she wrote her a letter by hand once every two weeks, on light paper—from the stock people buy in Otaru at the shop on Denuki Boulevard. Knew she fired from the right—short—with that short bracing of the shoulder with which instructors fire, not cadets.
He was leaning on these now. In order.
She was looking into his eyes.

The inhale was shallow, short—with that whistle in the upper part a lung makes when one air goes out and a different one returns. The right lung was working. The left—no. He heard it. He knew how many air volumes she had left. He was not counting them in metric units. He was counting them in breaths.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I will tell you."
"I know. Do not hurry."
"I must."

He held her head level. He knew this too—that the head had to be held level—that it must not be lifted, must not be lowered—because each shift of a degree shifted the lung, shifted the middle. He held it.
She held the pause. He saw by her throat—by the thin movement of skin above the right clavicle—how she gathered air. She was not gathering to breathe. She was gathering to speak.
"Kurosawa-san. Yoshida. Jindai-en. Yasuko-san. Kenji just sent."

One sentence. Delivered evenly—with the quiet professional tempo with which Sasaki once read long lists at briefings—with a half-second pause between each name, in which she took a small inhale and went on. Her voice did not tremble. She looked into his eyes as she spoke.
"I know," he said. "Hold on."

He said it evenly. He said "I know" because he had taken all five words into himself. He said "hold on" because that was all one could say to a senior—to a junior, or a junior to a senior, when between them lay what lay between them.
He held the handkerchief.
Kurosawa heard it. He knew this was the third. He knew how many were left.

He did not ask her how she knew. He knew this had been in the SMS Kenji had sent her by the car—half an hour before this minute—that she had kept in the side pocket of her jacket without drawing it out through the whole conversation in the second room. Kenji's pension registry. Yoshida Hiro, sixty-two. Director of Jindai-en, ninety-eight to nineteen. Cleaner Yasuko-san, seventy-eight, alive. That was what Sasaki had not managed to show him before the door exploded. That was what she had held inside her for thirty minutes.
That was what she had just given him.
She blinked. For the first time since opening her eyes.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I'm sorry."
"No."

He said it faster than he had time to think. It came from the same place you killed him had come from—when he had entered the second room. He did not have time to track these places in himself. He simply spoke.
"No," he repeated. "Not I'm sorry."
She did not object.

He felt—under his palm, under the handkerchief—that the rhythm of her breathing had begun to change. The inhale was becoming half a second shorter. The exhale—half a second longer. This was the normal course in pneumothorax. This was what the instructor had shown on the course. It meant the right lung was not enough. It meant the mediastinum had begun to shift.

He knew that with this he could do a countershift puncture with a needle in the second intercostal space along the midclavicular line. He knew how to do it. He had a needle—thick—in the medical kit of the car. He knew he needed forty seconds to run to the car.
He did not run.

This decision came not as a decision. It came as a fact. He knew that 110 was already on its way—twenty minutes—and 119 was already on its way—twenty minutes—and that the puncture, if he went for the needle, would be made in ninety seconds—and would be made on a mediastinum that had already taken a place not its own—and would not return.
He did not run.
He held.
She saw this in his eyes.
Her eyes did not reproach him. In that second they said to him: right. She had the right to say it. He had the right to hear her.
They did not hear anything else.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Hold on."
"I'm holding."
He said this for her. He said it the way a senior says to a junior when something is hard—not adding how exactly one holds. One holds with what one has.
She smiled.

The smile was brief—corners—not for him, and not for her—for something between—the same something she had returned the smiles from the department to over the last three years—when Ogawa joked quietly, when Kenji complained about the processor, when Kurosawa looked at her longer than he needed to, when he took from her hand the bento she had put on to warm for him, because she knew—because she knew many things.
"Tell Nao."
It came quietly. She said it with the air that was left.
"I will."
"Only tell."
He nodded.
She breathed.

The last inhale was the same as the fifth. It did not announce itself. It entered and did not come out to the end. It began in the right part and stopped in the middle—with the small hold with which a clock chain holds when the spring is no longer giving it anything.
She did not finish the word.
Her fingers on her right hand, which lay along her body, made a thin motion—not a grasp, not a reach—a small finger motion with which a person closes an invisible tap.
Then did nothing.
Kurosawa looked into her eyes.
The eyes did not close. She had not had time. She saw him. He saw her.
Outside the walls of the lighthouse the wind held its note. Twenty-three meters per second from the southwest.
Kurosawa did not move for one minute.

Then—carefully, with both hands—he lowered the back of her head to the concrete. He placed under the back of her head his own coat folded in four—having taken it off in three motions, without looking around—and placed the coat exactly where it needed to lie. He straightened the collar of her jacket—the same one he had once straightened on Ogawa—and closed the lower button of her coat. One. He did not fasten it to the end. He did not have the right.
Then he sat on the concrete beside her.
Not on his heels. Not beside her at half a step. Simply—sat—on the concrete, fully. Back to the desk with six clavicles. Face to her face.
The handkerchief with the monogram K.Y. lay on her chest—damp—the same one Ogawa's wife had given him for New Year twenty-five.
He did nothing more.

Beyond the second door, in the entry hall, the wind held the tin can he had knocked to the floor when he entered. The can did not move. It lay on its side. Kurosawa had known this in the morning when he entered, and knew it now. It was the same can. One detail in the room in which nothing had changed in this time—except one.

In the back room the wick of the oil lamp burned down. It had another ten seconds. It had zero. It burned down. In those same ten seconds Kurosawa did not look at it. The wick went out without a witness.
The wall lamp on the pillar kept shining evenly.
On the wall above the desk stood the word 美佐子. Three kanji. Plain gray pencil.
Kurosawa sat.
Outside the door of the lighthouse the wind held its note.
110 was forty minutes out.
119 was forty minutes out.

The SAT unit from the Obihiro precinct—forty-five minutes—because they came from a base at Hidaka-West through the crossing near Samani, because on the direct road under the Erimo ridge heavy transport from the Japan Sea side was not let through at night—and Kurosawa knew this from the twenty-three protocols, and knew it now.
He did not move for forty minutes.

He did not look at the watch. He did not look at her hand. He did not look at the word on the wall. He looked at her face—at that small area between the right temple and the edge of the hair—at the place where a fine pulse used to beat when she was concentrating—and where now nothing was beating.
He held his eyes there.

He knew—with that quiet corner in himself that knew about time before the rest of him—that in forty minutes the first SAT would come in from the entry hall; that he would have to rise; that he would have to unclasp his hands; that he would have to say three things—his surname, rank, and what was behind him. He knew these three things.
He would say them.
He did not move.
Beyond the wind—not far south of the lighthouse—the small outboard was going along the cliffs to one of the fishing coves of the Hidaka. Kurosawa did not think about it.
He thought about a few things. In an order not of his choosing.

He thought about the first morning Sasaki came into the department. It was January of two thousand. Ogawa was not yet senior inspector—he was a regular investigator on the second floor. Kurosawa himself still wore the dark blue tunic without a shoulder chevron—with the shoulder boards of keibuho—not full keibu. Sasaki came in a uniform blouse and gray skirt, from the lower floor, with a paper folder in her left hand and a coffee cup in her right. The coffee was for Ogawa. Kurosawa had remembered it then, because he had thought—briefly—that she was not one of those who in the first week guessed who in this second most needed to be warmed.

He thought about the day she first went with him to a site alone. It was June of twenty-two. The clavicle from Memuro. He remembered her steps behind him—even—not fast, not slow—with the tempo people walk who are not afraid.

He thought about the evening when she put a bento on the corner of his desk and did not say anything. That had been many evenings. He could have named each one separately—and could not have—because they were different evenings with one silence.

He thought about Nao. In Niigata. About how he would enter her apartment in two days. About what he would say to her, and in what order. About how long he would be there. About whether she would cry at once or after a day. About whom she would call afterward—and about the fact that he would have to call Kenji first—and Nao from the door of home. This he now knew.

He thought about the fact that he would not tell her one thing. He would not tell her that Sasaki had jumped. He would say that the shard had gone through the room and there was nothing to be done. He would say it the way it would be said in the protocol. He knew Nao would take this. He knew Nao would take this because that was how Sasaki had taught her—earlier—by the same fine method with which she had taught him many things he had absorbed without noticing.

He thought about Ogawa. About how if Ogawa had been here, Ogawa would have looked at him and said Kurosawa—and would have added nothing—and Kurosawa would have heard everything he needed to hear. Ogawa had not seen him for nine months now. Kurosawa began to feel the lack of his warm silence.
He took this away from himself at once. Not now. This would come later.
The wind over Erimo held its note.
Kurosawa sat on the concrete beside her.

He did not wipe the blood from the left corner of her mouth—a thin strip that had appeared on the fifth inhale—not because he could not, but because it was there, and to move it he had no right. It was hers. He left it.
Twenty minutes after her heart stopped, his right leg began to hurt—the one on which he sat on the concrete with the heel bent under him. He noticed the pain and forgot it.

Seven minutes later he felt his shoulders drop. There were no shoulders. There was a frame in which he sat. In the frame there still fit: the desk with the clavicles, the word on the wall, the lamp on the concrete pillar, the wind outside the walls, and Sasaki's body before him. Together five objects. Together one frame.
Ten minutes later he began to drip in the chest—not in the eyes—precisely in the chest—with that slow dripping motion of water dripping from the eaves at the end of March. He set that aside too.
At forty minutes the first steps from the entry hall came in. Two. Ambulance—paramedics—low rubber soles. Kurosawa heard. Did not turn.
He knew he would stand now.
He stood twenty seconds later.
The handkerchief with the monogram K.Y. remained on her chest. He did not take it.

The paramedics from Obihiro—two of them—came in with a radio and a stretcher. Kurosawa raised a hand. Palm down. They stopped. He gave his surname and rank, and stated the time breathing had stopped, and said that he had not moved the body. The younger paramedic nodded. The older knelt beside her. Kurosawa stepped back. Then one more step. He stood by the desk with the six clavicles and watched them do what they had to do.
Behind them, three SAT came in from the entry hall.
Kurosawa turned his head. Saw them. Gave a hand sign toward the back door. One of the SAT moved that way. Two remained in the first room.
That was all he said.
The word 美佐子 on the wall behind his back stood as it had stood.

p.emphasis: "Yukio-san. Yuri said you are a good person."

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty
section.p: The funeral hall stood in the east wing of Ichikawa-sōsai-jō, in the suburbs of Sapporo, past Nakanoshima Park. Kurosawa arrived forty minutes before the service began. He took from his pocket the fusa-nenju—a black rosary, bought yesterday at the shop near the Hodaiji temple, with two knots and one bead of bone. He had not held rosary beads since his father's funeral—and his fingers did not remember how to arrange them between thumb and index finger.

Beyond the glass facade of the hall lay a gray December afternoon. Snow was not falling—only the cold stood level—and the sign above the entrance (white on black, with the inscription "佐々木家告別式") reflected matte.
He entered.

In the entry hall were three staff in black with "受付" on their chests. He signed the book—hand steady, the name "黒澤 雪男" slow—and placed the kōden in a white envelope with a double black-and-white cord. Thirty thousand yen. He did not know if that was the right amount for a partner—there were no rules—and he placed what he placed.
He was handed a program of the service. One page. On it—the family name, place, time, name of the sekiheku-sōryo from Eshō-ji temple, Kita ward. In the lower corner—the kaimyō, five kanji:
He held the program between two fingers. Looked a long time.
Pure lotus. Pattern of the heart. Nun.

"Aya"—from her name. "Shin"—from her line of work. "Ren"—the symbol of Buddhist mourning. Purity is chosen by the family. He knew there was no one in this family to choose purity; Sasaki's father had died six years ago, her older sister too, and the decision had been made by the hōji-abbess of Eshō-ji, with Nao entitled to one word.
He put the program in his chest pocket.
Walked into the hall.

The hall was white, with a high ceiling of undisturbed plaster board. At the far end—an altar. In the center—the ihai with the same kaimyō, carved on dark lacquered wood. Before the ihai—Sasaki's photograph. Not from the field. In the uniform she rarely wore. She was smiling—not with the smile he knew—not the working, thin, short one—but a longer and softer smile, at the moment when someone had said something amusing off-camera. Kurosawa looked. Turned away.
Chrysanthemums stood around. White. Not one—forty, fifty, sixty. In a half-circle. A wall of flowers behind which the altar was as if behind a curtain.

On either side—rows of black chairs. People were already seated, quietly. Three of her former classmates from the academy. Chief Tanaka Ryosuke, in the first row on the left, with his wife. Endo, in a black coat, stood by a column. Kenji was in a black suit that clearly did not belong to him—with sleeves slightly too long—and stood by the exit like a man ready to flee.
Kurosawa nodded to Endo. She nodded back briefly.
He walked deeper in.

Nao sat in the first row on the right. Alone. Relatives on the mother's side were in Niigata and had not made it in time. She was in a black coat one size too large—old, probably her mother's—and in a black dress. Hair gathered in a low ponytail. Face quiet. In her hands—a photograph in a black frame. Not the one on the altar. Smaller. Worn at the corners. With a thin black ribbon across the upper left corner.

He studied it across two rows. Sasaki in it was in civilian clothes—a green windbreaker—standing on the pier of Otaru harbor with a fish in her hands. Summer. Before everything. Probably Nao had taken it herself.
Kurosawa sat across the aisle from Nao, two rows back. Did not go to her at once. Right so.
At two o'clock the priest came out through the side door. Small, thin, in a brown kōromo with a silk kesa over the left shoulder—and with a whistle-rin-cup in his hands. Walked slowly to the altar.
Sat. Placed the rin on a cushion.
Silence settled of itself.
He struck the rin.
A thin, long note went vertically.

Then he opened a small book and began reading Han-nya Shin-gyō—the Heart Sutra—in that special monotone voice which in Japan belongs neither to singing nor to speaking—and behind which Kurosawa repeated in himself three or four lines he had known since childhood from his mother.

p.emphasis: Kan-jizai bosatsu, gyō jin han-nya haramita ji, shōken go on kai kū, do issai kuyaku.

section.p: He knew the words. He did not know the meaning. His mother had once explained, once: "All things—form and emptiness—are one." He had not understood then. He did not understand now.
The whistle of the rin did not interrupt the reading.
The reading went for twenty-three minutes.
Then came the shōkō. The incense.
The participants approached the altar one by one. Family first.

Nao rose. She held the photograph with both hands, the way one holds a child—and walked to the altar slowly. Stood. Bowed before the ihai. Took from a small wooden bowl a pinch of dark powder, raised it to her forehead, sprinkled it into the metal kōro. A thin blue thread of smoke rose. Nao repeated. Three times. Bowed.
Kurosawa looked at her back. It did not tremble. She was walking her own—the one she had chosen herself.
Then went Tanaka. Then Endo. Then colleagues.
Then he.

He rose. Walked slowly. His left hand held the nenju. His right took a pinch. He raised it to his forehead. Did not sprinkle at once—held it two seconds. Looked at the altar. At the photograph. At the ihai. At the kaimyō.
He read the five kanji slowly—with his lips, without sound. One by one.
Sei.
Ren.
Aya.
Shin.
Ni.
Then sprinkled the powder into the kōro. Took again. Sprinkled again. Bowed his head. Two bows—deep, slow. Removed his hands.
Walked back.
To his place.
Sat.
The reading ended with one more note of the rin.

The service lasted an hour and a half. At the end the priest stood, looked over the hall and said one sentence quietly: "Aya-Shin-Ni is now on the other side, in the Pure Land. We who remain, we continue." Nodded. Left.
People began to rise.
Kurosawa remained sitting for a minute. Looked at the nenju in his palm. Then rose.
Walked to Nao.

She stood to the left of the altar, still holding the photograph with both hands, and waited while Endo and Kenji came up in turn. Endo said something brief to her—Kurosawa did not hear. Nao nodded. Kenji approached, laid a palm on her shoulder—for a second—and stepped back. Nao looked at him directly: "thank you, Yamada-san." Quietly.
Kurosawa came up last.
Stopped half a step away. Did not want to stand too close.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Nao-san."
"Thank you for coming."
"I had to come."
She looked at him. For a long time. The way Sasaki looked when she wanted to say something and could not bring herself to. That look passed down in families.
"Yukio-san," she said.
He nodded.
"Yuri said you are a good person."
Kurosawa was silent a second.
Then he went down on one knee—slowly—so as to be on her level. The photograph in her hands began to tremble. Nao pressed it tighter, with both palms. The tremor dropped.
"Yes, Nao-san."
"Yuri isn't coming back, is she?"
"She isn't coming back."
She held the photograph.
"But I will come," said Kurosawa. "If you allow it."
Nao nodded. Once.
Said nothing more.
He stood.

At the exit from the hall—a small table with kōden-gaeshi—little chocolates in black-and-white wrappers with the monogram "佐々木." Kurosawa took one, put it in his chest pocket, not for eating—so as not to insult the family with a refusal.

On the sidewalk in front of the hall a black sedan was waiting. The driver was a young sergeant from the department whose name Kurosawa did not remember—he took him by his position. Nao was to go to the cremation directly: Hiragishi crematorium, half an hour's drive. Kurosawa offered to accompany her there.
She nodded.
He opened the rear door for her. She got in. He went around the car, got in on the other side.
The sergeant pulled onto the highway without a word.
Nao placed the photograph face down on her lap—so that no reflections from the windows fell on it.
Kurosawa looked ahead.
The Kannon-neiyu highway hummed under the wheels. The sky gray. Streetlamps already on, though it was three.
He wanted to say something. Did not say it.

Nao looked out the side window. Did not cry. Looked at something beyond the glass—at a filling station going by, at trees, at the metal fence of a cemetery on a bend. Her palms lay on the photograph. Fingers thin, with short-clipped nails—the same as Sasaki's—but Nao wore on the middle finger of her right hand a thin silver ring Sasaki had never worn.
Kurosawa noticed the ring.
Did not ask.
A kilometer on, Nao pressed her forehead to the glass. Briefly—for a second—and straightened again. Kept looking out the window.

Around the bend came new cable poles, then a longer row of low residential buildings, then a park belt without fences, with the bare skeletons of trees. Nao did not try to follow them with her eyes. They passed beyond the glass on their own, and she let them.

At an intersection the sergeant braked. A young woman was pushing a child in a stroller across the road. The child was asleep. No one in the car said anything. The yellow light turned green. The sergeant moved off.
Kurosawa looked at Nao. She was still at the window.
The crematorium appeared around a bend.

A plain building of gray concrete. A wide arch over the entrance. Two chimneys on the far side. Japanese sign, white on gray. He had been here once—when they buried his father—but remembered nothing except that it had smelled of hot concrete.
The sergeant stopped the car.
Kurosawa opened Nao's door.
She got out. Turned out to be a head shorter than him. The photograph again in both hands, face up.
Looked at the building.
"Yukio-san."
"Yes."
"You'll stay to the end."
"Yes."
She nodded. Went ahead.
Kurosawa went after her—half a step behind and slightly to the left—the way partners walked when they did not know what was waiting inside.
He knew.

In the entry hall of the crematorium they were met by a staff member in gray uniform. He led them to a small waiting room—narrow, with a dozen wooden chairs, a coffee machine, and one low table with a popular magazine two months out of date. Endo and Kenji arrived ten minutes later. Tanaka with his wife too. Silent.

The cremation lasted an hour forty. Kurosawa sat upright, hands on his knees. In the chair beside him Nao held herself the same way. Once she placed the photograph face down on her lap—and Kurosawa looked at her briefly—and she caught his glance—and nodded, and turned the photograph face up again.
He knew it was not right to turn it back. That had been her choice, and he should not have intervened. He looked away.
An hour and forty minutes later the staff member returned.
"Family of Sasaki-san. This way, please."
Nao stood. Kurosawa stood. He let her go ahead.
They entered the hall of farewell to the bones. Kotsu-age.

In the center of the room stood a low metal table. On it lay bones. Cremation in Japan does not burn to ash—a skeleton remains, brittle, white, with that particular tint a stone has after frost. The bones lay in their order—legs at the bottom, then the pelvis, then the spine, then the shoulders, then the head. All familiar.

The attendant gave Nao and Kurosawa each a pair of long chopsticks—of two different materials (one wooden, one bamboo—so the pair would not match; a tradition Kurosawa remembered from childhood without explanation). Nao took her pair firmly.

The attendant indicated the first bone—small, from the right foot—and said: "We go from the bottom." Nao served first. The attendant helped her lift the fragment with the chopstick; Kurosawa caught it with the second from the other side; together they placed it in the covered urn—small, smooth, porcelain, white.
Nao held her chopstick level. Did not tremble. Kurosawa felt his chopstick slip for a second—and corrected.
Foot bone. Femur. Several ribs. Spine. Shoulders.

Last was the nodobotoke—a small bone from the second cervical vertebra, of a shape the Japanese read as "seated Buddha." The attendant showed it separately. He said: "This is the one who sat within him."
Nao nodded. Took with her chopstick first. Kurosawa from the other side. Together they lowered it into the urn.
The attendant closed the urn. Wrapped it in white silk cloth. Handed it to Nao with both hands.
Nao took it. Looked at it.
"This is her."
"Yes, Nao-san."
Nao did not cry.
Held the urn.
Kurosawa stood.

He felt—from this moment on—that he no longer had a partner. He had had her—up to this moment, while her bones lay on the table, while they laid them out with their hands. Now she was in porcelain. Now as a witness.
He placed a palm on Nao's shoulder. Not hard. For a second.
Removed it.
"Let's go," he said.
Nao nodded. Walked to the exit.
He followed.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-One
section.p: Prosecutor Fujiwara's office was on the fourth floor of the Chihō Kensatsu-chō, with a window on the parking lot and on the low gray roof of the fire depot across the road. Walls—light gray, with a single calendar—a court calendar, with dates of hearings underlined in red. The desk—dark, long, almost empty: a thin lamp, a black pen, a black cup with black tea, and one folder Kurosawa had brought an hour ago.
Fujiwara sat at the desk.

He was sixty. He always wore a black suit and the white cuffs of a shirt, with two simple silver cufflinks at the wrists. Hands—thin, with long fingers, no ring (he had divorced long ago). Hair combed back, parted on the left. Face—dry, very calm.
Kurosawa sat opposite. Hands on his knees.
Fujiwara was reading the folder slowly. He was not a man who read fast.
"Kurosawa-san," he said at last. "I have a question."
"Yes."
"You understand what you are taking on."
"I understand."
"This will not be an expert consultation on paper. It will be grounds against you personally, if he escapes."
"He will not escape."
"You have this on paper?"
"I have only Nakamura's word."
Fujiwara nodded. One palm turned a page. He read on.

Kurosawa looked past him at the calendar. At the date—the sixteenth of December—when the first hearing on the Takada case was scheduled (not his case; he knew only that it existed). The red underlining was thin, neat.

"Kurosawa-san. One time aloud," said Fujiwara. "This is not a reversal of the sentence. Nakamura has served twenty-two years. This is a temporary reclassification as an expert consultant in an active investigation, article 168 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with an electronic bracelet and assigned convoy. Legally he is in transfer between institutions. A motion to review the case you and I will submit no earlier than six months from now, and not from this desk. You understand this the way I have just said it."
"Yes."
"The deadline is the first of February," said Fujiwara, without lifting his eyes.
"The deadline is until there is a finale."
"That is not a deadline. That is a wish."
"I know."
"Kurosawa-san"—Fujiwara raised his eyes. "I am signing this not because you are right. I am signing this because I knew Ogawa, and Ogawa would have signed it first."
Kurosawa was silent.
"And one more thing," said Fujiwara. "If Nakamura steps off the step he cannot step off, you will have to stop him. Not me and not the leadership. You."
"I understand."
Fujiwara held his pen a second over the page. Then lowered it and signed. His signature was narrow, vertical, without flourishes—three vertical strokes and one horizontal.
Set another stamp. Red.
Closed the folder.
Reached it across the desk.
"Go."
Kurosawa nodded. Took the folder. Stood.
"Thank you, Fujiwara-san."
"Do not thank me," said the prosecutor. "Go."
Kurosawa went.

The Tsukigata correctional facility stood forty kilometers north of Sapporo, in the Ishikari valley, past a stretch of rice fields flooded in winter and locked in thin ice. The facility walls—gray concrete with two towers. The interior courtyard—paving, a small garden on the left, with two pines and low stones, in Japanese style—not for the inmates but for inspectors who come from Tokyo.
Kurosawa parked in the outer yard. Took the folder. Went through the checkpoint.
At the duty officer's post in the second zone he showed his document. The duty officer looked slowly. Read. Raised his eyes.
"One?"
"One."
"Transport?"
"Mine."
The duty officer nodded. Picked up the phone. Dialed the internal line.
Kurosawa waited. In the reception was a low plastic sofa, brown, with a scratch in the middle of the seat. He did not sit. He stood by the window, looking at the empty parking lot.
Twenty minutes later the doors from the internal block opened.
They brought out Toshi.

He was in gray civilian—a plain coat, dark trousers, dark shoes without laces. Hair short-shaved, as always. Face yellow from prison food. Thinner still since their last meeting. Kurosawa noted to himself: roughly two or three kilograms.
On his wrists—electronic cuffs, thin, with a blue indicator on the inside. One guard held the key. The other—the folder with the description.
Toshi looked at Kurosawa. Once. Did not say anything.
The duty officer signed one more paper. Handed the folder to Kurosawa.
"He's yours, Kurosawa-san," he said. "For everything that follows—you."
"Yes."

The guard removed the cuffs from the anchor bar, leaving only one bracelet on Toshi's left ankle. He did not offer his hand. Simply lifted his leg when it was needed, and lowered it when it was needed.
He walked through the checkpoint.
Through the doors of the outer vestibule—to the parking lot.
Kurosawa opened the right rear door of his SUV. Toshi got in. Did not ask whether he could sit in front. Kurosawa did not offer.
Sat behind the wheel.
The engine warmed for half a minute.
He pulled out of the facility.
The Ishikari valley ran flat on both sides of the highway. The rice fields were under ice. Straw goose decoys stood alone on the side roads, without geese. The sky low.
Twenty minutes they were silent.

Kurosawa looked ahead. Toshi sat in the back, behind his right shoulder. Kurosawa saw in the mirror the upper part of his face—eyes, nose. Toshi did not look at him. Looked out his window, at the fields.
At the twenty-first minute Toshi said:
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I am sorry about Sasaki-san."
Kurosawa did not answer at once.
He had known this phrase would come. Had known since yesterday, since the day before, since the time he filed the motion. Had known Toshi would say it himself, without a question.
"Thank you," he said at last.
"I underestimated her."
Kurosawa was silent.
"I thought," Toshi said, slowly, "that she needed no protection. Because she knew how to hold herself. That is a mistake. Everyone who walks beside you needs protection."
"You think it is I who lost her."
Toshi did not answer at once.
Kurosawa looked in the mirror.
Toshi answered evenly:
"No. I think it is he."
"You are sure."
"Yes, Kurosawa-san. I am sure of that."
Kurosawa nodded. Said no more.
The Ishikari valley ended. The outskirts of Takikawa began. The sky was the same.
For a few minutes they were silent again.

Kurosawa glanced at the fuel gauge—half a tank remained. He would not refuel at the nearest station—the timing was not right. In Takikawa he turned off onto a side road—he knew this loop from several previous operations—and came out onto a secondary road that ran parallel to the highway, with less traffic.
On the shoulder stood a kiosk with boxes in black bags—a small shop selling saman and coffee from a machine. Kurosawa did not stop. Toshi looked at the shop briefly—and turned back to the window.
Ten minutes later Toshi said:
"Where?"
"Otaru."
Toshi nodded. Once.
Was silent.
Then said:
"I knew."
Kurosawa looked in the mirror.
"You knew."
"Yes."
"Since when."
Toshi looked out the window. A long time. Then:
"Since the time I was a ward."
"Jindai-en."
"You already know."
"We know it is in Otaru. We found out the institution's name yesterday."
Toshi nodded.
"I was there from ten to seventeen. Then I left."
"You knew he was there now."
"I knew he was there until nineteen. I did not know he was there now."
"You did not know."
"He does not hold one room long, Kurosawa-san. I thought he had moved long ago. I was mistaken."
Kurosawa was silent.
He knew how Toshi used words. He knew that "I was mistaken" was not an apology. It was a fixation. Toshi never apologized.
"One more thing," said Kurosawa.
"Yes."
"Inoue Satoshi. You know him."
"Yes. He is two years older than me. He was also a ward."
"He knows."
"No."
"You are sure."
Toshi looked out the window. The road ran now past low fish drying-racks raised on piles—a summer zone for fish, empty in winter.

"Inoue is an orphan, like me," said Toshi. "The difference is that Yoshida chose me, and did not choose Inoue. Inoue he kept as the facade. Inoue does not know because it was not for him to know. He is a good person, Kurosawa-san. He loves Yoshida."
"This will be hard."
"Yes."
Kurosawa was silent.
"You are coming with us," he said, "because I want you to come."
"I know."
"You are coming because you can confirm what I cannot confirm."
"I know."
"But one more thing, Toshi."
"Yes."
"If you step off the step you cannot step off, I will stop you."
Toshi looked at him in the mirror.
It was the first time in the hour he had met his eyes.
"I know, Kurosawa-san," he said quietly.
Kurosawa nodded.
The road came out onto the highway that ran to Otaru. The sky was still the same—low, gray.
Kurosawa gave gas.
Toshi looked out the window.
Kurosawa heard his breathing behind him. Even.
Half an hour later Toshi said:
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"One question. Not for the record."
"Go on."

"Sasaki-san told me once—at one of the interviews when you had gone out to drink water in the corridor—that you drink green tea only from a thermos. That you never take it in bottles from a vending machine. Why?"
Kurosawa thought.
"Because from a thermos it is warmer," he said. "And from a machine it cools before I can open it."
"That is an answer."
"Yes."
"And the truthful one?"
Kurosawa was silent.

"Because I bought the thermos with her," he said. "In the third month of working together. We went into Tokyū Hands by Odori—and she held two, gray and black. I took the black. She took the gray. Since then I drink from it."
Toshi nodded.
"Thank you," he said.
"For what."
"For answering truthfully."
Kurosawa looked in the mirror. Toshi was looking out the window, just as before.
"Nakamura-san."
"Yes."
"You did not ask that out of curiosity."
"No. I asked because I wanted to show you," said Toshi, "that you can answer such questions now. Five days ago you would not have answered. That matters for where we are going."
Kurosawa was silent.
He knew Toshi was right.
He held the wheel steady.

The landscape past Takikawa slowly changed color. The rice fields ended—there began small rises planted with low conifers, and behind them—the first outskirts of Ishikari. The sky held the same gray density. Roads on this stretch were dusted with salt in winter, with a thin scrape under the tires; the engine ran evenly.
He saw in the side mirror the trailing car—Kenji—a kilometer behind them. Kenji kept his distance professionally. Kurosawa noted to himself: tell him the distance is right.
"One more thing," said Kurosawa.
"Yes."
"In Otaru. When we arrive. You speak only when I ask you. Not before."
"Yes."
"Inoue-san will recognize you."
"I know."
"It will be harder for him than for me."
"I know, Kurosawa-san. I will not hurt him."
Kurosawa nodded.
"One more."
"Yes."
"If Yoshida is not at Jindai-en, I will ask you to say where else he can be."
"I will say."
"You know."
"I don't know exactly. I know possibilities. I will say."
"Good."
Toshi looked out the window.
Kurosawa looked ahead. The sky and the road merged into one gray line on the horizon—and on that line the first outskirts of Otaru gradually appeared, white and thin under the low sky.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Two
section.p: Otaru lay under a low sky, with the port on the left and the Temiya slope on the right. Kurosawa turned off the highway onto a narrow road that climbed between two rows of old wooden buildings—former warehouses from the Meiji era, now converted into ceramic workshops and shops for tourists. It was past four in the afternoon. The streetlamps had already gone yellow. Kenji drove in the second car, half a kilometer behind; Toshi—with Kurosawa.

The children's home Jindai-en appeared around the bend. Kurosawa recognized it from the photograph Kenji had sketched last week—but on site the building was longer and darker than he had remembered from the shot.

Wooden, two-story, Taisho style, with a wide overhanging eave and black tile. The main building stood deeper on the lot, behind a low stone enclosure. To the right of the main block—an annex from 1972, concrete, simpler, without exterior windows. On the facade—one small enameled plaque with the black inscription "神代園," without any image.
Kurosawa parked by the fence. Kenji's car pulled up behind. Kenji got out, closed the door softly, came over.
"Sir," he said.
"We're going in."
"Toshi?"
"With me."
Toshi got out of the rear door. The cuff on his ankle was concealed under his trouser leg. He stood evenly, without tension.
Kenji looked at him briefly. Did not greet him.
They walked to the main entrance.
The entry doors were wide, wooden, with two glass panels in the upper part and a metal handle in the form of a ring. Kurosawa rang the side bell.
Half a minute later the door opened.

A middle-aged man opened, in a gray cardigan and an apron over a shirt. He was about fifty-two—with thin round glasses, smoothly combed dark hair with two white threads at the temples, and a gaze Kurosawa noted from the threshold as kind. Not perceptive. Kind.
"Yes?"
"We are from the prefectural police," said Kurosawa. "Kurosawa Yukio, Missing Persons unit. This is Yamada, consultant. This is Nakamura. We come without appointment. My apologies."
The man looked at him for a long time. Then at the credentials Kurosawa held out. Then at Kenji. Then at Toshi.
Looked at Toshi a second longer.
"You are Inoue-san?"
"Yes. Inoue Satoshi. I am the director."
"We would like to speak with you. It concerns your predecessor."
Inoue nodded slowly. Did not ask which predecessor. He knew there was only one who mattered.
"Come in," he said. "It is not the best hour—the children are just coming back from school—but I will take you to my office."
He stepped aside.
They entered.

The genkan was wide, with two rows of cabinets for children's shoes along the wall. In the first row of cabinets were twenty or so pairs of small slippers, winter boots—all standing evenly, with tags with names written in careful, childish hand. In the second row—adult staff shoes.
It smelled of linseed oil and, faintly—probably from the kitchen deep inside—of boiled rice.

Kurosawa took off his shoes. Kenji too. Toshi—with Kurosawa's help—crouched, took off his shoes, placed them evenly, like the children. The cuff was visible now. Inoue saw and held his gaze on it for a second—then turned away—did not ask.

Inoue led them down the corridor—wooden floor, worn, warm to the touch through socks. They passed the kitchen (a woman in a white apron looked out from it, nodded to Inoue, disappeared); passed doors from behind which someone could be heard playing the first bar of Sakura Sakura on a piano—and stopping, and starting again; passed a wall with old photographs in black frames—graduating classes of wards, rows of children in front of the main building, each shot with a small metal plaque below it giving the year.

Kurosawa noticed: in the 1993 graduation photograph, in the second row, was a girl with hair combed back, with a thin serious face, thirteen or fourteen years old. He recognized her from another source, from another photograph of an older age, in a white medical cap. He did not stop. Did not point.

Kenji noticed that Kurosawa did not stop. Kenji also did not stop. But when they had passed, Kenji briefly touched Kurosawa's wrist with his left elbow. Not as a gesture. Simply as contact. Kurosawa understood: Kenji had recognized her too.
Toshi passed without looking at the wall.

Inoue's office was at the end of the ground-floor corridor, with a view of a small inner garden with one low maple. Desk—dark, old, with a new computer. Two cabinets—with paper files. Walls—with two children's drawings in frames and one photograph.
Kurosawa looked at the photograph.

Inoue, about twenty years younger, in a white shirt, stood next to an older man in a gray suit. The older man—short, thin, with a shaved head, thin features, dark deep eyes. He was resting his hand on Inoue's shoulder. Neither was smiling. Photo—approximately 2005–2007.
Inoue saw where Kurosawa was looking.
"That is Yoshida-sensei," he said.
"I know."

Inoue looked at Kurosawa for a long time. Then nodded. Pointed to a low table in the corner with four chairs. All sat. Inoue brought from the kitchen a black tray with four cups of hōjicha tea, set it down, sat opposite.
"I will not go around in circles," said Inoue. "You have come to me about Yoshida-sensei. What has happened."
Kurosawa was silent. Held the cup in his hands, did not drink.
"Inoue-san. We have grounds to believe Yoshida Hiro is implicated in a series of crimes in Hokkaido. Over the last six years."
Inoue looked at him.
Said nothing.
Then laughed briefly. Not loud. Not rough. Simply with one exhale, with his head turning to the side—to the window—and back.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"Forgive me. That is not the laugh of disbelief. That is—I simply do not know how otherwise. You are saying such a thing about the man who raised me."
"I know."
"Yoshida-sensei is a holy man."
Kurosawa nodded.
Did not argue.
"Let me explain why I say that," said Inoue. "I was received into this home in 1985. I was eight. My mother had died. My father was alive, but he was not there. You understand."
"I understand."

"Yoshida-sensei was then a teacher. Junior. He was twenty-three. He noticed me in the first week. I had clothes from the previous home that were small for me—the sleeves ended at the elbows—and Yoshida-sensei brought me his own sweater. In the evening. Quietly. Without witnesses. Simply put it on my bed and left."
Kurosawa was silent.
"He did that always. Not for me. For everyone. Only in such a way that no one saw. He did not like being seen. And he did not like being thanked for it."
"You believe him."
"Kurosawa-san. I do not believe him. I know him."
Inoue looked into his cup.
"He raised me. He taught me. He put me in this position when he left. I will not hold you by the hand. Say what the suspicion is. I will hear it."
Kurosawa looked at Kenji. Kenji nodded imperceptibly.

"Inoue-san. We have every ground to enter your archive now. I have a prosecutor's warrant. I have brought it with me. But I do not want to enter without your permission. I know your permission matters more than paper."
Inoue looked at him.
"Kurosawa-san. I will not refuse you. I only want to understand why you have come."
Kurosawa was silent a second.
Then said:
"I am looking for my brother."
Inoue did not reply.
Not at once.
He put the cup down slowly on the table. Did not look at anyone. Looked into his cup.
Was silent for thirty seconds.
Then raised his eyes.
"Your brother."
"Yes."
"You think he is here."
"I do not think. I know."
Inoue looked at Toshi. For the first time since the start of the conversation.
"Nakamura-san."
Toshi nodded.
"It is so."
"You know this."
"I know."
Inoue looked into his cup again.
For a long time.
Kurosawa waited. Kenji also waited. Toshi sat evenly, with palms on his knees.
Finally Inoue said:
"What do you need."
"Permission to go down to the basement. The archive. The medical journal. The ward records from 1980. And—the keys to the 1972 annex."
Inoue did not respond at once to this.
To the basement and the archive he nodded. Nodded once. Then longer.
To the annex—he did not nod.

"The 1972 annex has been under reconstruction since 2005," he said. "I do not have keys. Yoshida-sensei always kept them himself. He told me, when I took over the home, that the keys would turn up later. I did not press. I had no reason."
Kurosawa nodded.
"I understand."
"You think that in there…"
Inoue did not finish.
"That is what we are going to find out," said Kurosawa.
Inoue placed his palms on the table.
"Kurosawa-san. I trust you because you came in yourself and told me about your brother. I do not trust you because you are a policeman. These two things are different inside me."
"I know."
"Go down. I will give you the basement key. I will inform the staff you are conducting an archive audit of the last decade. I will not tell the children about you."
"Thank you, Inoue-san."
Inoue nodded.
Stood.
Went to a cabinet. Took a set of keys from the lower shelf, three on a fob. One—long, brass, with a small brown leather tab. Second—flat, iron. Third—with a red tag.
Held them out to Kurosawa.
"The long one—basement door. The flat one—iron cabinet with the medical journal. The red—the box with personal files up to 2000."
"Thank you."
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
Inoue looked at him.
"If you find your brother," he said, "I want you to know one thing."
"Yes."
"I did not know."
"I know, Inoue-san."
"And one more."
"Yes."

"If you do not find your brother, but find something else about Yoshida-sensei, I will not ask you for leniency. I only ask that you remember that he was my one. And that otherwise I would not have lived."
Kurosawa was silent.
Then nodded.
"I will remember."
Inoue nodded.
He pointed at a door in the corner of the office. The door was small, wooden, with a bolt.
"The basement is that way."
Kurosawa rose.
Kenji rose too.
Toshi remained seated.
"Nakamura-san will stay with me," said Inoue. "I know him. I am not afraid of him."
Kurosawa looked at Toshi.
Toshi nodded.
"All right," said Kurosawa.
He walked to the door in the corner.
Slid the bolt back.
The door opened.
Behind it a staircase went down.
Kurosawa lingered on the threshold for a second. Looked back—Inoue stood at his desk, hands at his sides, looking at Toshi.
Toshi sat evenly, with the same palms on his knees.
"Inoue-san," said Kurosawa. "One more thing."
"Yes."
"The kitchen. Who works there?"
"Suzuki-san. Our cook. In her thirties. Since 2015."
"Can we ask her not to ask about anything?"
"I will tell her."
"Thank you."
Inoue nodded.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"If I need to tell the children something after you leave, I will say you were archive auditors. Is that acceptable?"
"Yes."
"Good."
Kurosawa looked at him longer than he needed to.
"Inoue-san."
"Yes."
"I will not ask you to forgive me when this is over."
Inoue did not reply at once.
He looked out the window at the maple in the inner garden. The maple was bare, with a thin layer of snow on the lower branches.

"I will not forgive you," said Inoue at last. "Because you have nothing to be forgiven for. You are doing what you must do. These are different things—doing what you must, and what has to be forgiven."
"I understand."
Inoue nodded.
Kurosawa turned back to the door in the corner.
Kenji stood beside him. Held the backpack in his left hand, the flashlight in his right. The flashlight was small, thin, with a double battery—the thing Kenji never parted with.
Kurosawa nodded to him.
Kenji nodded back.
They went down.

p.emphasis: "This is the body Kurosawa-san signed for in 2022 as Ren."

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Three
section.p: The stairs were steep, wooden, with wide treads that sagged in the middle from seventy years of walking. Kurosawa went down first. Kenji after him. The beam of the flashlight found on the first step below a switch—old, rotary, with a bakelite knob. Kurosawa turned it. Two bulbs under the ceiling lit up yellow.
The basement was low. Ceiling—one meter eighty. Kurosawa tilted his head ten degrees and walked. Kenji—straight.

The space extended deeper under the main block. Shelves stood perpendicular to the stairs—eight rows, of wood darkened by dust, with metal corner braces. On each shelf—folders. Not cardboard boxes—operational folders with muslin ties, with stickers of years and codes.
Here lay all the paper memory of Jindai-en, since 1970. Fifty-eight years.

Kenji placed his backpack on the floor in the central aisle. Took out his laptop—not to work with now, but for the scanner he intended to switch on later. Took out a pair of thin cotton gloves. Handed one pair to Kurosawa.
"Yoshida first," said Kurosawa. "Personal file."
"Yes."

They went to the fourth shelf—by year of appointment as director, 1998. Kenji knew the layout from the inventory Inoue had shared last month (he had thought then that this was a routine check). Personal files of administration ran on the left, in alphabetical order.
Kurosawa ran his fingers along the spines. Found: 吉田 博.
Thin folder. Two centimeters. Pulled it out.
Placed it on the low working table by the stairs. The table was old, with two hanging lamps. Kurosawa switched one on.
Opened.

Here lay forty years of service. First was the position card of 1986, when Yoshida was taken on as a teacher of the younger classes. Photograph—Yoshida at twenty-four, in a black suit, with short hair and the gaze of one who had not yet decided whether he was a person or a habit. Second—a copy of his diploma from Kyōiku Daigaku Hokkaidō, faculty of pedagogy. Third—a stack of pages with an internal filing: a copy of the graduation thesis of 1986.

p.strong: The Restoration of the Personality of a Traumatized Child Through Role Therapy.

section.p: Kurosawa read the title page three times.
Academic supervisor—Mori Katsuya.
Date of defense—the twenty-eighth of March, 1986.
Grade—shū (highest).
He turned the page.
The work was long—forty-nine pages. He did not read. He glanced through.
Three things caught his eye.

First—chapter three, "Methodology of Reproduction." Yoshida described how, for a child who had lived through traumatic loss, it was possible to reconstruct "the key moment at which the child got stuck"—and to lead them through it once more—"with a different ending." He wrote that this was "not therapy in the medical sense." "It is the actualization of a choice that was not made."

Second—page thirty-nine, "Example from personal experience." Yoshida, at twenty-four, in his graduation work, wrote about his own "key sticking place"—"at a pier at the age of eight." He named neither the place nor the event. Only—"the pier, morning, water, and a sister who did not come up."
Third—the epigraph. At the very end, after the conclusions, in hand, in the same restrained script with which he wrote phrases in the rooms:

p.emphasis: There is nothing more terrifying than a moment that does not end. Restoration is not about beauty. Restoration is about the edge.

section.p: Kurosawa closed the thesis.
Kenji stood beside him. He had been reading over his shoulder. Said nothing. He did not need to.
"Medical journal," said Kurosawa.
Kenji nodded. Went to the seventh shelf—there stood an iron cabinet, locked with a flat iron key. Kurosawa opened it. Took out a thick journal in a black cloth cover.
Jindai-en Staff Medical Journal, 1985–2019.
They opened it on the page where names ran vertically, and years and license categories horizontally.
Far right column—sanitary license, obtained 1990. Kurosawa ran a finger along the row.
License to work with narcotic preparations—not obtained. Sanitary veterinary access—not applicable. Medical license (rin-i)—not obtained.
"No access to propofol," Kenji said quietly.
"Yes."
"He did not obtain it through himself. Never applied. He did not enter through the entry point of the system."
"Then through someone."
"Then through someone with access. A nurse. A clinic. Niigata."
Kurosawa nodded.
Wrote the date of the medical license in his notebook. This could be cross-referenced with the health department's registry—but it was already clear.
He put the medical journal on the working table.
He opened Yoshida's personal file further. Inner page—work history:
• 1986–1998—teacher of the younger classes.
• 1998–2019—director.
• 2019—application for retirement "for reasons of health."
• 2019—appointed honorary consultant (unpaid, without duties).
• 2019—forwarding address for mail: Genshō-an, Hidaka, PO Box 7.
Kurosawa looked at the address for a long time.
"He has been there the whole time," he said.
"Yes."
"Hidaka."
"Yes."
Kenji was silent, then added:
"And he comes here when needed."
"Yes."
They moved on to the wards' personal files.
Kenji knew what to look for. He was laying out the alphabet: Japanese, by surname.
K—Kurosawa.
Kurosawa Ren.
Thin folder. Half a centimeter. Sticker: "Kurosawa Ren, b. 1977." Date of admission—not 1985, as with the others. Date of admission—April 2022.
Kurosawa opened it.

First page—not a ward's card in the usual sense. It was a form of a different type: ward-patient of the psychiatric wing, distance form of care. Kurosawa had never seen such a form before. It had space for a doctor and a guardian, not for a child and parents.
Patient's surname: Kurosawa Ren.
Date of birth: 3 November 1977.
