Condition: long-standing major depressive disorder with elements of catatonia, post-traumatic reaction.
Date of admission to distance care: 1 April 2022.
Guardian: Yoshida Hiro.
Kurosawa turned the page.
Second page—quarterly medical reviews. Entries in Yoshida's hand.
July 2022: "Condition stable. Patient calm. Takes food unassisted. Quiet-register communication."
October 2022: "Patient chose physical activity—15 minutes per day. Sleep normal. Conversations—about his sister."
Kurosawa stopped at "his sister." There had been no sister. But with Yoshida, from childhood—Misako.
"He was writing about himself," said Kurosawa.
"This is his doctrine," Kenji said quietly. "The patient is himself. Ren is restoration."
Kurosawa nodded. Continued.
January 2023: "Condition improved. Patient draws."
April 2023: "Patient asked about his younger brother. It was explained that the brother is not ready."

Kurosawa felt something in himself stop quietly. Not his heart—not his heart "pounding"; he had long been from the profession in which such combinations of words did not exist. Simply quietly stopped.
He read the line once more.

p.emphasis: Patient asked about his younger brother. It was explained that the brother is not ready.

section.p: He placed his palms on the table.
Kenji watched him. Said nothing.
Kurosawa continued.

July 2023: "Condition stable." October 2023: "Condition stable." January 2024, April 2024, July 2024, October 2024: "Condition stable." January 2025: "Patient asked about his daughter. It was explained that the daughter is safe."
Kurosawa turned to the end.
Last entry—October 2025. "Condition stable. Patient reads."
There were no entries for 2026, 2027. None for 2028.
"He stopped keeping the journal in 2025," said Kenji.
"Which means Ren was no longer 'stable.'"
"Or he knew he had entered a phase where the entries would be different."
Kurosawa was silent.

He looked at the registration form once more. At the date—the first of April 2022. And—at the stamp at the bottom of the form: the stamp of the chief physician of the psychiatric wing of Jindai-en, with a signature.
Jindai-en had no psychiatric wing.

Kurosawa knew this from familiarity with the institution's registry. Jindai-en had a children's ward, and a small medical station, and an isolation room in case of illness—there was no psychiatric wing.
"This is a forgery," he said.

"Yes," said Kenji. "He backdated the file when Ren was already with him. So that in case of a check—if someone came with a question—there would be a form. 'I care for him at a distance. Patient of the psychiatric wing.' There was no wing. There was a form. The form is paper."
"He had this in the second week after Ren disappeared."
"Or the third. No later."
Kurosawa closed the folder.
Placed it on the table beside Yoshida's personal.
Kenji had already moved on—to the letter M.
Pulled out a second folder. Thicker.
Mizuki Michiko, born 1978.
"That's her," said Kenji.
Kurosawa came over.
They opened it.
Date of admission—1985. Date of departure—1993. Niigata Medical School, 1993–1998. Specialization—nursing.
Further—a clipping from the graduates' journal of 1998, with a photograph. In the photo—Michiko, twenty years old, in a white nurse's uniform, with hair combed back, with a thin serious face.
Kurosawa looked. The face was the same as on the wall in the corridor—in the row of graduates of 1993—only older.
Kenji turned further.
The last official entry—2002. "Employed by the Niigata Woman's Clinic, third point of psychiatric support."
Further—blank.
But at the bottom of the page, in pencil, in fine writing, in Yoshida's hand:
"Michiko became Ayano," said Kenji. "He renamed her."
"When."
"In 2003. That is when he first 'called' her. From the thesis theory—'role therapy.' The name—also a role."
"Then this Ayano is not Ren's daughter. It is she."
"Yes, Kurosawa-san. It is she."
Kurosawa nodded.

He knew now that he had separated the two Ayanos even earlier—but only now was he holding paper confirmation in his hands. This was the woman from the Niigata clinic. Not the twenty-year-old daughter of Ren. This—a fifty-year-old nurse, with a double name, with two lives folded one into the other.
Kurosawa placed the Mizuki folder beside the two others.
Kenji went deeper into the shelves.
He knew he was looking for one more thing.
He pulled from the second shelf on the right edge a folder—thin, with a sticker "Takahashi Yuji, b. 1999, incomplete graduation."
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
Kenji placed the folder on the table beside the others.
Opened it.
Takahashi Yuji—22 years old. Ward from 2010 (age ten) to 2017 (age seventeen). After 2017—wardship at distance by Yoshida on "temporary-transitional status." Last entry in the folder—April 2021.

p.emphasis: Takahashi left home on a tour bus to Kushiro. Did not return. Missing report filed 3 May 2021.

section.p: Added in pencil, in the same terse hand of Yoshida:

p.emphasis: Found 6 June 2021. Sea. Identified by dental chart 15 August 2021.

section.p: Kurosawa looked at the date.
He knew what would come next. Did not want to know.
Kenji turned the page.

On the reverse a copy of the identification protocol was inserted. Body of a man, age approximately 20–25, height 174, thin build, heavy decomposition (two-three months in the water), identification impossible by appearance. Identified by dental chart.
Copy of the dental chart, overlaid on a diagram of the dental arch.
Kurosawa looked at the chart.
Did not understand at once.
Then understood.

This was the dental chart he had signed in 2022—when they had come to him from the Otaru morgue and shown him a copy of the card—and said that it matched Ren's dental record. And he had looked once then, and seen that it matched—and signed. Had not paid attention that it was that particular card—only that it matched.
Now he was holding the original in his hands. Not a 2022 copy. The 2021 original, from Takahashi's October file.
It was the same card.
That is.

That is, in the Otaru morgue in 2022 they had shown him not Ren's card. They had shown him Takahashi's card—with a new label pasted in the upper corner, "Kurosawa R." He had looked then. He had signed then.

Coroner Kawai Tatsuya—the same one who had died in 2024—had stood beside him and said that "dental match high." Kurosawa had believed him because he had no reason not to believe him. He had not examined the card himself then.
The body in the sea—was Takahashi.
Yuji, twenty-two years old.
Thin. Light-haired. Approximately the same build as Ren.

Died alone somewhere in early 2021, at sea. Body incidentally washed up in Kushiro. Decomposed. Identified by teeth with a swapped label—a year later, released to the Kurosawa family as their brother.
Buried in Ren's grave.
Exhumed in 2027 by Endo.
Kurosawa did not move for a long time.
Kenji stood beside him. Kept a hand on his shoulder. Said nothing at first. Then said quietly:
"Kurosawa-san. This is the body you signed for in 2022 as Ren."
"I know."
"It is Takahashi."
"I know."
"And this means one thing."
Kurosawa looked at him.
"Yes," he said. "It means Ren was already at Jindai-en in 2022. That he has been alive for six years."
"Yes."
Kenji opened his backpack. Pulled out a thin blue folder—with Endo's sticker, with a red diagonal band.
"One more, Kurosawa-san. Endo sent it two weeks ago. I did not show it earlier—was waiting for physical confirmation. Now we have it."
Kurosawa opened the folder.

Inside—three pages. First—the DNA-expertise protocol of the exhumed body from the grave of Kurosawa Ren, forensic laboratory at Hokkaido University, Endo's signature. Second—comparison sample: your archival, Kurosawa Yukio, taken in 2019 during a scheduled medical exam at reattestation (stored in the department bank). Third—comparison sample: Kurosawa Ayano, daughter, voluntarily given in March this year through the school nurse at the lyceum in Niigata.

"The conclusion is one," said Kenji. "On both axes. The body in the grave has no family match either with you as brother, or with her as daughter. Not Ren. This is a biological 'no,' not just a paper one."
Kurosawa looked at the conclusion. Two match figures—both below the threshold with which the court works. Both—with a period.
"So there were already two proofs," he said quietly.
"Now three," said Kenji. "DNA. Dental chart. Takahashi's personal file. On three independent lines."
Kurosawa closed the folder.

Three folders lay on the working table beside each other: Yoshida, Mizuki-Ayano, Takahashi. Plus—the distance medical form for Ren. Plus—the medical journal with the absence of a propofol license. Plus—Endo's blue folder with the DNA.
Six papers. Six lines that had previously run through separate lives.
Now they converged on one point.
Kenji placed a palm on the table. Did not speak.
Kurosawa looked at the stairs.
"I'm going to Yasuko-san," he said.
Kenji nodded.
"I'm still here. I need to log this. I'll scan everything."
"Don't hurry. Three copies. One—in the prosecutor's safe by evening."
"Yes."
Kurosawa went to the stairs. On the first step he stopped.
"Kenji."
"Yes, sir."
"Thank you."
Kenji nodded. Said nothing more.
Kurosawa came back to the table.
One more thing.
"One more," he said.
"Yes."
"Yoshida's cabinet in the administration office. He left it here when he went in 2019?"
"Yes. Inoue said it stands in his old place. He did not move it."
"It needs to be opened."
"The cabinet is not here. It is on the second floor."
"I know. That is for tomorrow."
"Yes."
Kurosawa returned to the three folders. Opened Yoshida's folder once more at the first page. Read again quietly.

At the end of the 1986 position card was a paragraph he had passed over on the first pass. In the fine hand of a secretary: "The candidate had his interview with director Mori Katsuya on the twenty-first of March 1986. The director gave a recommendation without questions. The candidate is a former ward of the home, 1970–1980. Has no personal relatives."
"Kenji," he said.
"Yes."
"This confirms the biography."
"Yes. He grew up here, was educated here, came back to teach, became director. Half a century in one building."
"One room."
"What?"
"In his work he wrote that a person got stuck on one moment. He himself got stuck on one building."
Kenji nodded. Did not speak.
Kurosawa closed the folder for the last time.
He held his palms on the table. For a second.
Then took his hands away. Stood.
Kurosawa went up.

p.emphasis: "Kurosawa-san. If your person is there—please, take him home."

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Four
section.p: Kurosawa came out of the basement into Inoue's office—closed the door behind him, turned the bolt. Inoue was sitting where he had been sitting. So was Toshi—with the same palms on his knees, in the same position, with the same two cups on the low table, which had now gone cold.
Inoue stood when Kurosawa came out. Kurosawa looked at him. Did not look long—but not fleetingly either.
"Inoue-san," he said. "I need to speak with Yasuko-san."
Inoue nodded. Did not ask why. He had already understood that the same people did not come back from the basement—so there was no point in asking.

"She is in the sitting room, on the ground floor, in the west wing. She sits there in December in the afternoon. It is her tea time with the children—but today the children are on an excursion to the port, they come back after five."
"Thank you."
Inoue looked at Toshi, then at Kurosawa.
"Nakamura-san stays with me."
"Yes," said Toshi. "I'll come to you when you call."
Kurosawa nodded.
He walked out into the corridor.
Walked slowly.
Passing the wall with the graduation photographs, he stopped. Once. Looked at the year 1993. At the girl in the second row—at her—at Mizuki, at the future Ayano. Looked for six seconds.
Then walked on.

The sitting room was in the west wing, with small windows that gave on the garden. Low ceiling. Walls paneled in light wood—old, worn, with two holes for clocks, of which only one still hung: small, round, with Arabic numerals and a dark wavy second hand that moved with a thin "tick."

In the corner of the room was a low wooden platform with tatami, and on it—a low table with two cushions. On the table—one thin teapot (the color of wet slate), one cup (white, with a thin crack across the bottom, traced in a thin golden line of kintsugi), and a small bamboo box for chopsticks, empty.
On the cushion on the left sat a woman.
Yasuko-san.

Kurosawa knew her from the photograph Kenji had sent from the pension registry. But in person, she turned out thinner. Seventy-eight years old. Small in stature. Back straight. Hair gray, combed back short, with a thin black pin above the left ear. Clothing—dark gray kimono of everyday cut, with a modest sash tied in two or three wraps. Hands—on knees, palms up, the way they are held by a person who is used to holding them.

Her face was of a kind familiar for Japanese women of her generation: thin bones, high cheekbones, with eyes that had dropped slightly with age—but had not lost a focused look. Such a look Kurosawa remembered in his mother.
She looked at him when he stopped in the doorway. Did not seem surprised. Did not rise.
"Kurosawa-san."
He nodded.
She had known his name before he gave it.
"Yasuko-san."
"Come in. Sit down."

He came in. He had already taken off his shoes at the genkan. Sat opposite her, on the right cushion—stretching his legs under the low table. Not the Japanese way. He knew he could not do it the Japanese way anymore; he was forty-seven, and his legs would no longer allow it.
Yasuko-san glanced at his legs—not with a look of judgment—and gave a brief nod.
"That will be more comfortable. Do not torment yourself."
"Thank you."
She took from the other side of the table a second cup—small, white, without a crack—and set it before him. Poured tea from the pot.
The tea was hōjicha—the one she made for the children. He knew by the smell.
He took the cup. Drank one sip. Held the cup in his palms.
"Yasuko-san."
"Yes."
"Inoue-san said you have been here since 1972."
"Since 1972. I came at twenty-two. Now I am seventy-eight."
"You remember Yoshida-sensei as a child."
"I remember. He was eleven when I came. He was quiet. Quieter than the others."
"What else do you remember."
Yasuko-san looked into her cup. For a long time. Then raised her eyes.

She looked at Kurosawa directly—that look Kurosawa had already known—from two hours ago, when Inoue had looked at him with it—the look that meant a person already knew what a guest had come with, and was only waiting for the guest to ask the question himself.
"Kurosawa-san," she said quietly. "You are looking for room number six."
Kurosawa was silent.
Looked at her.
Then nodded. Once.
"You know about it."
"Have always known."
"You went in."
"I did not go in. But I knew."
Kurosawa placed the cup on the table. Kept his hands on his knees.
"Tell me," he said.
Yasuko-san did not answer at once.
She took her cup. Drank one short sip. Set it down. Looked into the cup.
"My mother was a cleaner here before me. Do you know that?"
"No."

"Her name was Yasue. Yasuko is my name, chosen in her honor, with one different kanji. Mother came here in 1946, when the home took in the children of the war. She was taken on for cleaning because she had lost her husband at the front. I was born in 1949. I grew up here, in the service room, with my mother. Not as a ward—as the cleaner's daughter."
"I understand."
"In 1972 my mother fell ill with her lungs. I came in her place. I was twenty-two. She died in 1976—here, in the room next door—but she had time to work with me for four years."
Kurosawa nodded.

"Mother," Yasuko continued, "in 1975 made one duplicate key. The original of the key belonged to Mori—the then director. He kept the key in his desk. Mother did the cleaning in his office every morning, before he came in. One day she took the key—brought it to a locksmith on Hanazono-chō—had a copy made—and returned the original to its place the same day. No one noticed."
"Why did she make the copy."

"Because the annex had just been built in 1972, and it contained rooms where cleaners were not invited. Mother did not like rooms where she was not invited. That was her principle. She used to say: 'Where you do not go, something grows that you do not want to see later.'"
"I understand."
"She passed the key to me in 1976, when she lay down. She said I would never use it. But that I should keep it. And that I should know where the entrance was."
"You did not use it."
"I did not use it. Neither mother nor I. We kept it."
"Why."
Yasuko-san looked at him.

"Because we knew we should not. A cleaner in a children's home is, in a certain sense, the quietest of all who work there. Not because we are timid. Because a child in the home sees the cleaner every day—and must know that the cleaner does not bring trouble. A cleaner who has entered a room to which she was not invited is a cleaner who has eaten the child's trust for tomorrow. Mother and I decided the key would be for the day someone came in who was not a cleaner."
"I understand."
"You are not a cleaner."
"No."
"You are a brother."
Kurosawa was silent.
He held the cup.
"I knew you would come," said Yasuko. "I did not know when. I only knew you would come."
"How."

"Because Yoshida-sensei left two days ago. He went to Erimo alone. He would not have gone to Erimo unless he was certain you would come here. He took to Erimo something he could not fail to take. So here he left something he could not fail to leave."
Kurosawa looked at her.
"Yasuko-san."
"Yes."
"You do not love him."
"Kurosawa-san. I do. But that is second. First, I understand him."
"You understand what he is doing."
"I understand that he is doing what he would rather not do. These are different things. He is not bad. He is stuck. The difference is that the bad can be judged, and the stuck must be freed."
"Freed."
"Yes. Led out. Shown the end. Only not by me. I am the cleaner. Not my end."
Kurosawa was silent.
He knew how to hold a silence. Yasuko-san knew too.
She looked into her cup.
Then said:
"The key."

She drew from the sleeve of her kimono a thin cloth handkerchief. Unfolded it on the table. Inside lay a single key—long, black, metal, with a plain groove on the head. From 1975. Fifty-three years old.

"This is the key to the outer doors of the annex corridor. Not to room number six. That room Yoshida-sensei rebuilt in 1998, after Mori's death—a new lock—and I did not make a copy. In 1998 I could no longer—Yoshida-sensei was director now—and I had no access to his desk."
"I understand."
"But," Yasuko-san looked at him, "when you open the outer doors, you will go down the corridor to room number six itself. The door of the room is not locked."
"Why."
"Because Yoshida-sensei went to Erimo. He knew he was turning you toward them. This is his doctrine. He does not enter when he chooses that you should enter."
Kurosawa nodded slowly.
He understood. He had read the graduation thesis half an hour ago.

"The annex has been marked 'under reconstruction' since 2005," Yasuko added. "Since then I do not enter. Inoue-san does not either. Only Yoshida-sensei had a key. But the outer doors of the corridor are the old ones, from 1972. A new lock was never put on them. In 2005 they simply put up the sign 'repair' and closed them."
"My key fits there."
"Yes."
Kurosawa took the key. Held it in his palm. It was cold. Metal, with a thin layer of dust on the bit—a long dust—the dust of 1975.
He put the key into his left inner pocket, next to the chest pocket where the nenju lay.
"Yasuko-san."
"Yes."
"You want to tell me something more."
She looked at him. For a long time.
Then, quietly:
"Kurosawa-san. If your person is there—please, take him home."
Kurosawa did not answer at once.
He placed his palms on the table. Looked at her.
"I will," he said finally.
She nodded. Once.
Took her cup. Drank a sip.
"And one more thing."
"Yes."
"Yoshida-sensei will come back. Not today. Later, maybe tomorrow. He always comes back when he goes to Erimo. It is his ritual. He never stays at Erimo longer than two days."
"I know."
"You will not stop him from coming back."
"No."
Yasuko-san looked at him.
"Thank you."
Kurosawa nodded.
He stood—slowly—the knee had gone numb. Bowed once, deeply.
Walked to the door.
At the threshold he stopped. Turned.
"Yasuko-san."
"Yes."
"You have known him since childhood."
"Since eleven."
"What should he be called. When I see him."
Yasuko-san thought.
"By surname," she said. "Yoshida. He will not correct you. He does not like to give himself as Hiro. Hiro is his childhood name. He is Yoshida now. That is the one who has named himself already."
Kurosawa nodded.
Left.
Walked down the corridor. Did not look at the wall of photographs this time.

In Inoue's office he took Toshi. Kenji had already come up from the basement with two bags of scanned material. Kurosawa showed him the key in his palm. Kenji nodded—once—and glanced at his watch. Half past five in the evening. The children would soon be back from the port.
"Inoue-san."
"Yes, Kurosawa-san."
"We are going to the annex. Through the yard."
Inoue looked at the key in Kurosawa's palm.
Saw. Understood. Did not ask.
Nodded.
"Go," he said. "I will be here."
Kurosawa nodded.
He walked out of the office.
Kenji after him.
Toshi—with a slight lag, as always.
They went through the genkan. Put their shoes on. Kurosawa opened the exterior doors of the main block.
The yard was gray. Sky low. On the side wall of the annex was a small metal entrance—gray—with the sign "工事中" ("under repair") on an enameled plaque, faded.
Kurosawa walked toward it.
The key in his pocket.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Five
section.p: The annex kept its own air apart from the rest of the house. Yasuko-san walked ahead with a short step, the key in her right hand—the same key her mother's brother had cut for her in seventy-five out of brass, its teeth worn down to flat grooves by fifty years of one and the same turn. Kurosawa followed her two steps behind, as one follows the elderly—without hurrying, without drawing closer, keeping the gap in which she could stop.

They went down a concrete slope from the back side of the main building—to the lower yard, dusted with the first gray snow. In the yard stood two iron pails of sand, a wooden shovel with a cloth-wrapped handle—and a metal door painted the same gray-beige color as the whole annex of seventy-two. The door had no plaque. Only, around the lock—a brass rim, worn to yellow.
Yasuko-san stopped half a step from it.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes, Yasuko-san."
"I did not go in. Since seventy-five. I will turn the key and wait upstairs. If you need anything—call."
"Thank you."

She inserted the key. Turned it slowly, with two clicks—with the small resistance a key takes in a lock that has not been looked into in a very long time. The door yielded half a finger. Yasuko-san did not push it wider. She took out the key. Put it in the pocket of her apron.
"Take with you only what you can carry yourself."
Kurosawa nodded.
She turned and walked back to the stairs. Kept one hand on the concrete rail. Did not look back.
Kurosawa waited until her steps had faded into the upper corridor. Then pushed the door.
Behind it was a corridor.

Straight, long, with a ceiling at the height of a man's stature plus a palm. Walls—gray concrete without plaster, with small streaks where over these half-centuries damp had risen. One lamp in the ceiling in the middle of the corridor—of the old kind, in a metal wire cage—and one just like it at the very end, twenty-two steps away—both burning with an even yellow light. Yoshida had left them on. Kurosawa noted this and did not stop.
Twenty-two steps. He counted them in his mind—not because he wanted to count, but because the counting kept his hands at his sides and his shoulders lowered.

At the seventh step he noticed the smell—warm, domestic, with that light note of boiled rice that came through the door once every two days. At the twelfth—he heard, from outside, behind the metal door at his back, in the yard, one drop fall from a downspout onto concrete. One short sound. At the nineteenth—the ceiling of the corridor became half a palm lower—it was not so, only seemed so—and Kurosawa walked on.
At the very end—a door of dark wood. Brass handle. The order in the handle was old—from fingers that touched it every day—and the bronze had that thin sheen a hand gives, not a rag.
He put his palm on the handle.
The handle was warm.

Warm in the way the handle of a door is warm to a room in which someone lives. Not hot—warm to human temperature—with that thin note of wax from fingers that stays on brass from daily touch. Kurosawa held his palm where a man's fingers had held their palm six years running—and there was no sharp feeling—only that things touched become warm, and things untouched—cold, and that this handle knew its daily warmth without him.
He opened.

p.emphasis: This was not a discovery. In the annex steps rang from the concrete clearly—right, left, right—and over the years he had learned to recognize Yoshida-sensei's steps from the ground floor. The steps that had entered the corridor a few minutes ago were different. Heavier. Two: women's steps, small—and then men's, even. The women's steps had turned back. The men's—had not.

He set the book aside on the low stool beside the bed. It was a small book in a gray paper cover, with one kanji on the binding—an old translation of a Chinese poet Yoshida-sensei had brought him in the winter. He was reading it slowly. One page in the morning, one after the midday meal. Today he had read one, because he was not used to reading after the midday meal without Yoshida-sensei, who would be drinking tea nearby.
The step stopped outside the door.

In that pause he had time to think about Yoshida-sensei. About how yesterday Yoshida-sensei had placed the book on the stool and said: "Ren, I will be gone for a few days." He had not said where. Had not said when he would return. Had not said what to do if someone else came. Yoshida-sensei did not say many things—not because he was hiding them, but because he considered: if it was needed, he would say.
He had time for one thing—to pull the blanket from his feet—and the door opened.

section.p: The room was small. Four tatami, slightly worn along the central path. One lamp on a low stand beside the bed, in a glass shade of cream color. Washbasin in the corner, low, with a single tap. Portable toilet in a niche behind a screen of rice paper. Walls—tatami, from floor to ceiling, with thin bamboo stitching every half-meter. One low bed by the far wall, with a plain cotton blanket in beige stripes.

On the side wall, at shoulder height—a small shelf. On the shelf—a single porcelain figurine without a face. Fifteen centimeters tall, smooth, in the form of an empty cone. Kurosawa saw it in one second—with that peripheral vision a policeman keeps separate—and forgot it at once, because a thin man was rising from the bed in front of him.

The man was in a gray cotton pajama. Hair to the shoulders, gray in patches. Face—clean-shaven, skin pale. Hands slow. He did not sit up straight at once—he raised his torso from the bed calmly—the way one rises who has already lived through several guests over the years and knew that the guest was not in a hurry.
He put his feet on the floor. Did not stand.
Kurosawa stood on the threshold. Did not step further than the first tatami.
The man raised his head.
"Yukio."

Kurosawa recognized the voice half a second before the face. The voice—low, soft—the same one that had sounded in the receiver in the year twenty-two from Otaru on a January evening, when they had arranged to meet at a kissa-ten.
"Ren."
Pause.
"It's me," said Kurosawa.

Ren looked at him. Looked for about twenty seconds—without haste, without fear, with that slow focus that comes when the eye has not held something at this distance in a long time. Then sat upright. Lowered his right hand onto his right thigh. Tapped with a fist. Once. Slowly.
"It's you."
"You came."
"Yes."
Kurosawa took half a step inside. No more. Went down on his knees on the threshold—a motion older than himself—and sat on his heels. Placed his palms backs down on his thighs.
Ren watched him calmly.
"Yukio," said Ren. "Does Yoshida-sensei know you are here?"
Kurosawa considered his answer. No longer than needed to find an honest word.
"I don't know."
Ren nodded. Lightly. With that particular nod with which one hears a truth that changes nothing.
"He knows everything."
Kurosawa was silent.
Ren looked past him—into the empty part of the corridor beyond the door. Then back at him.

p.emphasis: Yukio was grayer. The lock above his left temple had gone white—not gray—and one eye held more wrinkles at the outer corner than the other. His coat was black. He had not worn such coats in his youth. Mother would have said that a man in a black coat looks older than he is.
Mother had died when he was five. Yukio had been one. This was long ago.

section.p: He did not know how long. He knew that between the time when they had sat at the kissa-ten on the second floor of Otaru station and Yukio had asked for black coffee—and this now—some time had passed. Yoshida-sensei used to say that time now was not important. That when it was important, he would say so.

p.emphasis: He tapped his fist on his thigh. Once. The hand did this by itself, when it met something new. Yukio was something new. Yukio was something old.

Behind Yukio's shoulder the corridor stretched long and dim. In this corridor six years ago there had been nothing—so Yoshida-sensei had said. He had said: "Ren, when you wake up, you will be in a room, beyond which is nothing. That will be good. You will be able to rest." He had done just that. He had rested. He had not asked what was beyond the corridor. There was no sense in asking about what did not exist.
Now beyond the corridor stood Yukio, and Yukio was in a black coat.
He tapped his fist on his thigh again. Quieter than the first time. Only for himself.

section.p: "Yukio," said Ren. "How long has it been?"
Kurosawa held the pause. Not because he did not know—but because he did not want the words to come sooner than they were needed.
"Six years, Ren."
Ren was silent for a long time.
Kurosawa counted the seconds mentally—not to know the number, but because the number kept his shoulders lowered. Ninety. One hundred. One hundred twenty.
"And Ayano?" said Ren.
"Alive," said Kurosawa. "In Niigata. Twenty years old."
Ren did not move. Looked at his own knees. At the thin fabric of the pajama over the bones that showed. Right hand on right thigh, calmly. Left—on left.
"Twenty."

Kurosawa nodded. Nothing needed to be said. He understood that Ren was now counting in his mind what Kurosawa had counted on the way here—and that between them for these twenty seconds there was nothing but arithmetic that neither of them wanted to do.
"Ayano," said Ren once more, quieter.
"Yes."
"Twenty."
"Yes."
Ren lowered his head. Did not weep. Breathed evenly.
Kurosawa sat on the threshold. Did not draw closer.

He knew that with one motion now he could disturb that thin thing on which Ren held—the thin thing Yoshida had sculpted for six years—and he did not want to. Not out of pity for Yoshida. Out of care for Ren. Ren was holding now on the fact that he knew the rules of his room—and that Yukio, having come into it, had accepted those rules without inquiring in advance.

He looked at Ren calmly. Noticed. Hands—dry, with a thin layer of winter chapping on the knuckles—not thin, but drained in that particular calm sense that comes from long years in one rhythm: rise early, read one page in the morning, eat twice, read the second page after the midday meal, lie down early. On the back of the left wrist—a flat mark from a watch that had been taken off and put on every day for years—and no watch on the wrist itself. Ren did not wear it. Yoshida-sensei took the watch away at night and returned it in the morning—Kurosawa guessed this in one second—and now there was no watch because Yoshida-sensei had not returned it yesterday.

Hair—longer than Ren used to wear it—but tended. The gray lock above the right ear had gone fully white. The skin of the neck—thin, without a sun-tan. Face clean-shaven. Someone had shaved Ren today. Kurosawa did not know who. Knew it was not Ren himself.
He looked past Ren's shoulder—at the shelf with the porcelain figurine.

Fifteen centimeters tall. Porcelain white, with a thin cream tint in the folds. Form—an empty cone, body without arms, without a face—only a suggestion of shoulders and a light curve where a neck ought to be. On the front face—a vertical line scratched with a needle, shallow. In the Japanese tradition such figures were called hitogata—"in the likeness of a person"—paper or clay dolls into which, during a Shinto ritual of purification, sin, illness, evil were transferred. Then they were burned or sent down the water.
Kurosawa had known this since his father's house. His father had a book about ō-harae—the great purification at the end of the year—and read it in winter, when he drank.

p.emphasis: Yoshida had been transferring something onto Ren for six years.

section.p: He held this thought for one long second. Then closed it, the way one closes the lid of a box that holds things better not kept open.
He did not move.
Did not move further.
Outside the corridor, from the far end, in the lower yard, somewhere, one drop fell from a downspout onto concrete. One sound. Then silence again.
Ren raised his head.
Looked at Kurosawa.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Did you come alone?"
Kurosawa thought.
"No."
"How many?"
"One is with me now in the house. Another—will be here in an hour."
"Who."
"Toshi Nakamura. You do not know him. And Kenji Yamada. You do not know him either."
Ren nodded. These names told him nothing. But he nodded.
Then—looked past Kurosawa's shoulder again. Into the corridor.
Kurosawa did not turn. He knew no one was there. Yet.

p.emphasis: He sat upright and thought about how Yukio for six years had thought he was dead. Yoshida-sensei had never told him that directly. But one evening—a year or two ago—Yoshida-sensei had said: "Ren, you are resting from the world now." He had not asked then what that meant. He knew he would ask when Yoshida-sensei was ready to say.
Yoshida-sensei was always ready to say. Only not about this.

He thought about Ayano. About how at six in the morning of January in the year twenty-two she had been drinking milk from the bowl in which he was supposed to have buckwheat. About how she had said then: "Papa, are you coming today to pick me up from the drawing club?"—and he had said: "I'll come."—and had not come.
This was not imagination. It was a number. He held it on his tongue like a smooth stone.

He thought about Yukari. The wife who had left in the year nine. He remembered her well—the motions of her hands as she cut onions in the kitchen—but did not remember the color of her voice in their last years together. When she had said: "Ren, I can't anymore."—had she said it thinly, or deeply, or evenly? He did not remember. He knew only that she had said it the way a person says it when she does not want to hurt by leaving.
Yoshida-sensei had asked him once: "Ren, are you angry with her?" He had answered then: "No." Yoshida-sensei had nodded. With the nod with which a truth is received that need not be proved.

It had been—it seemed—recently. Yoshida-sensei always sat in seiza on the tatami beside his bed and asked two or three questions per visit. No more. He would answer. Yoshida-sensei drank tea and listened. Then left.
Now beyond the door stood Yukio. Yoshida-sensei was somewhere. He did not know where.
He did not ask. He was not in the habit of asking.

section.p: Kurosawa looked at the watch on his wrist only once—to know he had begun counting at fourteen thirty-four—and did not look again.
One minute.
A second.
A fifth.
Ren once turned his head—to the right—hearing some sound outside the door. Kurosawa heard it too: far, from the upper floor—Inoue was speaking with Kenji on the phone, quietly. Then silence again.

At the sixth minute Kurosawa noticed the book on the bedside stool. Gray paper cover. One kanji on the binding. He read it from seven paces away—「静」, "quiet." Later he would recall it had been a translation of Du Fu—not the early Du Fu, but the quiet Du Fu of his last years in the boat. Ren was reading him slowly.

At the seventh minute Kurosawa noticed Ren's left hand. On the back, between thumb and index finger—a thin white scar Ren had received at twelve, when he was cutting paper for a collage and Kurosawa, eight years old, had pushed his elbow. There had been blood then, and Aunt Kiyoko—Ren's future wife did not yet exist—had stitched the cut with kitchen thread and scolded Yukio quietly, so as not to wake their father.
The scar was the same.
At the eighth minute Ren said, very quietly:
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Don't leave now."
"I'm not leaving."
"Stay."
"I'll stay."
Kurosawa did not move. Neither did Ren.
Another drop fell in the lower yard. Another.

Beyond the corridor wall, somewhere far in the upper floor of the main building, a clock with a tower mechanism struck the half hour. Kurosawa heard it through the concrete as a thin vibrational stroke. One. Then a long vanishing of the sound.
He sat.
Ren sat.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Is it winter outside?"
Kurosawa looked at the ceiling of the room—not because the answer was there—but because that is what a person does who is gathering a simple fact in his head before speaking it.
"Yes, Ren. Our first snow was the night into Wednesday."
"In Otaru."
"In Otaru."
Ren nodded.
"Yoshida-sensei said this year's winter would be quiet."
"We'll see," said Kurosawa. "He may be right."
Ren thought.
"Will you let it live out for him?"

Kurosawa was silent. He knew Ren was not asking literally now. Knew Ren was placing on the table now—between them—everything he knew about Yoshida-sensei, and that this "everything" held on one understanding: Yoshida-sensei would decide for himself. Kurosawa allowed the pause to be what it was.
"We'll see," he said.
Ren nodded once more. Accepted this answer as one accepts a neutral weather.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"I'll stay here a little longer."
"Stay."
Kurosawa did not move. Ren did not move either. Between them—seven tatami, one lamp, one porcelain figurine on the shelf, and one book on the low stool, open on a page Ren had not yet read.
The room held them both.

section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Six
section.p: Toshi came into the corridor at fifteen forty-two. Kurosawa heard his steps on the eighth—because Toshi had set his foot down deliberately heavier than his normal step, so that Kurosawa would hear. Toshi did not hold his hands in front of him in the cuffs; the guard, senior sergeant Yamaguchi, walked two steps behind him, with the key in his right hand and the holster fastened on the clasp.
Kurosawa turned his head. Did not stand.
Ren saw his movement and turned his head too, calmly—with the same slow focus with which he had been looking at everything new the whole time.
Toshi stopped a meter from the door. Did not enter. Yamaguchi—likewise.
"Kurosawa-san," Toshi said very quietly.
"Yes."
"He has come."
"How?"

"On foot from the station. He came by train. From Hidaka he traveled overland—on foot to Samani, from there by taxi to Obihiro, then a train through Sapporo. Two days on the road. Yasuko-san is with him in the sitting room. Kenji says for me to call you."
Kurosawa nodded.
"Tell Kenji to keep the camera on the sitting room on his screen. Tell Yasuko-san to bring Yoshida-sensei up here. Alone. Without you, without the sergeant."
Toshi looked at him for one second.
"Yes."
"Thank you."
Toshi turned and walked back down the corridor. Yamaguchi—after him. The footsteps died on the upper floor. Then silence again.
Ren looked at Kurosawa. Looked until he saw Kurosawa did not intend to explain.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Yoshida-sensei is coming here."
"Yes."
"That is good."
Kurosawa did not answer. Ren noted this—and did not note it at the same time. Nodded. Lowered his right hand onto his right thigh and left it there. Did not tap.
"Yukio," said Ren, still more quietly. "Is Yoshida-sensei coming here for me, or for you?"
Kurosawa turned his head. Looked at Ren for one long second. Then said, with the small yielding with which one places on the table a thing Ren wanted to see:
"For himself, Ren."
Ren thought.
"That is also good," he said quietly. Not an evaluation. A statement of a fact he held calmly in his eyes.
Kurosawa did not answer.
Kurosawa waited.

He heard, upstairs, the doors of the sitting room open. Heard two voices sound—a quiet man's and a quiet woman's—and steps begin on the stairs. One pair of steps, then another. Yasuko-san went first—by the custom of the hostess—Yoshida-sensei walked half a step behind her.

Kurosawa rose. Not at once—with the pause in that second when the body asks the head whether it is ready, and the head answered: ready. He stood upright. Placed his feet shoulder-width. Kept his hands at his sides.

Ren saw this and also rose. Not at once—with the same slow motion—but stood. Placed his feet awkwardly, with the uncertainty that comes after six years without proper shoes. Stood five seconds, found balance—and did not sit back down.
Yasuko-san appeared on the threshold. Nodded to Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa-san. Yoshida-san."
"Thank you, Yasuko-san."

She took a step back into the corridor. Yoshida passed her. Yasuko-san did not look at him. She turned and walked back toward the stairs—with the same calm short step with which she had come—with a hand on the concrete rail.
Yoshida stopped half a step from the threshold. Did not cross.

He was exactly as Kurosawa had seen him on the Erimo lighthouse—in the same gray coat below mid-thigh, the same dark leather shoes, the same thin face with high cheekbones. Only now—after two days on the road: on foot from Hidaka to the Samani pier, taxi across the valley to Obihiro, train through Sapporo to Otaru—his lips were thin and dry. The coat carried the smell of carriage dust and the dry trace of rain on the collar. The shoes had dried on top, but in the crevices of the soles still held a crumb of gravel from the Obihiro station.
In his right hand Yoshida held a small case. Black, with a brass latch, the size of a medium book.
He looked past Kurosawa's shoulder—at Ren.
Ren looked at him.
"Yoshida-sensei."
"Ren."
Yoshida smiled. With one corner of the mouth. One motion carried through to the end. The way a person smiles who comes home after a long journey and sees that the home has held together without him.

He turned his gaze briefly to the small porcelain figurine on the shelf of the side wall. Looked at it for one second—with that calm eye with which a master looks at a thing he has placed by his own hand in the place where it was to be. Did not correct anything. The figurine held its place on its own. He was satisfied with that.

Then he looked at the bedside stool. Noted the open page in the book—at the place where Ren had left it when he heard the steps. The corner of his lips lifted briefly once more. He kept in his memory which page Ren was to have read today after the midday meal—and saw that Ren had not read it.
This did not sadden him. This did not console him. He merely noted it.
Then Yoshida looked at Kurosawa.
"You found him."
Kurosawa looked into his eyes. Did not narrow. Did not turn away.
"I am arresting you."
Yoshida nodded. Lightly.
"I know. Let me finish. This is my doctrine."
Kurosawa was silent.

He heard through the walls of the annex—far above, in the sitting room—Kenji say something to Yamaguchi. The plastic of the holster clicked ringingly. Yamaguchi's steps came up to the stairs of the annex and stopped.
Kurosawa did not move.

He knew that this scene could be closed now with a single motion. One gesture of the hand—and Yamaguchi would come down, two more from the yard would come up, Yoshida would be laid into steel, driven to the district station, given a card there, prints taken, put in a cell. Judicial expertise, investigation, indictment, court, verdict. Three or four years of process. In those years Yoshida would write a book about the doctrine. A public book—in soft cover—and in it there would be a paragraph about Ren, soft and warm, which Kurosawa would not be able to read without thinking about his second of inattention on Erimo.
He knew this.
He held his hands at his sides.
Yoshida stepped over the threshold.
He came into the room—evenly, without haste—and stopped a step from Ren. Did not draw closer. Did not touch. Only looked.
"Ren."
"Yes, sensei."
"Yoshida-sensei must go."
Ren watched him.
"Where, sensei?"
"To my sister."
Ren looked past Yoshida's shoulder into that same empty part of the corridor beyond the door he had looked into a minute ago. Then back at him.
"To Misako."
Yoshida smiled a second time. Just as briefly.
"To Misako."
Pause.
Ren lowered his head. Did not weep. Breathed evenly. His right hand slowly went to his right thigh and remained there. Did not tap.
Yoshida turned to Kurosawa.
"Do not take from him what I gave him."
Kurosawa did not answer.
Yoshida waited for an answer two seconds. Then—with the small yielding with which one hands the word to a person who prefers not to give it—nodded.
Kurosawa looked at him.

Then—not because he decided, but because the body decided before the head—Kurosawa lowered himself to his knees. Not on the threshold—he had stood on the threshold long enough. Now he entered the room, took three steps past Yoshida, and sat on the tatami a meter and a half from him, on his heels, with his palms backs down on his thighs.
He sat as his father had sat at New Year's bowings—evenly, without haste, with that straight back that the body holds by itself when the head has released it for a few minutes.
Yoshida saw this. Did not understand at once. Then understood.

He also lowered himself. Slowly—with that slow motion of a person whose knees have known seiza for forty years and had begun in those forty years to hurt little by little. His left hand came to his left knee back down. His right—to his right.

They sat opposite each other. Three tatami between them. The case with the brass latch lay on the tatami half a step from Yoshida's right knee. Ren on the bed behind Yoshida's back—did not move. Toshi on the threshold—did not enter.
Kurosawa looked at Yoshida.
"You killed him."

It came—as it had come at the Erimo lighthouse—before he had time to think from what place in himself he had said it. But this time he knew from which. From the same place from which the question had not come out at the lighthouse.
Yoshida held his gaze.
"Yes," he said quietly. "Yes, Kurosawa-san. I killed him."
Pause.

"Not in the sense in which people kill with a knife. In the sense in which a person kills who takes from another six years of his life. I killed him. I say this to you now because you need to hear it. At the lighthouse I told you I preserved him. That was true. It was also not the whole truth. I preserved him by what I took from him."
Kurosawa was silent.
Yoshida did not look away.
"I owe you this word," he said. "I give it to you."
Kurosawa looked past Yoshida's shoulder—at Ren. Ren sat upright on the bed, with his hands on his thighs. Did not interfere. Did not look.
"You did not ask him."
"I did not ask."
"You thought for him."
"Yes."
"Six years."
"Yes."
Kurosawa turned his eyes back to Yoshida. Did not raise his voice. Did not lower it.
"Misako."
Yoshida blinked once.
"Yes."
"You think it is she there, in Ren's head."
Yoshida looked at him for a long time. Did not answer at once. Then said—with the same quiet even voice with which people speak a phrase they have held in themselves sixty years:
"I do not think, Kurosawa-san. I know."
Pause.

"I know this not the way science is known. I know it the way a fisherman knows there will be a storm tomorrow when the water turns two shades darker before it can be seen from the shore. I know this in myself. Do not ask whether it is true. The truth and what I know—are different things. I know."
Kurosawa nodded. Not in agreement. In acknowledgment that he had heard.
"You placed her there."
"I did not place her there. I only left the door open."
"That is your phrase from Erimo."
"Yes. It is my one phrase. I repeat it because I have no other."
Pause.
Kurosawa looked at his own knees. At the thin fabric of his dark trousers. At the dust from the corridor—a small gray thread that had caught on his cuff. Did not shake it off.
"Sasaki," he said.
Yoshida did not answer at once.
"Yes."
"That was your choice."
Yoshida lowered his chin half a finger. Not a nod. Something more.
"Mine. Not hers."
Kurosawa nodded again. The same way.
"You chose."

"I chose. I did not choose her. I was choosing you. I set the back door with the timer, with the calculation that it would be blown through in the second you looked at it. I did not calculate that she would leap. But I did calculate that if she did leap, I would not argue with it. That is what you wanted to hear from me. I say it to you."
Kurosawa was silent.
"You owed her," Yoshida added. "I did not owe. That does not comfort. I know."
"No," said Kurosawa. "It does not comfort."
Pause.

Toshi outside the threshold shifted his weight from his right foot to his left. The steps did not ring—Kurosawa heard it by the thin rustle of his trouser fabric against the jamb. Yamaguchi stood two landings up. No one came down.

Kurosawa noted this. He understood that if Toshi took half a step forward now and said one word—Yamaguchi would come down in ten seconds, and the scene would change. Toshi did not take the half step. Toshi held his silence the way one holds a key in a pocket when it is not yet time to open with it.
Kurosawa accepted this.

He knew—with that thin corner that knew about his next actions half a second before the actions themselves—that legally he ought now to rise, give the order to Yamaguchi, put steel on Yoshida, drive him to Otaru. That this was the line he had served for twenty-three years.
He knew it.
He did not cross it.
He held his palms on his thighs, backs down—as Yoshida held his—and allowed these two pairs of hands to hold themselves the same in two bodies that held different things inside.
"Yoshida-san."
"Yes, Kurosawa-san."
"How many years have you waited for this."
Yoshida thought. He counted not for himself—he knew—but so that Kurosawa would hear the figure slowly.
"Twenty-three."
"Since Otaru in two thousand and five."
"Since Otaru in two thousand and five."
"You saw me there."
"I saw you there."
"You chose."
"I chose you."
Pause.
Kurosawa nodded. Accepted.

He understood—with the slow clarity with which an investigator in the thirtieth year of service understands—that he had just been given three things he had been searching for through three books. That it would not lighten. That it would now live in him apart from his actions. That this was what Yoshida wanted to finish in himself. Not confession. Testimony.
Kurosawa was witnessing.
Yoshida saw it.
"Now it is possible," he said quietly.
Kurosawa looked at him.
"Yes."
Yoshida rose from the tatami. Not quickly. The body knew how to rise from seiza after a long sitting—and it rose.

He took a step to the center of the room. Lowered the case onto the tatami beside his right foot. Took off his coat—unhurried—hung it on the brass hook above the washbasin, the same one on which for six years Ren's spare pajama had hung. Unfastened the cuff of his right sleeve. Rolled the sleeve up to the elbow.

On the forearm—two fingers below the elbow crease—was an IV cannula. Already inserted. Since yesterday. Held in place by a strip of white plaster wound with thread so it would not slip. Port closed with a rubber plug. Trocar clear, with a thin notch for tubing. Ayano—the former Michiko from Jindai-en, the current nurse at the Niigata clinic—had come to him the day before and placed the cannula herself, with cold hands and without a word. Yoshida had summoned her with a single line from the payphone at the Obihiro passenger station on Tuesday evening, as he stepped off the train. One line was old, learned forty years earlier: "Get ready, come." Ayano had come to Genshō-an on Wednesday by the night train, placed the cannula on Thursday morning, and left back the same day. Kurosawa saw this only now. He understood it had been impossible to see the first time.

Yoshida sat down on the tatami. A plain motion of seiza—knees on the tatami, heels under the buttocks—with the naturalness with which a person sits who has accumulated three or four thousand hours in this pose in a lifetime. Right hand came to right knee, back down.
He opened the case.

Inside: one syringe with twenty milliliters of clear liquid, in a plastic sheath. One short luer-lock adapter. A thin swab with isopropyl alcohol in a sealed sachet. One small pack of cotton. Everything laid out tidily—not like a nurse's kit, but the way a master lays out an instrument he has long been preparing.

Kurosawa recognized the propofol at first glance. Not by the label—there was no label—but by the characteristic milky-clear note of the liquid in the syringe, with that light pastel impression the lipid emulsion gives. Twenty milliliters. Standard induction dose for an adult. Ayano had calculated it to the milligram. Kurosawa was placing in his head one check mark—"Michiko-Ayano, Niigata clinic, theft via wholesale warehouse"—and closing the folder.

Yoshida broke the syringe's seal. Fitted the adapter—with two fingers—with the thin click a luer-lock gives when it seats evenly. Broke the seal of the swab. Wiped the port of the cannula. For one second he held the syringe in the air—not to think—but so that the liquid in the syringe would settle, the way water settles in a cup when it has just been poured.
Yoshida raised his eyes. Looked at Ren.
"Ren."
"Yes, sensei."
"Do you remember, I told you that one day I must leave?"
"I remember."
"This is it."
Ren nodded. The way a pupil nods who has carried for ten years in his bag one sentence from a teacher and has now taken it out, unfolded it, seen that it is the same.
"Yoshida-sensei."
"Yes, Ren."
"Thank you."

Yoshida looked at him for a long time. Then—with the small yielding with which a person allows himself to step half a palm off the rules of politeness—touched with his right hand the right corner of his eye. Did not wipe anything. Simply touched. Then returned the hand to its place.
"You are welcome, Ren."
Pause.
Yoshida turned his gaze from Ren and looked at the syringe. Held it in his right hand. The left hand lay calmly on his left knee, back down, with open fingers.
Kurosawa was watching. Did not interrupt.

He understood—with the slow clear understanding with which an adult hears for a second time a tale told to him in childhood—that what was happening now was the last conversation of a master with the one pupil who had received him. That this was a farewell. That this was a ritual. That no court would have a procedure for this—because no court writes procedures for what it does not see.
He held his hands at his sides.
Toshi stood in the doorway.

He came in quietly—Kurosawa heard one short step behind him—and stopped where the room ended and the corridor began. The cuffs on his wrists did not clink. Yamaguchi behind him did not step into the annex—stood on the stairs two landings up—and Toshi had come alone.
Toshi looked at Yoshida. Then at Kurosawa.
"Kurosawa-san."
One word. Quietly. Without request, without command. Only a statement of fact: he was here, he was waiting—and a question, whether Kurosawa wanted this fact to have a continuation.
Kurosawa looked at him.
"No, Toshi."
Toshi nodded. Lightly. Accepted the answer.
He took half a step back. Now he stood on the threshold itself, but did not cross. Watched. Did not move.

Yoshida did not notice these two things—not because he did not see them, but because he no longer needed to see them. He held the syringe in his right hand and the adapter in his left. Connected the syringe to the port. Clicked. Pulled the plunger back half a millimeter—to make sure the tubing held in the vein. Saw a thin red thread in the clear short segment between the cannula and the port. Nodded to himself.
Then he pressed the plunger.
Not fast. Not slow. Evenly—with the same steady force with which one pours water from a ceramic pitcher into a cup—and the plunger went down evenly.
Yoshida looked not at the syringe—at Ren. Looked with that particular quiet gaze with which a master looks at his last piece placed on the shelf. Not with pride. With attentiveness.
Ren held his gaze. Did not turn away. Did not weep. One hand lay on his right thigh, calmly. The other—on the left.
Kurosawa sat on the threshold.

He noted the time in himself—not because he wanted to count, but because the counting kept his shoulders lowered. Yoshida had begun the injection at sixteen zero-two. In fifteen seconds the plunger would reach the end. Another twenty seconds—the liquid would enter the bloodstream to the heart. Propofol, through six to eight loops of vascular circulation, would reach the brain and bind the GABA receptors. Then—sleep. Then—the thin long inhale a body takes before a long exhale. Then—a quiet exhale. Then—silence.
Kurosawa watched.

He knew propofol in this dose and at this speed gave a sweet sleep—not suffering. Knew a person felt only a brief warmth in the vein, then light dizziness, then—sleep. Knew breathing would fall silent at the second minute, the heart at the third. Knew that in the medical dictionary this was called induction. In obituaries this word would not appear. It would be: "passed away in his sleep."

He knew also that this could be stopped now only by one motion—snatch the syringe from Yoshida's hand—and that this motion would be a violation of something for which he had no word. Not the law. The law demanded that motion. Not conscience. Conscience was silent in him.
He allowed the thing for which he had no word to hold his hands at his sides.
Yoshida drove the syringe to the end. Carefully disconnected it from the port—with one finger held the plug—and put the syringe back into the case. Closed the case. Did not rise.
He sat in seiza on the tatami, evenly—with that evenness with which a person sits who has kept his back straight for forty years and knew no other posture—and waited.
One minute. Did not move.
Kurosawa looked at him.
"Yoshida-san."
Yoshida raised his eyes. Not at once. With the small delay with which a person answers his own name when anesthesia is already holding him by the shoulders.
"Yes, Kurosawa-san."
"I have arrested you."
Pause.
"You knew this."
"I knew."
Yoshida looked at him calmly. Another pause. Then—with that thin evenness with which one holds a cup when the hand is already tired but still sets it down straight—he said:
"Thank you."
Kurosawa nodded. Did not answer.
Two. The thin color was leaving the face, the fingers, the backs of the hands. The head lowered half a palm forward. No heavier.
Ren stood by his low bed. Did not move. Looked at Yoshida.
Kurosawa did not look at Ren.
At the second minute and ten seconds Yoshida quietly—with the evenness with which one speaks the last note of a chord—said one word:
"Misako."
Pause.
Then another pause, longer than the first. Then a third, longer than the second.

At the third minute Yoshida's chest made one slow motion up and did not make the motion down. His hand—the one which had held the empty fingers of the syringe half a minute ago—lay back down on his right knee calmly, with a thin layer of old wax on the fingernails from rubbing the skin of the Kannon in Genshō-an.

He did not fall. His posture held him another thirty seconds after he had left it. Then the left shoulder blade slowly leaned to the side—not sharply—and Yoshida lowered onto his side, onto the tatami, with a motion that was natural to the extent that natural is the motion of a person falling asleep on a futon.
He lay there.
His legs remained in seiza. The right palm—the one in which the syringe had just been—came to the tatami beside his face, open, palm up.
The room held its air apart.
Kurosawa stood.
Did not go to Ren at once. For a minute he stood where he had stood. Looked at Yoshida on the tatami. At the empty palm, open up. At the lock of gray hair that had fallen onto Yoshida's forehead.

He understood—not as a thought, but as a thin sensation in the chest—that this scene would be tried in him longer than its memory would last. That Prosecutor Fujiwara from Otaru at three in the night would phone him and ask: "Kurosawa-keibu, why did you not intervene." That he would answer: "There was nothing to intervene in." That this would not be a truth and would not be a lie. That Fujiwara would not be satisfied with that. That the applications of the internal disciplinary commission would be taken up for review. That Tanaka Ryosuke in Tokyo would sign his retirement. That all this was long, slow machinery—that had now only begun.
He allowed himself one full pause. Not to think. To let the pause be.
Then he turned his head.

Ren stood on the same spot beside the bed. Did not weep. Breathed evenly. His right hand slowly rose and touched the corner of his eye—wiped nothing—only touched. Then dropped back onto the right thigh.
Kurosawa took a step into the center of the room.

Did not draw close to Yoshida. Passed him at half a step. Lowered himself onto the tatami beside Ren—at the distance at which one usually sits down beside an elder brother at a low table—and sat on his heels. Kept his hands to himself. Did not touch Ren.
Ren looked at him.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Stay."
"I will."
Kurosawa sat. Ren sat. Yoshida lay.

Toshi quietly turned back to the stairs and went out into the lower yard. Kurosawa heard through the walls—far, in the lower yard—Toshi saying briefly, calmly, in the same quiet voice of his, one phrase after another into the receiver to Sergeant Yamaguchi. "Yamaguchi-san. Call a doctor. Call SAT. Call the prosecutor from Otaru—Fujiwara. There is a body in the annex. Kurosawa-keibu is here. Room six. Do not hurry. No one is hurrying anywhere."
Kurosawa heard him through the concrete as a thin vibrational stroke. One. Then the long vanishing of sound.
He sat.
Ren sat.
Yoshida lay.
Beyond the corridor wall a drop fell from a downspout onto concrete.
Another.
Then silence again.
At the third minute after Yoshida's death, Ren turned his head. Not quickly. Calmly, with the same slow motion with which he had done everything through these six years.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Yoshida-sensei will not come again."
Kurosawa looked at him. Did not hurry with an answer.
"He will not, Ren."
Ren nodded.
"This is what he wanted."
"I know."
"This is not what you wanted."
Kurosawa thought.
"No, Ren."
"But you did not hinder."
Kurosawa was silent. The silence was the answer.
Ren nodded once more. Accepted. Then said, very quietly:
"Thank you."
Kurosawa turned his head. Looked at him for one long minute. Then said:
"What do you thank me for, Ren."
"For being here when he went."
"That was not for me."
"I know."
Kurosawa nodded. Did not turn his gaze away.
"I will stay with you until evening," he said. "Then doctors will come for you. One from Jindai-en, one from Sapporo. You will be taken to a center. It is not a prison. It is a home. I will come."
Ren thought.
"You said this to me once already."
Kurosawa waited.
"In Otaru," said Ren. "At the kissa-ten. You said: 'See you at New Year's.'"
"Yes."
"We did not see each other."
"No. We did not."
Ren looked at his own knees. Was silent. Then—with the small yielding with which a person allows himself one unnecessary word—said:
"Now we will."
Kurosawa nodded.
"Now we will."
The room held its air apart.
Beyond the corridor wall, in the lower yard—another drop fell from a downspout onto concrete.
Then silence again.
