section.subtitle: Chapter Twenty-Seven
section.p: Ren was transferred to Teine Kōseikai on Tuesday. In a gray Toyota HiAce with tinted glass, with two paramedics and a nurse in a white coat, and a coffee thermos on the front seat. Kurosawa followed in his own car. The drive from Otaru to Sapporo took sixty-eight minutes. The first snow lay along the shoulders in a thin band and disappeared under the wheels of those who had left the city earlier.

At the center, Ren was received by Dr. Sase—short, forty-eight years old, in a restrained blue sweater over a white shirt. He did not ask questions. He held the folder with Endo's transfer letter—Endo had signed it from Tokyo on Thursday—and nodded with a thin nod. Kurosawa remained in the vestibule until evening. He was asked not to worry about Ren. The room chosen was small, with one window facing south. Bed—low. Table by the window.

At five he went up with an orderly to the room. Ren sat on the bed in the gray pajama—the same one in which he had been taken out of Jindai-en—and was reading the same book in the gray paper cover. The orderly left. Kurosawa stood on the threshold.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"The window faces south."
"Yes."
"Yoshida-sensei said that a window facing south is good. In winter there will be sun."
"Yes, Ren."
Ren nodded. Went on reading.
Kurosawa stood one minute more. Then said, quietly:
"I'll come to you tomorrow."
"Good."
He went out. The orderly closed the door after him soundlessly.
He drove home at nine in the evening. Did not go into the kitchen. Lay down on the futon in his work shirt.
Toshi gave his testimony two weeks later.

In Prosecutor Fujiwara's office in Otaru—the same Fujiwara who in twenty-six had signed the warrant on Toshi over an unpaid tag—a long office with two windows and blinds that were always raised two thirds. Toshi sat on a wooden chair in gray civilian, with the cuffs removed for the testimony. Yamaguchi stood behind him, with the key in his right hand.

Toshi spoke briefly. Answered Fujiwara's questions with one or two sentences. About the network—said what he knew. About Jindai-en—said he had never been there. About Ren—said he had not seen him until the day of Yoshida's arrest. About Yoshida—said: "He is my teacher. I did not have a pupil of my own. I will not hand over what I did not have."
Fujiwara entered this in the protocol.
Then Toshi added—not for the protocol but for Fujiwara personally:
"Kurosawa-san in that minute had nothing to do. And he did nothing. It was not a crime. It was witnessing."
Fujiwara said nothing. Wrote the word "witnessing" in a notebook to the side. Not in the protocol.

Five days later the prosecutor's office moved Toshi's case from the accusation of complicity to the accusation of failure to report. In a week Fujiwara petitioned the Otaru court to replace imprisonment with a probationary term. The court accepted. Toshi walked out of Tsukigata on Thursday at four in the afternoon. Kurosawa did not come. Toshi did not look back.

He took the bus north, to Furano. To the cabin he had left in January. Kenji later found him by satellite aerial photography: the chimney was smoking. Toshi did not appear at the Furano-mini for rice and tea for two weeks running. On the third—he came once, bought rice and tea, and did not buy anything else. Kenji closed the query.
Kenji closed out the network in three weeks.

Eight clavicles of the nine columns of Erimo cape were returned to families. The ninth column stood empty—the same empty column, the ninth—with two terns that landed on it once every two days. Kenji left it. Wrote in the report: "Empty. No niche." Tanaka Ryosuke read the report and did not ask.

Two children from Yamagata, who had "disappeared" in eighty-eight and ninety-three from the children's homes of Jindai-en and Sanbi-en, Kenji identified through dental charts via the archive of the Hokkaido district dental association. Both families in Yamagata still existed—elderly parents, another daughter—and Kenji went to them himself, by train, with two small boxes. In each box—one clavicle, wrapped in white silk cloth. Kenji bowed both times. Did not speak for long.

Michiko—the former ward of Jindai-en, the current nurse of the clinic in Niigata, whom Yoshida had taught to call herself Ayano—was arrested two weeks after Yoshida's death. In her apartment on the second floor of an old building in the Higashi-Niigata quarter they found: three ampoules with residues of propofol in the refrigerator, two empty cannula boxes in a drawer under the bed, one small porcelain figurine without a face on the nightstand. Michiko did not resist. Did not speak.
Kurosawa went to her on Monday.

The Niigata detention center stood north of the station, in a gray concrete box of sixty-seven, built between two residential buildings as if inserted there so that no one would see it from a distance. Kurosawa showed the guard his retirement ID—a green card with a red stripe in the lower corner—and the expert-consultant credential Kenji had issued him the previous week. The guard nodded. Did not ask.

In the interview room stood a table of molded plastic, two chairs, and one window covered with frosted glass. The fluorescent lamp under the ceiling had one dead strip out of four. Kurosawa sat. Placed a small canvas bag on the table.
She was brought in ten minutes later.

She was in a hospital shirt—the same one in which she had been arrested at the clinic—ironed, clean, with two plain ties at the back. Hair gray, short. Face thin. Kurosawa had never seen her—only in the photograph from the Jindai-en archive—and now recognized her at once by the eyes. Michiko was in herself. Not tear-stained. Not empty. In herself.
The matron left her by the chair and stepped out into the corridor.
Michiko sat. Placed her hands on her knees. Backs up.
Kurosawa opened the canvas bag. Took two things out of it. Placed them on the table between himself and her.

Two porcelain figurines without faces. Fifteen centimeters tall each. One—from the Jindai-en archive, of the year eighty-eight, from the inventory number Yasuko-san had written down for him on a scrap of paper in December. The other—from the search of her apartment, from the nightstand. Kurosawa placed them beside each other—at a hand's distance from one another—the way one places cups on a table when drinking tea together.
Michiko looked at them.
Not at once. First she looked at the table. Then at her own hands. Then at the two figurines. Did not reach for them. Did not touch.
Kurosawa waited.
"Michiko-san," he said quietly.
She turned her eyes to him.
"You waited for him forty years."
She did not answer. Breathed evenly.
Kurosawa nodded. It was not an answer. It was the acceptance of silence as an answer.
"He is dead."

Michiko lowered her head. Not fast. Slowly—with the slow motion a head makes that leans not because it has lost the strength to hold itself, but because it has decided in itself to acknowledge something.
It was not a nod.
It was a bow.
Kurosawa saw it. Did not show he had seen.
"I know you loved him."
Michiko raised her head. Looked at him for a long time. Kurosawa held the gaze.
"I am no longer Ayano," she said.
The voice was quiet, even—the same voice with which a nurse speaks to a patient who has just woken from anesthesia. Not empty. Not in tears. In herself.
"I know," said Kurosawa.
Pause.

Kurosawa did not hurry. He placed his palms on the table beside the two figurines—did not draw closer, did not touch—and sat. Michiko sat. Two figurines without faces stood between them—a forty-year-old and a twenty-five-year-old—the same hand had made them both, with the same long fingers with the small scar on the right index.
Three minutes.
Kurosawa heard through the walls of the detention center the thin sound of the ventilation—even, like the noise of water in pipes—and did not move.
Michiko did not move.
Then Kurosawa stood.
Did not take the figurines. Left them on the table—both—at the same hand's distance from one another in which he had placed them.
"Michiko-san," he said quietly, from the door.
She did not look at him. She was looking at the two figurines.
Kurosawa went out. The matron stood in the corridor—did not look into the room—and Kurosawa nodded to her. She did not immediately close the door. Then, understanding—she did.
Michiko remained sitting motionless. Kurosawa knew this walking down the corridor. He did not look back.
At the first questioning with the investigator of the prosecutor's office the next day, Michiko answered in one sentence:
"Yoshida-sensei is dead. I am no longer Ayano."
Then she fell silent. Then she said nothing more.

Endo—alive, consulting from Tokyo—reviewed the case and wrote one page in which she described the psychological structure of a sleeper assistant without an ideological shell. Kenji read it. Kurosawa read it. Neither of them asked how Endo held those two words—"psychological structure"—evenly inside her.

Ayano—Ren's daughter, twenty years old, master's in art history in Niigata—was not informed of Michiko's arrest. Kurosawa asked Tanaka to have her name removed from the protocols and replaced with "witness-relative." Tanaka signed without a word. Ayano herself did not ask—she had not known Michiko and was not to know. Kenji arranged with Nao—and Nao arranged with Ayano in a thin conversation over tea on Sunday—that Kurosawa would come to Ayano in Niigata in December. Ayano nodded. Did not ask more.
Kurosawa filed his retirement on Monday.

He placed the resignation on Tanaka Ryosuke's desk at eight thirty in the morning—while Tanaka was still drinking tea from the thermos he had brought from Tokyo—and stood two paces from the desk with his hands at his sides. Tanaka took the resignation. Read it. Did not sign at once. Held the pen in his right hand, cap toward himself, another fifteen seconds. In those fifteen seconds he looked at Kurosawa. Not evaluatingly. Not with reproach. With the calm gaze with which a division chief who had come from Tokyo to this post only two years ago looks at his predecessor—and sees: what had happened at Erimo, and what had happened in Jindai-en, were not two cases into which one could fit an official conclusion; this was one life of one officer.
Tanaka placed the pen on the resignation. Wrote his own name. Then signed. Said nothing. Returned a copy to Kurosawa.
Kurosawa bowed. Not deeply.
"Kurosawa-keibu," Tanaka said only one thing.
"Yes."
"Go home."
Kurosawa bowed once more. Left.

In Tanaka's reception, his secretary—a young woman from Tokyo, thirty-two years old—did not lift her eyes from her monitor. That was correct. Kurosawa walked to the stairs. On the third-floor landing he passed Aoyama—the same Aoyama from the homicide unit who had been with him in Shiretoko in twenty-seven—and Aoyama nodded. Kurosawa nodded back. They did not stop.
He packed a box in his office on Tuesday evening.

One box of brown cardboard, the size of two volumes of a school dictionary. Into it he put: the folder on the Kurosawa Ren case, closed, with a red "archive" sticker; the photograph on the desk—a small one in a plain wooden frame, showing the family house in Otaru, taken in seventy-five in March; the porcelain cup with a thin crack in the bottom, from which he had drunk coffee for fourteen years; the yellow paper with the duty roster that had lain in the pocket of his coat since July of twenty-eight together with the sheet "Kurosawa" from the Erimo cape; the small key to the side drawer, which was now needed by no one.

He held one more thing in his palm before laying it in. One postal envelope, cream, thin, without an address—the one that had come to him in the autumn of twenty-seven with a photograph of the Erimo lighthouse and the line "seven days. Alone. Or with one. Not more." The envelope had been kept in the lower left drawer along with a pair of old pens and one eraser. Kurosawa looked at it for one long second. Then placed it in the box.

One more thing. From the upper right drawer, from under the stapler—a small ring of cheap silver, with a thin engraving, in the shape of a simple band without a stone. Ren's ring. Toshi had passed it to Kurosawa the week before—had come from Furano by bus alone—had kept it for himself for three years in a scrap of white cloth, in a tin box on the upper shelf above the bed, and had said: "Kurosawa-san, this is Ren's. Yoshida-sensei left it with me for safekeeping in twenty-five, when he was teaching. He did not explain. I preserved it." Kurosawa nodded, took the ring. Did not ask how. Now he placed it in the box with the rest.

One more thing. The small bundle of soft paper that Sasaki had set on the dashboard of the car thirty minutes before the Erimo lighthouse. Kurosawa had taken it from the car that day—himself, without a sound—when he handed the keys back to the patrolmen. He had kept it with him for three months. Had not unwrapped it. Now he unwrapped it above the desk. A small porcelain figure without a face, in a blue kimono—an ichimatsu-ningyō—the one Ayano-the-nurse had sent to Nao in Niigata in October. Sasaki had taken it, brought it to Sapporo, kept it with her to the lighthouse. Had wanted to show him. Had not had the time. Kurosawa wrapped it back in the same paper. Placed it in the box.

One more thing. Ren's drawing—the one Ren had given him at Teine Kōseikai the last weekend, folded in four. Kurosawa did not unfold it. Did not want to look at it in the office. He placed it in the box last, on top.
That was all.
He closed the box. Wound tape around it once—evenly—and set it under his left arm.

The office held its light without him. The fluorescent lamp under the ceiling hummed thinly—at the same note it had hummed for all fourteen years—and Kurosawa heard it separately, as something that would hold on here after he was gone.
He switched off the desk lamp. Did not look back.
He walked out of the department at eighteen forty-five.
Kenji's car was in the parking lot. Kenji sat behind the wheel with the window rolled down. Phone in his hand. Kurosawa came up, placed the box on the roof of the car. Kenji lowered the phone.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Kenji-san."
Kenji was silent half a second.
"I'm going to Nao's in Niigata on Friday. I want to show her Yuri-san's photo album. The one she made in her master's."
Kurosawa turned his head. Looked at him calmly.
"Good."
"You don't mind?"
"No."
Kenji nodded. Did not hold the gaze long.
"Kurosawa-san."
"Yes."
"I will come to you."
"I know."
"Once every two weeks. Monday evening. Tea."
"Good."
Pause.
"Kenji-san," Kurosawa said quietly. "One thing."
"Yes."
"Nao-san. Do not hurry. She is young. She is at work. Do not hurry."
Kenji looked at him calmly.
"I am not hurrying, Kurosawa-san."
"Good."
Kenji nodded. Kurosawa took the box off the roof of the car, tucked it under his right arm. Said no more. Walked across the lot to his car. Held the box level.
Kenji watched his back until Kurosawa sat behind the wheel and started the engine. Then he raised his window. Drove off.

Kurosawa sat in the lot another minute. The box lay on the passenger seat, under his right hand. He looked through the windshield at the department building. At the fluorescent lamp in his former office on the fifth floor—that rectangle of yellow light someone had left on after his exit—and did not go back to switch it off.
Then he started the engine and drove home.

section.subtitle: Epilogue
section.p: Kurosawa went to Niigata on Thursday in mid-December.

The journey took him two days—from Sapporo by ferry to Hakodate on Wednesday evening, then the night train to Omiya, then a change to the direct line to Niigata with a lunch stop at Takasaki. He traveled slowly now. He had time. Ayano was waiting for him at four in the afternoon at a café on the second floor of Niigata station—small, with nine tables—with large windows onto the suburban line.
He arrived ten minutes early. Ordered coffee, black. Placed a small gray briefcase on the table—the one he now carried only for what he did not want to hold in his hands.
Ayano appeared at four zero-two.

She was tall—like her father—with thin features, in a dark green coat with a high collar. Hair gathered in a plain bun. In her hands—one book in a white cover and a small satchel from the university library. Twenty years old—Kurosawa knew—but in that second she looked two or three years older. Not because she looked worn. Because she held her back straight, the way people hold it who have spent two years in a master's program and learned to sit six hours over a single cup of tea.
She saw him. Came over. Did not bow. Placed the satchel on the neighboring chair and sat opposite.
"Uncle."
"Ayano-san."
"Thank you for coming."
"Nothing to thank."
She glanced at his right hand—at the briefcase. Did not ask. Ordered tea. The waiter brought it a minute later. Ayano held the cup in both palms—did not drink—and looked at him.
"Uncle," she said. "Why so long?"

Kurosawa looked out the window. Beyond the glass a suburban-line train was pulling in—gray, with a green stripe along the flank—and stopping at platform five. He waited until the train had stopped. Then turned his eyes back to her.
"I didn't know," he said.
Ayano nodded. Not in forgiveness. As a sign of hearing.
"Did he recognize me?"

Kurosawa did not answer at once. He knew—with that thin corner that knew the answer before he was asked—that the truth would not be the one she hoped for, and not the one she needed. He held the pause long enough for the words to find their place.
"He remembers you at fourteen," he said. "The way he saw you last, on the morning of the year twenty-two."
Ayano lowered her eyes to the cup. A thin steam rose and disappeared.
"I don't remember him grown," she said.
"Yes."
Pause.

Kurosawa opened the briefcase. Took out one thing. A thin white paper, folded in four. Did not put it on the table at once—held it one more second in his hand—then unfolded it and placed it before her.
Ren's drawing. The one Ren had given him last Tuesday. A small room. One lamp. A low bed. A shelf with a porcelain figurine on the wall.
Ayano looked.
Looked for a long time. Did not touch the paper. One palm on the cup. The other on her knee. Her face did not change.
Then, quietly, she said:
"He draws the room."
Kurosawa nodded.
"Every day."
Pause.
"He wanted you to see this."
Ayano turned her eyes to him. Looked at him for a long time. Kurosawa held the gaze.
"Is he waiting for me?"
Kurosawa thought. Not to find a word—but to let the truth settle.
"He is always waiting there."
Ayano nodded.
Then—with the short motion of one who has made a decision without hesitation—said:
"I will come. At the new year."
"He will be glad."
Pause.

Ayano folded the drawing in four, carefully, with the motions with which her father and her uncle had folded small papers from their journals when they were to be kept. Put it in the inner pocket of her coat. Did not look at Kurosawa's briefcase. She knew there was something else there. Did not ask.
"Uncle."
"Yes."
"Thank you again."
"Nothing to thank, Ayano-san."
Kurosawa rose first. Ayano too. Her train left at six. His—the night sailing back to Hakodate. He bowed. Ayano bowed. Not deeply.
They walked out of the café separately.
Beyond the station snow was falling in the same thin vertical grain Kurosawa had left in Sapporo in the morning and met here again in the evening.
Winter in Sapporo held its form. Snow was falling thinly, without wind—in that straight vertical grain that begins early in January and lasts until midday without a break.

At Teine Kōseikai it was two degrees warmer than outside, and in the vestibule it smelled of a citrus floor cleaner—the same one used at medical institutions in Hokkaido since the nineties. Kurosawa took off his coat in the cloakroom, hung it on a wooden hanger with two metal clips. Left his shoes on the lower shelf, put on gray guest slippers of soft felt. Nodded to the volunteer girl at the desk. She nodded back.
He went up in the elevator to the third floor.

Ren's room was at the end of the corridor. A door of thin light wood, with a small brass plate: "Kurosawa Ren." The brass was new—installed six weeks ago, when Ren had moved from the temporary room on the second floor here. Kurosawa looked at it with a quiet attachment—the attachment a person keeps for things that ought not to be theirs, but are.
He knocked. Twice. Lightly.
"Yes," said Ren from inside.
Kurosawa opened.

He stood on the threshold one long second. Not because he could not enter. Because to make the step from the corridor into the room of a brother who for six years had lived behind different walls is a motion the body makes more slowly than the head. He allowed the body to find its rhythm.
Then he entered.

The room was small. One window facing south, at the lower part of which stood the lower edge of the white sill, and beyond it—snow—snow steady, distinct, with the vertical black lines of the cedars that stood in the yard of the center, the way they stand in place where they were set. Bed by the far wall, made up with a plain cotton blanket in beige stripes. Table by the window. On the table—a stack of white A4 paper, about ten sheets, and a metal box of pencils. In the box—two "HB," one "2B," one sanguine, one graphite stick without a jacket. That was all.

Ren sat at the table. In a gray sweater, in gray cotton trousers. His hair had grown a little longer than it had been in October—Dr. Sase had not insisted on a haircut—and one lock of gray above the right ear lay on his shoulder. He held a pencil in his right hand. His left hand on the sheet, pressing the corner of the paper down.
Drawing.

Kurosawa came in quietly. Closed the door behind him. Sat on the chair on the far side of the table, at the distance at which one usually sits down beside a brother with whom one holds a long silence. Did not look into the sheet.
"Yukio," said Ren, without lifting his head.
"Yes."
"The snow today is quiet."
"Quiet."
"I looked out the window this morning for twenty minutes. Then sat down to draw."
"What today."
Ren thought.
"The room."
"Again."
"Again."
Kurosawa nodded. Did not look at the sheet. He looked past Ren's shoulder—at the snow outside the window.

Ren continued drawing. The pencil moved across the sheet thinly, with the slow precise rhythm that comes when the hand knows its motion and does not ask the head. Kurosawa heard the thin dry rustle of graphite against paper—and one line, and a second, and a pause, and a third.
So they sat for about fifteen minutes.

Outside the window snow was falling evenly. In the corridor beyond the door quietly—once every seven minutes—a nurse walked past with a tray, and the steps of her rubber slippers could be heard through the thin wood. Then silence again.

Kurosawa thought about the family home in Otaru. About the room on the second floor in which he and Ren had lived together until Yukio at seventeen had gone to Sapporo for university. In that room there had been two beds—one by the east wall, one by the west—and between them a low table with two drawers. Ren used to read on his bed until eleven at night. Yukio would fall asleep earlier. Sometimes Yukio woke at two in the morning and saw that Ren's lamp was still on. He did not wake him. Only turned onto his side and fell asleep again.
That was a long time ago.
Kurosawa thought this, and did not say it aloud.
Ren went on drawing.
At half past one, a nurse knocked at the door—young, in a white coat, with the name "Haraguchi" on her badge—and opened it half a palm.
"Kurosawa-san. Kurosawa Ren-san. Tea time."
Kurosawa turned his head.
"Thank you, Haraguchi-san. Five more minutes."
"All right. I'll set the cups in the sitting room."
She closed the door. The steps in the corridor faded.
Ren raised his head. Looked at Yukio as if past him—with that particular slow focus he had always had after Jindai-en, and which Dr. Sase called "correct." Not illness. Not recovery. A way of being.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Will you come tomorrow?"
Kurosawa thought. Not longer than needed to find an honest word.
"I will, Ren."
"I will wait for you."
"I know."
Ren nodded. Lowered his head. Continued drawing.

Kurosawa sat on the chair calmly. Did not move. Let the pause be what it was. He knew that everything between them held now on one fact: he had come today, he would come tomorrow—and that this fact for Ren mattered more than all the words Kurosawa could or could not say. In the same way the snow outside the window held on one fact: it was falling.
Five minutes later Ren set down the pencil.
Looked at the sheet. Nodded to himself. Then folded it in four—carefully, slowly—and pushed it half a palm toward Yukio. Did not hand it over. Simply pushed it.
"Yukio."
"Yes."
"Take it home."

Kurosawa took it. The folded sheet lay in the palm without weight. He did not unfold it. Held it a second, then put it in the chest pocket of his sweater—the way one puts a sheet one is to keep whole until evening.
He did not look at the drawing. He kept his eyes on Ren.
"Thank you, Ren."
"Yes."

In the sitting room of the center Haraguchi-san poured Ren green tea in a white cup with a thin crack in the bottom. For herself, too. For Kurosawa she brought coffee in a porcelain mug with the center's logo—a plain black circle with the inscription "手稲厚生会" on the side. Kurosawa thanked her. Sat beside Ren on the low sofa. Did not speak.
Ren drank his tea slowly, in small sips. Held the cup with both hands. Looked out the window. Haraguchi-san tidied unobtrusively. Did not intrude.

At three Kurosawa rose. Bowed to Haraguchi-san. Offered Ren his palm, back down—not for a shake, but for that short touch Ren allowed himself once per visit. Ren, with his right palm, touched Yukio's palm for a second. Then took his hand back.
"Until tomorrow, Yukio."
"Until tomorrow, Ren."
Kurosawa walked out of the room. Haraguchi-san accompanied him to the elevator. In the elevator she said:
"Kurosawa-san, Ren-san drew longer today than usual."
"How long."
"Three hours. Morning and after the midday meal. We put the drawings in the lower drawer of the desk. He wants that."
"Thank you, Haraguchi-san."
The elevator stopped on the ground floor. Kurosawa got out. In the cloakroom he put on his coat and shoes. In the vestibule the volunteer girl nodded to him. He nodded back.
Beyond the glass doors of the vestibule snow was falling in the same vertical grain the morning had begun with.
He walked out into the snow.

On the way to the car he stopped for a second. Not because he had felt something—he did not feel anything then—but because on the side path stood the winter rowan with small red berries, dusted with the thin white grain—and he liked how that color held in the gray day. He stood three seconds. Then walked on.
In the car he started the engine. The heater came in with a thin note in half a minute. He pulled out of the center's yard. On the way back to Misei the radio was off. He did not turn it on.
Kurosawa came home at six in the evening.

The city held the snow. He parked in the lower yard of the building—the same building in Misei where he had lived for twelve years—and rode up in the elevator to the fourth floor. The corridor smelled of drying linen from apartment number forty-eight—old Mr. Onda dried his laundry on the balcony and left the window open. Kurosawa forgave him that smell.
He opened the door of his apartment. Took off his shoes at the genkan. Hung his coat on the wooden hook. Walked into the kitchen.
One lamp above the kitchen table. He switched it on—yellow soft light, with a thin note from the old filament—and did not switch the rest on.
On the chair beside the table stood the box from the department. From Monday. Not yet unpacked.
He set it on the table.
Sat in his usual place—back to the window, facing the stove. Set the mobile phone to silent, placed it to his right beside him. Then opened the box.
He took things out one at a time.
First—the Kurosawa Ren folder. Placed it on the table to the left. Did not open.

Second—the photograph of the family home in Otaru. Placed it to the right. Looked at it one second. Wooden facade, low, with a roof pitched to the right. He had grown up in it from four to eighteen. Ren—from eight to twenty-two. His mother was no longer in the photograph.
Third—the porcelain cup with the crack. Set it in the center. Did not brew coffee in it.
Then—the yellow paper with the duty roster. Placed it below. Did not read.

Then—the sheet "Kurosawa" from the Erimo cape. Unfolded it—for the first time in a year and a half—read it. It was blank. Only one word, in black pen: Kurosawa. Not "inspector." Not with a first name. Only the surname. Yoshida had written it with his right hand, with that small slant of the letters Yoshida had held since middle school. Kurosawa looked and folded the sheet back.
Then—Ren's ring. Small, silver, in the scrap of white cloth from Toshi. He unwrapped the cloth. Placed the ring beside the cup. Folded the scrap of cloth neatly, placed it under the ring.

Then—the photograph of Misako. The one Yasuko-san had given him at Jindai-en in December when he had come last to collect the last of Ren's things. A small black-and-white card, with thin serrated edges, from nineteen seventy. An eight-year-old girl in a sundress with little flowers, with two braids—standing on pier number two—laughing into the camera. Behind her shoulder—the sea of Otaru in a summer misty haze. Kurosawa placed the photograph to the left of the cup.

He looked at it for one minute. At the thin line of the horizon above the girl's shoulder. At the calm sea. At the pier Misako would fall from a month and a half later and not surface. At the twin brother—Yoshida at eight—standing off-camera, holding the camera. That was his hand that pressed the shutter. Those were his eyes that saw Misako in that moment.
Kurosawa looked away.

Then—the photograph of Sasaki Yuri. Nao had sent it in November. From an envelope with three prints, she had written: "Yukio-san, of these three Yuri told me she loved this one most. One I keep for myself. One for you. One for Kenji-san." Kurosawa had chosen the middle one—Yuri in uniform, next to the department car, her face turned three-quarters to the camera, with that short smile with which she had held every working day. He set the photograph to the right of the cup.

Ren's drawing lay separately. In the chest pocket of the sweater, folded in four—the one Ren had given him after the midday meal today. Kurosawa had not yet unfolded it. He kept it closer to the heart, not on the table. Not yet.
Four objects on the table. Only what could be carried by one hand. Only what held in the light of a single lamp.

He stood. Went to the stove. Poured water from the ceramic pitcher into a Turkish coffee pot—twenty-two grams of coffee, three hundred thirty grams of water—and set it on a low flame. Stood by the stove. Looked at the water.
The mobile phone vibrated once.
He looked at the phone. The screen showed a number he knew.
He took the receiver to his ear at the kitchen threshold. Knew it was Nao. Nao called on Monday and on Thursday evening—once a week to him, once a week to Kenji—and today was Thursday.
"Yukio-san."
"Nao-san."
"Kenji-san was with me on Sunday. Showed me the photo album. The one Yuri made in her master's."
"I know."
"Thank you."
"Nothing to thank."
Pause.
"Yukio-san."
"Yes, Nao-san."

Nao thought. Kurosawa heard her breathing on the other end. She breathed quietly, with that small note Sasaki Yuri had had too—when she was preparing to say something she had held in herself for three weeks.

"Yuri had one book at my house. Old. About rabbits. A children's one. She brought it in twenty-twenty-one—she was staying with me temporarily then, before her new apartment—and she forgot it when she left. Forgot—that's not true—I think she left it for me. Did not say so directly."
"Yes."
"I keep it on the lower shelf by the window. I look at it once a week."
"Yes."
"Would you like me to send it to you?"
Kurosawa was silent for a long time.

He stood at the kitchen threshold, with the phone in his right hand, with his palm on the wooden frame of the jamb. The water on the stove was beginning to sound. Thinly, not yet boiling—with the note that comes half a minute before boiling.
He allowed the pause to be what it was.
"Yes, Nao-san. Send it."
Pause.
"Thank you," said Nao.
"Nothing to thank."
"Good night, Yukio-san."
"Good night, Nao-san."
He placed the phone on the kitchen table—beside the cup—and turned back to the stove.

The water came to a boil half a second later than he expected. He took off the pot. Poured coffee into the porcelain cup with the crack. Steam rose in that vertical thread easy to break if one places the cup poorly. He set the cup level.
Sat on the chair with his back to the window. Held the cup with both hands. Warmth passed through the porcelain into his palms—that thing that always comes later than a person expects it—and stayed.
He took a sip.
The coffee was plain. Hot. The way he liked it.
On the table before him—four objects. The sheet "Kurosawa." The photograph of Misako. The photograph of Sasaki Yuri. Ren's ring.
He looked at them for a long time.
Then drew from the chest pocket of the sweater the folded sheet. The one Ren had given him today. Held it in his palm one more second.
Placed it on the table beside Yuri's photograph. Smoothed it with his fingers. Carefully.

The drawing was plain. A small room. One lamp. A low bed. Walls without ornaments. Washbasin in the corner. One shelf with a porcelain figurine on the wall. All—in pencil of medium hardness, with thin distinct lines and one soft shading fill in the lower left corner, where in the real room it had been darker.
Kurosawa looked for a long time.
He placed his right hand on the table beside the drawing. Did not touch the paper. The palm settled on the board two centimeters from the lower edge of the sheet. Held it there.
The bed in his brother's drawing was not where it had been.
Yehor Selin is the author of «The Doll Maker Files».
